item.title: [SCMP] Huang Qifan, China’s political tumbler, falls after a decade of close corruption calls
item.description:
For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign.

Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over.

The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption.
item.content:encoded:
For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign.

Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over.

The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption.

Bo and Sun were both members of the Politburo, the pinnacle of the party’s power, and their downfalls were two of the biggest political earthquakes the country has seen in recent decades. Yet Huang survived.

Huang, 74, was also very visible after he left public service in 2018. Rather than retreat to retired obscurity, Huang kept up a busy schedule of interviews and conferences across the country, firing hot takes on China’s economic issues.

So when news of the corruption investigation into Huang finally came on Tuesday, it was a surprise to many – not only because it involved one of China’s most celebrated economic technocrats, but also because it came so long after the political tremors around him appeared to have stopped.

“Subjecting someone like Huang, who had emerged from many previous rounds, to a formal corruption investigation, before the fifth plenum sends a very serious message to the whole party: corrupt officials should not harbour any illusions of escaping detection,” said a Beijing-based political scientist, who declined to be named due to sensitivity of the matter.

“There is no political ‘tumbler’ and no safe landing for corrupt officials in the anti-corruption fight.”

The fifth plenum is a party meeting scheduled for October 26-29 in Beijing at which the organisation’s inner circle will discuss and adopt a landmark document to “deepening party self-governance”.

The event is expected to focus on tackling systemic corruption, tightening internal political oversight, and eliminating organisational loopholes across the bureaucracy and state sectors.

While many anti-corruption investigations into retired senior officials go unnoticed and unannounced, Huang’s unusually heavy speaking schedule made his downfall difficult to hide from the public.

The South China Morning Post understands that Huang was originally scheduled to deliver a keynote speech in Beijing on October 25 and another in Hangzhou the next day.

Before Tuesday’s announcement, word got out that he would miss the Hangzhou event. An employee at AIA Group – the organiser of the October 25 speech in Beijing – said they had not been able to reach Huang or his secretary since Monday.

Huang’s reputation as a tumbler goes back to his relationship with Bo, the charismatic and swashbuckling Politburo member who ran Chongqing from 2007 to 2012.

As Bo rolled out his ideologically charged “singing red songs and smashing the dark forces” campaign, Huang was the administrative and economic brain behind the policies that became known as the “Chongqing model”.

The model combines state-led capitalism, aggressive public-welfare provision, and foreign direct investment with a populist revival of revolutionary Maoist culture and a heavy-handed public security crackdown.

Positioned as an alternative developmental path to China’s coastal, market-driven consensus, the model gained national and international attention as a potential blueprint for addressing rising wealth inequality, regional imbalances and social stratification.

The two men projected an image of an unshakeable governing duo. During the national parliamentary “two sessions” in Beijing in March 2010, Huang famously described his working relationship with Bo as “like a duck to water”. He was also a magnet for reporters at the annual meetings, readily answering questions about the economy and Chongqing.

That alliance faced a critical test in February 2012, when Bo’s estranged police chief, Wang Lijun, fled to the US consulate in Chengdu, triggering one of China’s biggest political scandals in decades.

Following the diplomatic stand-off, Bo was removed from the party’s leadership. He was later sentenced to life in prison on charges of bribery, embezzlement and abuse of power.

The aftershocks hit many of Bo’s subordinates in Chongqing, as the municipality’s new leadership headed by caretaker party chief Zhang Dejiang, repeatedly pledged to “eradicate” Bo’s “toxic influence”. Despite the chaos, Huang remained in position.

In November 2012, Sun took over from Zhang, becoming Huang’s new partner and direct supervisor.

Like Bo before his fall, Sun was also seen as a political rising star. He relied on Huang to maintain the city’s administrative machinery and drive double-digit economic growth. Huang, it seemed, had weathered the Bo saga unaffected, and was among six regional officials to be part of President Xi Jinping’s delegation to the United States in 2015.

The political ground shook beneath Chongqing again in 2017, just months after Huang stepped down as the city’s mayor. Sun was rounded up in anti-corruption investigation during a trip to Beijing for a top-level meeting, and ultimately sentenced to life imprisonment on corruption charges.

The southwestern metropolis again pledged to clean up the negative influence of a disgraced party boss and again Huang appeared to sail through the controversy. Huang stayed on in his semi-retired role in the national legislature as vice-chairman of the National People’s Congress Financial and Economic Affairs Committee, finally stepping down in March 2018.

Even after his retirement, Huang, respected as a capable economic manager, remained an influential intellectual heavyweight. Affiliated with prestigious platforms including the China Centre for International Economic Exchanges, the China Finance 40 Forum and Fudan University, he had a towering media profile, offering perspectives on a wide range of economic issues.

In 2021, he warned that the business models of Chinese internet firms would no longer work in the coming decade, slamming them as “taking advantage of weaknesses in human nature to entice purchases”.

In 2022, Huang warned that China’s property market had reached a turning point, questioning whether the country could sustain its decades-long construction boom.

As recently as May this year, he described China’s record US$1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025 as “shocking”, urging Beijing to rebalance trade through a combination of gradual yuan appreciation, tariff cuts and improved benefits for workers.

He is known among various lecture organisers as exceptionally proactive and eager to take the podium, and is said to have told organisers that he is willing to talk on any issue.

He is also believed to be in good health for his age, with a fondness for steak and cigars.

His confidence was built on decades of economic policy experience.

Born in Zhuji in Zhejiang province in 1952, Huang rose through Shanghai’s industrial bureaucracy.

Entering the municipal party and government apparatus in 1983, he was deeply involved in the early development and opening of the Pudong New Area.

In October 2001, he was transferred to Chongqing as a vice-mayor, overseeing the city’s industrial policy, state-owned assets, taxation and financial sectors before becoming mayor in January 2010 – a post he held for nearly seven years.

Under his stewardship, Chongqing logged consecutive years of double-digit GDP growth, routinely outpacing the rest of the country.

Huang promoted the Chongqing-Xinjiang-Europe freight railway, and attracted Hewlett-Packard and Foxconn to build an electronics manufacturing hub in the city.

He also pioneered the municipal investment vehicle modelled on Singapore’s state fund Temasek and kept runaway property speculation in check through strict land-supply management and an expansive public rental housing programme.

Huang’s downfall follows a smaller earthquake in Chongqing. Since 2022, the anti-corruption drive has sped up, targeting more and more senior officials across the country.

Chongqing was hit hard, with seven other high-ranking provincial officials coming under investigation since then. The most senior of the seven was then-mayor Hu Henghua, who came under the microscope in March, triggering another shake-up across the administration.

The investigation into Huang comes less than two weeks before the party’s fifth plenum, which brings together the hundreds of full and alternate members of the Central Committee.

The Central Committee’s ranks have been thinned by the anti-corruption campaign, with 34 of its 205 full members under investigation or stripped of their status as deputies to the National People’s Congress.

The Beijing-based political scientist said Chongqing had been the epicentre of China’s most disruptive political tremors over the past two decades and the investigation of Huang nearly a decade after retirement showed Beijing’s resolve to clean up Chongqing’s factional legacy, allowing no perceived seniority to impede its continued organisational housecleaning.

Not all are that surprised by Huang’s fall.

His family’s commercial dealings cast a persistent shadow over his administration. In Chongqing, the extensive business footprint of his son was “an open secret” among political and business circles, according to sources familiar with the situation.

“Many in Chongqing’s government and financial circles know his son very well, as Huang Qifan is widely regarded as the ‘godfather’ of Chongqing’s state-driven financial vehicles, which can mobilise a lot of resources,” said a source who worked with Huang.

The source said the younger Huang quickly immersed himself in China’s capital market deals.

item.title: [SCMP] Cloudy outlook? How haze crisis is testing Singapore’s events economy
item.description:
When Daniela Cruz arrived in Singapore last week, hazy skies obscured the picture-perfect sights she had seen on social media, offering a different view of the city state from the one she had expected.

The 27-year-old bank associate had travelled from Australia for the Formula One Singapore Grand Prix, but the smoky weather dampened her experience. “The buildings we saw on social media were covered in haze, and it made conditions extremely hot and humid,” she said.

The haze blanketing Singapore’s skies over the three-day event raised fears of disruption. On Thursday, a day before racing began, motorsport governing body FIA said the conditions could potentially restrict entertainment acts and outdoor activities.
item.content:encoded:
When Daniela Cruz arrived in Singapore last week, hazy skies obscured the picture-perfect sights she had seen on social media, offering a different view of the city state from the one she had expected.

The 27-year-old bank associate had travelled from Australia for the Formula One Singapore Grand Prix, but the smoky weather dampened her experience. “The buildings we saw on social media were covered in haze, and it made conditions extremely hot and humid,” she said.

The haze blanketing Singapore’s skies over the three-day event raised fears of disruption. On Thursday, a day before racing began, motorsport governing body FIA said the conditions could potentially restrict entertainment acts and outdoor activities.

This was not the first time the marquee event had faced uncertainty due to haze. In 2015 and 2019, organisers introduced precautionary measures, including health advisories and the sale of N95 masks, while both editions of the night race proceeded without major disruption, as did last weekend’s event.

The poor weather did little to diminish the novelty of the night race, which drew a crowd of more than 300,000 this year.

But while Singapore managed to keep one of its flagship events running, the recurrence of haze could weaken the city state’s appeal as an international events hub, observers said. Smaller events have also faced cancellations as air quality deteriorated, with conditions showing little sign of improving.

The stakes are significant for a city that has invested heavily in attracting international visitors and major events.

From its debut in 2008 until 2024, the Singapore Grand Prix generated more than S$2.2 billion (US$1.72 billion) in incremental tourism receipts, with the figure for 2025 still being calculated, Trade and Industry Minister Gan Kim Yong said in February.

Singapore’s meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) sector is another important contributor to its visitor economy, with tourism receipts from the segment reaching S$2.3 billion last year, a 35 per cent increase from S$1.7 billion in 2024.

Dedicated sports fans were unlikely to be deterred from future editions of the Singapore Grand Prix, one of the most distinctive events on the F1 calendar, said Guy Llewellyn, an assistant professor at EHL Hospitality Business School.

“A single hazy weekend is unlikely to outweigh its unique atmosphere, entertainment line-up, and broader appeal as a destination,” he added.

But first-time and leisure travellers who viewed the event as part of a wider holiday experience could be discouraged from revisiting the night race and Singapore, Llewellyn said.

For Cruz, the smooth traffic flow and multitude of activities during the grand prix set a high bar for future races. But she gave the concerts, which featured American singer Lana Del Rey and Swedish pop star Zara Larsson, a miss to avoid having to walk long distances in the heat and haze.

“Regarding the haze, we can tolerate a level similar to the weekend’s, but a worse level would lead to us reconsidering visiting again.”

Foggy road ahead

In recent weeks, air quality in Singapore has deteriorated amid an increase in hotspots in neighbouring Indonesia and unfavourable weather, raising concerns over outdoor activities across the city state.

While the F1 race avoided disruption, some domestic events have been cancelled or suspended. The fate of coming activities remains uncertain as the government prepares contingency measures for worsening pollution.

Air quality in recent weeks has stayed primarily in the “unhealthy” range, with the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) reading staying between 101 and 200. The city state recorded its highest reading this year of 192 on the opening day of the grand prix on Friday.

Singapore recorded its highest PM2.5 reading this year – which reflects the average concentration of fine particles in the air – on Wednesday, peaking at 288 in the western region.

As at 5pm on Wednesday, the PSI reading remained in the “unhealthy” range, rising to 175 in the west.

Some Singaporeans have chosen to stay indoors, with others donning masks outdoors.

Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu on Saturday said the government had contingency plans in place across different air quality levels, and would distribute masks to eligible Singaporeans, such as the elderly or those in lower-income brackets, when the PSI exceeded 200 – deemed to be in the “very unhealthy” range.

Several public sports centres shut their doors on Wednesday, and the city state’s health promotion agency, which organises workout sessions and nature walks, has cancelled all outdoor activities since Saturday.

A number of running events have been suspended in recent weeks, including a ticketed 5km run at Sentosa on Sunday.

In 2015, thick haze led to the cancellation of the first night of finals at the FINA World Cup. PSI levels entered the “hazardous” range of above 300 that year.

Organisers with events slated for October told This Week in Asia they were prepared to suspend activities if the situation worsened and would heed advisories and regulations set out by authorities.

The National Environment Agency advises the public to avoid prolonged strenuous outdoor physical activities if air quality is in the “very unhealthy” range, while those with lung conditions are asked to refrain from being outdoors altogether.

Singapore’s sports agency advises organisers to consider suspending or modifying outdoor activities, and review the risks of conducting events in air-conditioned settings, when air quality levels enter the “very unhealthy” range.

Decisions on cancelling or modifying the Garmin Run Marathon Series on October 25, which 6,000 had signed up for, would be made a day before the race, a spokesperson said.

Garmin Run Club has cancelled multiple practices due to the haze in recent weeks and advised runners to adjust their training plans depending on the day’s haze levels.

Local club JRT Volleyball Academy cancelled training sessions on Saturday after forecasts showed air quality could deteriorate into the “very unhealthy” range.

Coaches were tasked with monitoring air quality and readings before and during sessions, said director Jerry Teo.

Observers urged event organisers to prioritise safety over commercial viability.

According to Llewellyn, destinations that adapt and manage health risks effectively are better placed to protect their reputation in the long run.

“Contingency planning can no longer be treated as an occasional disruption. It needs to become part of standard event management,” he said.

Zilmiyah Kamble, senior lecturer in hospitality and tourism management at James Cook University Singapore, said while the haze created “considerable uncertainty” for outdoor events, the city state was likely to remain an “attractive choice” as organisers were also assessing “the destination’s broader capacity to manage health, safety and operational disruption”.

item.title: [SCMP] Will South China Sea’s code of conduct remain elusive as deadline looms?
item.description:
A long-awaited code of conduct (COC) for the South China Sea risks becoming a toothless agreement, analysts have warned, as Beijing and Southeast Asian nations scramble to hammer out a deal by the end of 2026.

More than three decades since it was mooted, the proposed pact has remained gridlocked over how to balance competing territorial claims among China and four rival claimant states – Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines.

Maritime experts speaking at a conference in Kuala Lumpur this week agreed that the code was not meant to settle sovereignty disputes and were divided on whether it could keep the peace.
item.content:encoded:
A long-awaited code of conduct (COC) for the South China Sea risks becoming a toothless agreement, analysts have warned, as Beijing and Southeast Asian nations scramble to hammer out a deal by the end of 2026.

More than three decades since it was mooted, the proposed pact has remained gridlocked over how to balance competing territorial claims among China and four rival claimant states – Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines.

Maritime experts speaking at a conference in Kuala Lumpur this week agreed that the code was not meant to settle sovereignty disputes and were divided on whether it could keep the peace.

“If anything involves clarifying maritime rights, not only China but also the Philippines and Vietnam will not accept a binding COC,” Ding Duo, a researcher at China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the Maritime Institute of Malaysia’s 9th South China Sea Conference on Tuesday.

Ding said the biggest obstacle was the COC’s scope, arguing that it should focus on maritime states managing their activities and preventing confrontations rather than settling territorial differences.

Claimant states held differing positions on which activities should be permitted or restricted under the agreement, including operations involving external powers, he added.

“Such differences should be settled within the COC platform,” he said, adding that disputes should not be resolved elsewhere.

Asean has repeatedly called for restraint and clear rules under the COC, which was first proposed in 1992, to manage disputes in the contested waterway.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations and China exchanged draft proposals in 2000 but failed to reach an agreement on such a code. Instead, they signed a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties (DOC) in 2002.

Consultations on the code resumed in 2013, and negotiators began working on its draft text in 2018.

The code was intended to set operational rules for parties in the disputed waterway to ensure that incidents at sea would not escalate into conflict, said Sumathy Perumal, acting director of research and senior fellow at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia.

“I don’t think [the] COC will impact maritime rights or maritime claims,” Sumathy said.

However, continued confrontations in the South China Sea had complicated negotiations and made it harder for parties to reach consensus on the code, she noted.

“The incidents on the ground [are] probably delaying [negotiations], and a lot more details [need] to be agreed upon by those intending to sign the COC,” she said, explaining that a mutually accepted framework was important to help China and Asean preserve peace in the waterway.

Questions persisted over whether the claimant states would accept legally binding rules that could restrict their activities in the waters.

“The fact a COC has not been realised until today is reflective of the fact that nobody seems to really want it. If they had wanted it, they would have really made it happen,” said Nazery Khalid, a maritime security expert and senior fellow at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia.

He said claimant states were reluctant to surrender their freedom to pursue competing maritime claims because binding rules could restrict activities currently permitted under the 2002 declaration.

“With a legally binding Code of Conduct, there are certain things that you cannot do any more, which you can do under the DOC,” Nazery said.

Reality at sea

On the water, maritime tensions – between several Asean claimant states and China, and among the Southeast Asian neighbours – have continued to flare over fishing grounds, offshore energy resources and disputed maritime zones.

Disputes between Malaysia and the Philippines have persisted over their overlapping claims in the waters off Sabah.

In June 2024, the Philippines submitted a claim to the United Nations to extend its continental shelf 350 nautical miles from Palawan, prompting Malaysia to file an objection over Manila’s move.

Tensions grew after Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr signed two maritime laws in November 2024 that Malaysia said infringed on its territory.

Malaysia also lodged two separate diplomatic protests in February and July ahead of Manila’s presentation of its continental shelf submission to a UN commission in July.

Malaysia and Vietnam also hold overlapping continental shelf claims in the South China Sea, despite having jointly submitted a claim to the UN in 2006.

In December 2019, Malaysia separately filed a submission to extend its continental shelf northwards into the waters around the Spratly Islands, prompting Vietnam to lodge its objections that the submission overlapped with its maritime entitlements.

Confrontations involving China have also been frequent across the region.

In January, a Chinese coastguard vessel entered Malaysia’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ) – the 200-nautical-mile band in which a coastal state holds special rights to marine resources – near the South Luconia Shoals off Sarawak on Borneo. The Royal Malaysian Navy’s offshore patrol vessel KD Kelantan had shadowed the Chinese ship since December 2025.

According to local media reports, Chinese vessels have maintained a near-continuous presence north and south of the shoals since 2014.

In October 2021, Malaysia’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Chinese ambassador to protest the presence and activities of Chinese ships, including survey vessels, in Malaysia’s EEZ.

While Beijing did not respond to the protest then, it claims the shoals as part of its Nansha Islands – known internationally as the Spratlys – and maintains that its coastguard patrols in the area are lawful operations within waters under Chinese jurisdiction, even as it prefers dialogue with Putrajaya to manage differences.

Philippine and Chinese vessels have also clashed in the disputed waters, with tensions rising in recent weeks despite a 2024 provisional bilateral arrangement meant to calm waters around the Second Thomas Shoal.

Last week, Manila accused a Chinese coastguard vessel of firing a water cannon and carrying out dangerous manoeuvres to delay the medical evacuation of an ailing Philippine Navy sailor from its grounded warship at the shoal by nearly 10 hours.

Beijing countered that it had allowed the evacuation on humanitarian grounds after prior notification, accusing Philippine vessels of using the mission to cause “infringements and provocations”.

That stand-off followed an incident in September in which Manila accused Chinese warships and coastguard cutters of blocking a Philippine resupply run to the same outpost – the first reported interception there since the 2024 arrangement was reached.

Chinese coastguard spokesman Jiang Lue accused Manila of breaking its commitments by conducting an unapproved mission. Philippine officials, however, maintained that the bilateral provisional understanding did not require Beijing’s prior consent.

In October 2024, Hanoi accused Chinese law enforcement personnel of assaulting Vietnamese fishers near the archipelago. China disputed the account and maintained that its authorities had taken lawful steps to stop Vietnamese boats from fishing illegally in waters claimed by Beijing.

China asserts sweeping claims across the South China Sea based on an 11-dash line drawn on a Chinese map in 1947, which it later reduced to a nine-dash line in the early 1950s.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled that Beijing had no legal basis to claim historic rights over resources within the nine-dash line, which exceeded its maritime entitlements under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).

Beijing rejected the ruling, maintaining that the tribunal lacked jurisdiction over the dispute.

In July, China’s Foreign Ministry reiterated its opposition, insisting that the decision would not affect its territorial sovereignty or maritime rights in the South China Sea.

“The so-called ‘award’ is nothing but a worthless piece of paper that is illegal, null and void, and has no binding force,” China’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement in response to the 10th anniversary of the ruling.

Nazery said the stakes in the South China Sea were high because it sat astride one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes and had become a focal point of great-power rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

“The last thing we need in Asean is to be adversely affected by the so-called great-power rivalry,” he said, warning that Malaysia must navigate differences carefully while maintaining its long-standing policy of neutrality and non-alignment.

While the fundamental question for Putrajaya was whether parties would respect existing international law, particularly Unclos, it must also maintain sufficient naval and surveillance capabilities at sea to protect its EEZ, Nazery said.

“You can talk all you want about safeguarding your maritime sovereignty, but typically you need the assets to back it up.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why did Hong Kong’s 11 Skies fail and can the megaproject be rescued?
item.description:
The roar of plane engines and the hustle and bustle at Hong Kong International Airport’s Terminal 2 present a stark contrast to the pin-drop silence at the adjacent 11 Skies commercial complex.

A South China Morning Post reporter who travelled between the two places in early October found minimal footfall at the shopping centre, with the bright and airy environment of the airport terminal replaced by dim, stuffy and boarded-up corridors, and poor air conditioning amid the simmering outdoor heat.

Occupying a gross floor area of 3.8 million square feet, 11 Skies is a mammoth project at the airport. Seventy per cent of the space was originally earmarked for a mall with 800 stores and 120 food and drink concepts, and the rest equally divided between experiential entertainment facilities and grade A office spaces.
item.content:encoded:
The roar of plane engines and the hustle and bustle at Hong Kong International Airport’s Terminal 2 present a stark contrast to the pin-drop silence at the adjacent 11 Skies commercial complex.

A South China Morning Post reporter who travelled between the two places in early October found minimal footfall at the shopping centre, with the bright and airy environment of the airport terminal replaced by dim, stuffy and boarded-up corridors, and poor air conditioning amid the simmering outdoor heat.

Occupying a gross floor area of 3.8 million square feet, 11 Skies is a mammoth project at the airport. Seventy per cent of the space was originally earmarked for a mall with 800 stores and 120 food and drink concepts, and the rest equally divided between experiential entertainment facilities and grade A office spaces.

But only one of its three office towers currently houses some companies running businesses at the airport.

The rest of the space sits in gloomy darkness.

After months of market speculation, the fate of 11 Skies was decided in early October when Hong Kong’s Airport Authority and developer New World Development signed an agreement to end the latter’s nearly 50-year contract for the project.

With the authority back at the helm, the mall’s management plans to tear down the existing 11 Skies signature logo, reconfigure the retail space into an entertainment hub, bring in tenants and investors, and relaunch the project under a new name and identity.

New World, which has been mired in a debt crisis since 2023, relinquished its control of the property and paid a HK$2.3 billion (US$293 million) break-up fee. It will spend an additional HK$1.05 billion on works and services before handing operations over to the authority by April next year.

The majority shareholder, the Cheng family’s private investment vehicle Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, will grant the authority an option to buy New World shares. Although the call option gives the authority the right to buy 750 million shares at HK$3 each from Chow Tai Fook Enterprises within the next three years, it comes with conditions that call its feasibility into question.

This rare break-up in Hong Kong’s public works sector raises questions of moral hazard and the risks of setting a precedent.

Wei Lai, head of Lingnan University’s department of finance, said the surrender appeared to be a negotiated restructuring involving a substantial termination payment, asset transfer and other contractual obligations.

“On the question of moral hazard, I would be cautious about characterising the arrangement as allowing a private developer to return a project ‘at will’,” Wei said, stressing that the arrangement was different from an unconditional exit option.

“From an economic perspective, the more relevant moral-hazard question is whether this arrangement changes the ex ante incentives of developers in future projects.”

Debt-ridden partner in an ambitious project

New World’s exit had been under discussion for months.

As a key step in taking over, the authority set up a new subsidiary, IEC Holdings, to spearhead the Skytopia project, a HK$100 billion megadevelopment that will turn the airport into a destination for yachting, shopping, dining, wellness, culture and entertainment. The 11 Skies project is part of it.

The authority’s executive director for commercial, Cissy Chan Ching-sze, became CEO of IEC on October 1.

“We will soon rename 11 Skies and change its style in a cost-effective way to reflect a new identity so that we can go recruiting for tenants and investors,” Chan said shortly after New World announced the deal on September 30.

On the same day, the developer’s financial results and debt levels were also a focal point.

In 2023, signs of New World’s financial distress prompted it to seek ways to reduce or refinance its debts to boost liquidity.

The 11 Skies project was also a factor in the debt crisis. Under the original terms of the contract, the developer was required to pay a guaranteed rent or a revenue rent representing 20 per cent of the gross revenue from the project, whichever was higher. New World was due to pay the rent from 2027 until the end of the contract in 2066.

The early termination allowed the developer to shed the contract’s financial obligations.

As of June 30, the developer’s total debt stood at HK$143.3 billion. Net debt amounted to HK$126.3 billion, an increase of HK$6.2 billion during the financial year.

To ease its financial burden, the developer implemented seven measures to reduce debt, including asset disposals, capital expenditure optimisation and a decade-long suspension of dividend payments that ended last year.

Julian Lee Pui-hang, the authority’s executive director for finance, conceded that it had to bring forward the 11 Skies project by parting with the “debt-ridden partner”.

“How can we work with a debt-ridden partner going forward?” he said. “The deal represents the best efforts of the controlling shareholder.”

Exit deal triggers moral hazard?

Wei of Lingnan University said she did not think the existence of one exceptional and costly exit mechanism by itself established an expectation for developers to bid more aggressively or take greater risks.

“Where difficulties arise partly from unusually adverse market conditions rather than simply from poor project execution, an orderly restructuring may in some circumstances preserve more economic value than allowing the situation to deteriorate further,” she said.

Market financing introduced an additional layer of market discipline because lenders and institutional investors would assess the financial position, risk exposure and expected returns of the authority.

“That market discipline can reduce, though not eliminate, governance and moral-hazard concerns,” Wei said.

Ervi Liusman, senior lecturer at the hotel and tourism management school at the Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School, said allowing a private developer to surrender a contracted commercial property would theoretically constitute a moral hazard if the developer could avoid the commercial risks it originally agreed to bear without facing a penalty.

“Allowing a developer to exit at will without penalty will encourage aggressive bids, knowing that there is an exit option if the market conditions deteriorate,” she said.

Liusman said that, based on what was revealed to the public, the developer had to bear significant financial losses upon returning 11 Skies, which meant the project was not surrendered at will and therefore did not constitute a moral hazard or set a bad precedent.

The surrender of the infrastructure, the break-up fee and other related expenses dealt a blow to New World’s balance sheet.

It resulted in HK$18.32 billion in net impairment losses and provisions relating to 11 Skies in the year ending June 30, contributing to New World’s HK$26.8 billion net loss. The net loss widened from HK$16.35 billion a year ago.

“Because the Airport Authority remains accountable to lenders and investors, it has strong incentives to ensure that any decision to take back the development is commercially justified and capable of generating long-term value,” Liusman said.

If the developer incurred substantial losses and contractual penalties, the focus shifted from who absorbed the loss to which party was best placed to unlock the future value of the asset, she explained.

“The Airport Authority’s intervention may then be seen as a realistic restructuring of a strategically important asset rather than a transfer of risk from private sector to the public sector,” Liusman said.

Despite being wholly owned by the government, the authority has primarily funded its infrastructure, such as the HK$141.5 billion three-runway system, through issuing debt, charging departure taxes and drawing on internal resources. The authority also retained the dividend payments the government agreed to forgo for a decade until last year.

It rarely directly taps the public coffers.

Ken Ip Man-hon, associate director of Saint Francis University’s Innovative Incubation Centre, said whether private developers should be allowed to exit large public-facing projects when commercial assumptions deteriorated was a legitimate policy question.

“The bigger lesson is that long-term projects need both accountability and flexibility,” Ip said.

He said a long-term project could not realistically be based on the assumption that its original business model would remain optimal for decades.

The project was tendered in 2018, a record year for tourist arrivals in the city before unexpected disruptions arose amid the social unrest of 2019 and the Covid-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2023.

After the borders reopened, another unexpected trend emerged, with mainland Chinese visitors – the city’s largest group of inbound travellers – spending less and Hongkongers choosing to cross the border for leisure spending.

Chan of the authority said her team would reposition and reconfigure the 11 Skies retail space into an entertainment hub, offer more unique experiences for visitors and bring in new features from overseas.

Win-win arrangement?

Ip said the authority was moving in the right direction by expanding the project beyond conventional retail to include aviation activities, arts and culture, tourism and experiential entertainment.

“The more important question remains – that is, what activities benefit most from being next to an international airport?”

Tourism and entertainment were part of the answer, but Ip suggested that the site could also include higher education, executive education, professional training, research and innovation.

“If 11 Skies can become a mixed-use international gateway rather than simply a better shopping and entertainment complex, the new strategy could give the project a much stronger foundation,” he said.

Li King-king, a professor at Hang Seng University of Hong Kong’s department of economics and finance, said the early termination was a very special case and was potentially a win-win arrangement.

The break-up was driven by factors such as location, airport design, trends in the Hong Kong retail market, changes in consumer behaviour due to the internet and residents travelling to the mainland for leisure, he said.

“The focus is whether the whole of society, the entire Airport Authority, the whole of Hong Kong, benefits from this agreement,” Li said.

Delaying the project could incur costs and affect overall airport planning, and the parties had to make a choice, taking society’s overall interests into consideration, he added.

The authority is now racing to reconfigure and relaunch the 11 Skies complex in 2028, with plans to align the project with the ambitious Skytopia megadevelopment at the airport.

Skytopia is a strategic blueprint that aims to create a new landmark for Hong Kong that will serve as a major growth engine for the economy.

The ecosystem will include a 20,000-seat arena for world-class performances at AsiaWorld-Expo next to the airport, a yacht bay providing 500 berths, a water recreation area, art galleries and storage facilities.

It will also feature a promenade with leisure facilities and an autonomous transport system connecting Skytopia, the Hong Kong border crossing of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge and Tung Chung railway station.

“We expect the entertainment hub to serve as a platform for mainland companies to market their products to an international audience, and for international businesses to make inroads into the mainland market,” Chan of the authority said.

The authority aims to recruit top-notch entertainment operators and business partners globally to be a part of major Skytopia components in the 2028-29 financial year.

“It will be an attraction for locals, transit passengers and visitors,” she said.

Additional reporting by Lo Hoi-ying and Denise Tsang

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines rejects China’s calls for direct contact amid ‘miscalculation’ warnings
item.description:
The Philippine military has rejected calls to restore direct communication channels with its Chinese counterpart, despite warnings from Beijing that their absence risks “miscalculation” during confrontations and could further escalate tensions in the South China Sea.

On Tuesday, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said it would not communicate with its Chinese counterpart in advance of its maritime operations, arguing that such channels were ineffective without mutual respect for international law.

Retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, spokesman for the military’s operations in waters the Philippines considered its territory, said the channels had failed to improve trust, accusing Beijing of using them as a “smokescreen” for what Manila regarded as coercive and aggressive conduct.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippine military has rejected calls to restore direct communication channels with its Chinese counterpart, despite warnings from Beijing that their absence risks “miscalculation” during confrontations and could further escalate tensions in the South China Sea.

On Tuesday, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said it would not communicate with its Chinese counterpart in advance of its maritime operations, arguing that such channels were ineffective without mutual respect for international law.

Retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, spokesman for the military’s operations in waters the Philippines considered its territory, said the channels had failed to improve trust, accusing Beijing of using them as a “smokescreen” for what Manila regarded as coercive and aggressive conduct.

He also said the Philippine military supported Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s decision to suspend direct communication channels with China.

The Chinese embassy in Manila had called for such channels to reopen in a Facebook post on Monday, arguing that communication was essential to prevent misunderstandings and keep tensions from escalating.

“Everyone knows that no matter how difficult bilateral relations become, communication channels should remain open to avoid miscalculation and prevent tensions from escalating,” it said.

The embassy accused Teodoro of suspending military-to-military communication for what it called “political self-interest”, saying such a move “fuels mistrust, narrows the space for crisis management, and pushes frontline personnel closer to confrontation”.

The Philippine Department of National Defence (DND) responded on Tuesday by reposting a 2024 statement from Teodoro, in which he said he had barred contact between the department and the Chinese embassy since July 2023.

The statement followed the embassy’s claim that the armed forces’ Western Command had agreed with China on a “new model” for managing the situation at the disputed Second Thomas Shoal, including arrangements for resupply missions. The embassy said Teodoro and other key Philippine officials had approved the arrangement.

Teodoro denied the DND was involved in any such deal, saying there was no discussion of a “gentleman’s agreement” or a “new model” during a courtesy call by then Chinese ambassador Huang Xilian shortly after Teodoro took office.

“I reiterate that I have disallowed any contact between the DND and the Chinese embassy since the courtesy call of Ambassador Huang Xilian, a few days after I assumed office in July of last year,” Teodoro said in the statement.

“During the said courtesy call, there was no discussion or briefing on any ‘gentleman’s agreement’ or ‘new model’, which is contrary to the Chinese embassy’s pronouncements.”

Trinidad said the military supported suspending direct communication channels because dialogue could not be effective without trust and respect for international law.

“Bilateral dialogue will be effective if the messages match the actions on sea, air, and ground. Unfortunately, this has not been the case,” he said.

He rejected the suggestion that the absence of direct communication could increase the risk of miscalculation and further escalate tensions.

“The miscalculations happen when you are not following international regulations and international law,” he said, referring to incidents involving Chinese vessels that the Philippines says have entered waters it claims and attempted to prevent resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre.

The ageing warship, grounded at Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea, serves as a Philippine military outpost on the disputed maritime feature.

Trinidad said the Philippine navy and coastguard had the legal right to challenge the presence of Chinese vessels in waters claimed by Manila, arguing that such encounters served as warnings to the ships involved.

“So, don’t take it literally that they are not being warned, they are not being challenged,” he said.

He maintained that China’s “coercive and aggressive actions”, rather than the absence of a direct communication channel, were the main source of miscalculation.

The dispute over maritime activities in the South China Sea is rooted in competing claims and sharply different interpretations of international law.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal established under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea ruled that China’s historic-rights claims within the nine-dash line had no legal basis insofar as they exceeded the maritime entitlements permitted under the convention.

Beijing rejected the ruling, arguing that the tribunal had no jurisdiction and that the award was null and void. The ruling did not determine sovereignty over all disputed islands and reefs.

Competing accounts

The evacuation of a Philippine marine from the BRP Sierra Madre on October 8, after he suffered a medical emergency involving a nearly ruptured appendix, became the latest flashpoint in the disputed waters, with Manila and Beijing offering different accounts of how the operation unfolded.

Navy Captain Marissa Andres-Martinez said the Philippines would not seek China’s permission to conduct maritime operations in waters it claimed.

“Nothing was communicated to the Chinese coastguard,” she said of Manila’s response to the emergency.

Andres-Martinez said the navy would continue operations to sustain the soldiers aboard the vessel without seeking China’s permission.

The armed forces’ public affairs chief Colonel Xerxes Trinidad said other seafarers should also recognise the urgency of medical evacuations.

“The moment you call for a medical evacuation, it is something of concern that all. I think, a proper Navy or any seafarer would do to give way to that.”

His remarks came amid Philippine Coast Guard accusations that Chinese vessels had used water cannons against Philippine ships responding to the medical emergency.

China offered a different account of the incident.

On Friday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said the Philippine coastguard had “intruded the adjacent waters of Ren’ai Jiao, Nansha Qundao of China”, referring to Beijing’s names for Second Thomas Shoal and the Spratly Islands.

“The China Coast Guard took legitimate and reasonable measures to handle the situation in accordance with laws and regulations,” Mao said.

China had allowed the evacuation on humanitarian grounds after communication between the two sides but “individual Philippine officials have distorted facts and wrongfully accused China without showing the whole picture to the public”, Mao added.

The Chinese embassy in Manila on Monday urged the Philippines to tow away the “illegally grounded” warship and evacuate its personnel to end their exposure to risk.

On the same day as the medical evacuation, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr called for a binding code of conduct in the South China Sea during a speech at the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore.

Marcos said an agreement between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations was “absolutely necessary” to reduce the risk of further confrontations.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump’s ‘golden age’ push hands top science honours to big tech. Will it work?
item.description:
The White House’s bid for a US “golden age” of science should put China on alert, Chinese analysts have warned, but they remain sceptical as to whether President Donald Trump’s alliance with Silicon Valley billionaires can pull it off.

This comes as Trump, in another arguably unconventional move, handed the country’s highest science and engineering awards to top American tech bosses.

Elon Musk, head of electric-vehicle maker Tesla and aerospace manufacturer SpaceX, received the National Medal of Science, the US’ top scientific honour.
item.content:encoded:
The White House’s bid for a US “golden age” of science should put China on alert, Chinese analysts have warned, but they remain sceptical as to whether President Donald Trump’s alliance with Silicon Valley billionaires can pull it off.

This comes as Trump, in another arguably unconventional move, handed the country’s highest science and engineering awards to top American tech bosses.

Elon Musk, head of electric-vehicle maker Tesla and aerospace manufacturer SpaceX, received the National Medal of Science, the US’ top scientific honour.

Joining him in receiving the award at the “Science: A New Golden Age Summit” in Washington on Thursday were leading chipmaking chiefs Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices, as well as Google co-founder Sergey Brin.

Personal computer tycoon Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, the US’ most prestigious award for the category.

While entrepreneurs have previously won these awards, observers noted that it was unprecedented for tech executives to be honoured on such a scale – particularly given that the National Medal of Science had long prioritised scientists and researchers.

The award was established by Congress in 1959, while the technology medal was introduced in 1980.

All of this year’s recipients have close ties with the White House. Musk is widely considered a Trump ally despite their months-long public feud last year, while Huang, Su, Brin and Dell are all members of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology.

The companies they lead have also deepened their commercial ties with the Pentagon to varying degrees.

With artificial intelligence (AI) emerging as a major arena of the China-US tech rivalry, those enterprises are also critical players in the supply chain. At Trump’s state dinner last month for Chinese President Xi Jinping, Musk, Huang and Su were seated at the same table as the two leaders.

Sun Zhanqing, a special researcher at the South China University of Technology’s Institute of Public Policy, said the line-up of awardees showed that a “new type of power relationship” was taking shape in the US.

“Tech entrepreneurs’ standing in [shaping] resource allocation, technological road maps and the national science narrative is rising,” Sun wrote in a note on the think tank’s social media channel on Friday.

Still, he cautioned against conflating US tech executives’ growing influence over scientific research with scientists’ actual “capacity to create knowledge”.

“The Trump administration’s science awards may create a cycle that warrants vigilance,” warned Sun, who is also deputy director of the government-affiliated Guangzhou Academy of Social Sciences’ Urban Culture Research Institute.

Tech bosses’ resource advantages yielded more visible results, he said, earning them higher honours that in turn could reinforce their policy influence and ability to secure more resources.

“Ultimately, people may attribute the advantages created by this cycle to the idea that a certain group of people is inherently more creative,” he warned.

“A golden age of science cannot be judged solely by how glamorous the people standing on the podium are.”

An analysis by Xinzhi Observatory, a technology-focused channel owned by Shanghai-based news portal Guancha, also struck a sceptical note on last week’s US science summit.

Even as the Trump White House continued to cut routine federal funding for basic science, it was trying to tap the massive computing power and capital of private giants to rebuild US global leadership in research through so-called superintelligence, the piece noted, using Trump’s new preferred moniker for AI.

With entrepreneurs increasingly steering research, the purity of scientific inquiry and the public interest could face an “unprecedented test,” it cautioned. “Whether reliance on the patronage of tech oligarchs can truly open a new, enduring golden age of science remains a highly contested unknown.”

However, China could ill afford to let its guard down, the observers cautioned.

“The award ceremony was not merely a ‘symbolic arrangement’,” Sun said. “Big tech companies are taking part in national tech competition as technology developers.”

He cited the more than US$6 billion in science and technology investments announced by the Trump administration at Thursday’s event. This includes US$2.4 billion in contributions from 11 companies, including Nvidia, AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, to provide AI “science tools and compute credits” for researchers.

Xinzhi Observatory said the investment plans announced at the summit might reveal a blueprint for “stockpiling talent reserves for future industrial competition” – by pushing advanced computing capacity directly to the local level to spur broader basic innovation.

Thursday’s event built on “Science: A New Golden Age”, a report by White House Office of Science and Technology Policy director Michael Kratsios released in July.

It outlines a major overhaul of the framework for American science, whose foundations were laid by the 1945 report “Science, the Endless Frontier”, written by Vannevar Bush, director of the US Office of Scientific Research and Development during the second world war, while positioning itself as the 21st century successor to it.

Kratsios’ report argues that the post-war “linear model” of technological progress – flowing in sequence from university-based basic research funded through slow, consensus-driven peer review, to applied research, then to technological development and industry – no longer held in many fields.

It said US private companies dominated research spending, bureaucratic and funding structures were burdening scientists, and the fruits of American science often ended up helping rivals build their advantage due to decades of industrial offshoring.

It proposed prioritising funding for risk-taking individual scientists over “legacy institutions” and expanding the Genesis Mission – launched by the Trump administration in November to use AI to accelerate scientific discovery.

However, Kratsios’ report has drawn criticism at home, including over its ostensible aim to shift vast resources away from traditional academia towards big tech, effectively turning national research into a venture-capital model.

But Chinese observers say it could pose a challenge to Beijing, by shifting the gravity of US-China tech competition away from individual breakthroughs to how well each side governs its innovation system.

The report identified China as the first “peer-level competitor” to the US in research and development spending – driven by Beijing’s “all-of-society approach” to partnerships across sectors.

Strategically, the White House report was a “direct response” to China’s whole-of-nation approach to scientific research, said Zhu Yanmei, dean’s adviser at the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute.

She warned in a July post that regardless of future administrative shifts, its core propositions – that science must serve national competitiveness, that federal funding must pursue quantifiable gains in technological sovereignty, and that AI must be treated as national infrastructure – had probably become consensus in US strategic circles.

She also cautioned that the problems highlighted in the US report – bureaucracy, conservatism and inefficiency – mirrored chronic flaws in China’s own research system.

“What China needs is not simple benchmarking or a reflexive response but a profound reflection on its innovation paradigm. In criticising America’s own ailments, the report has inadvertently held up a mirror for China,” she wrote.

“For China, the report’s biggest takeaway may be this: a true science and innovation power is measured not by the number of papers or the scale of funding but by whether its institutions can keep generating ‘crazy ideas’ and turn them into ‘world-changing forces’.”

Beijing is also moving to streamline its research system.

Guidelines issued last Friday on developing new productive forces called for boosting the role of companies as the main force in scientific and technological innovation, and for supporting capable private firms to lead major national technology projects.

In April, Xi called for an open, inclusive innovation environment that tolerated failure and placed greater weight on AI-enabled basic research.

item.title: [SCMP] Slain model Abby Choi called ‘birthing machine’ by ex-father-in-law, court hears
item.description:
The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her a “birthing machine” and tried to assault her before he allegedly plotted with his two sons to kill her three years ago, a court has heard.

Choi’s partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, recounted on Tuesday a bitter argument between the influencer and her former in-laws in what he said was a watershed moment leading to a breakdown in the relationship in mid-2022.

Choi was previously married to Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, who is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and his father Kwong Kau, 68.
item.content:encoded:
The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her a “birthing machine” and tried to assault her before he allegedly plotted with his two sons to kill her three years ago, a court has heard.

Choi’s partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, recounted on Tuesday a bitter argument between the influencer and her former in-laws in what he said was a watershed moment leading to a breakdown in the relationship in mid-2022.

Choi was previously married to Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, who is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and his father Kwong Kau, 68.

Testifying for the first time in the High Court, Tam also said Choi had given his family a false impression that her former in-laws were leading a good life, because she feared her two children from her previous marriage would be disparaged in their new home due to their background.

Tam said he was not surprised initially to find out that Kwong Kau was the registered owner of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin, before she told him the flat was in fact bought using her money.

“When I saw the Kadooria flat was in Kwong Kau’s name, I did not deliberately ask [Choi] about it because she had been telling me all along that this family was doing OK,” Tam said.

Kwong allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the upscale property and enlisted his two sons to help kill the 28-year-old on February 21, 2023. Prosecutors argued the flat was only registered in his name to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty.

The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the burial of Choi’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial began last month.

Tam said his family’s wealth grew significantly after his father, who founded the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian, received part of the profit from selling the brand to a Japanese company for HK$1 billion.

He said he first met Choi around the end of 2013 and early 2014, when he briefly returned from Australia during a break in his studies to meet up with her then-husband Alex Kwong, his former classmate.

He said Alex Kwong “totally disappeared” after one day in 2015, the same year he began the process to divorce Choi and absconded from criminal proceedings arising from his alleged involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case.

Tam said he did not probe further after Choi said her then-partner was safe, because he thought she had somehow managed to find a way to contact him.

“I came out very often with Abby afterwards. We took care of her children together, and love grew between us as time went by,” he added.

The court heard Tam and Choi formally started dating in December 2015 and held a wedding banquet a year later, although they never registered their marriage. The model gave birth to their daughter in September 2016, and their son was born three years later.

Choi lived with her partner’s family at a luxurious residence on Begonia Road in Kowloon Tong and received up to HK$300,000 monthly from Tam’s father to cover the couple’s expenses.

Tam said the two children Choi had with Alex Kwong lived separately with two domestic helpers initially at a flat in the Laguna Verde estate in Hung Hom, before the socialite decided to move them to the Kadooria development in 2019 because it was closer to her Kowloon Tong home.

The witness highlighted a heated argument between Choi and her former mother-in-law, Jenny Li Sui-heung, on a day when the influencer’s elder daughter had a fever at the Kadooria home in June or July 2022.

According to Tam, the model was angry at Li for telling Alex Kwong to stay away from the child because she could infect him.

“My understanding is that Abby was at that time accusing Li Sui-heung of preferring sons to daughters,” he said.

Kwong Kau, who joined the row, reportedly lunged at Choi and hurled curses at her after he accused the influencer of assaulting his wife.

“And then Kwong Kau said: ‘Who do you think you are? You’re just a birthing machine’,” Tam continued.

Tam said the elder Kwong attempted to attack Choi a second time, but he intervened to prevent the former police officer from hitting the model.

He said Choi then barred Kwong Kau from visiting the residence. She also told Tam they needed to cut ties with the Kwong family, whom she described as horrible and ungrateful.

Defence lawyers also grilled a police officer helping to lead the investigation of the case.

Detective Constable Ko Yan-ki, who was originally not expected to take the witness box, was cross-examined over his text conversations with Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, in the months preceding the trial.

The messaging logs were produced as evidence after the officer contacted Cheung while she was giving evidence last week about her purported ownership of a flat at Whampoa Garden. She later clarified that she did not own the property.

Ko rejected the prosecution’s suggestion that he should have avoided contact with Cheung while her testimony was ongoing, saying he needed to make prompt inquiries on new information regarding her property ownership.

The messaging records also showed that Cheung had a monetary dispute with a friend she met at a mahjong parlour earlier this year.

Cheung said she was alleged to have owed HK$1.6 million, but she insisted the debt was settled seven years ago. She also revealed that she once lost “a few tens of millions of dollars” while gambling at a mahjong parlour in Jordan.

Ko said Cheung’s alleged debts did not catch his attention when he investigated the case, adding that he could not ascertain whether her claims about gambling millions of dollars away were true or exaggerated.

The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] Is this the best time for US strategists to push for abandoning ambiguity on Taiwan?
item.description:
For nearly five decades, the United States’ Taiwan policy has centred on strategic ambiguity by not declaring whether it would intervene militarily in a potential Taiwan conflict.

This policy – designed to deter Beijing from using force while preventing Taipei from formally declaring independence – is being challenged by realist US strategists amid a broader debate over America’s role in the world, growing constraints on US military might and a shifting regional balance of power driven by China’s military rise.

A small group of realist US strategists is pushing for the US to rule out military intervention over Taiwan to avoid the possibility of a catastrophic war between mainland China and the US. Experts said this idea, despite still being a minority view, was at least opening debate on the long-standing one-sided policy.
item.content:encoded:
For nearly five decades, the United States’ Taiwan policy has centred on strategic ambiguity by not declaring whether it would intervene militarily in a potential Taiwan conflict.

This policy – designed to deter Beijing from using force while preventing Taipei from formally declaring independence – is being challenged by realist US strategists amid a broader debate over America’s role in the world, growing constraints on US military might and a shifting regional balance of power driven by China’s military rise.

A small group of realist US strategists is pushing for the US to rule out military intervention over Taiwan to avoid the possibility of a catastrophic war between mainland China and the US. Experts said this idea, despite still being a minority view, was at least opening debate on the long-standing one-sided policy.

“When US officials first adopted strategic ambiguity over Taiwan, China’s military was no match for that of the US. This is no longer the case,” wrote Jennifer Kavanagh, director of military analysis at the Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, in an opinion piece late last month.

“At the same time, the American military suddenly seems fragile, lacking the advanced munitions and naval forces it would need for a major power conflict and facing serious vulnerabilities in its basing infrastructure.

“Simply put, the US military remains the strongest in the world, but its ability to outlast China in a war over Taiwan is now in question.”

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not formally recognise the island as independent, although Washington is committed to supplying it with defensive weapons and opposes any forcible takeover.

Kavanagh told the South China Morning Post on October 8 that of her many modelling efforts looking at what would be required to break through a blockade of Taiwan, the bottom line was that neither Beijing nor Washington could defeat the other side.

“The conflict would start with some kind of intense war. [In the modelling, the] US typically runs out of air-defence missiles and offensive missiles before China does, even if China depletes stockpiles,” she said.

“My assumption is that China blockades Taiwan and just bleeds it out. And there’s not so much the US can do.”

In a research report published on September 10, Kavanagh not only proposed ending strategic ambiguity over Taiwan but also argued for replacing US mutual defence treaties with Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia with narrower security partnerships.

The report also said the US should move most forces away from positions near mainland China in the first island chain – a string of US-led chokepoints along an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines – towards a smaller presence centred farther east around the second island chain, stretching from Japan through Guam to Papua New Guinea.

Her proposal drew strong pushback within US national security circles, was called a “bombshell” and “radical”, and was deemed to be Communist Party “talking points”.

“When I started arguing this, I was trying to be careful how I phrased what I was saying in the way that would make it clear that I was arguing for something that I thought was in US interests,” said Kavanagh, explaining how her position had become more direct since she first made the argument earlier last year.

“The US foreign policy is in a period of flux. And people are debating what the US role in the world should be.

“Being clear and direct about alternatives and options that the US has, and making a strong case for why this is in the US’ interest contributes to the debate.”

Kavanagh belongs to a school of foreign policy that rejects military interventionism in favour of military restraint, narrow national interests and a focus on domestic strength. Since last year, she has written several reports and published opinion pieces proposing a Taiwan non-intervention policy.

From the late 1990s until recently, a group of US foreign policy scholars and analysts has advocated restraint and argued that Taiwan’s importance does not justify risking a war with Beijing.

In 1998, Ted Galen Carpenter, now a senior fellow at the Randolph Bourne Institute and the Libertarian Institute, advocated continued arms sales but explicitly ruled out military intervention in a policy paper he wrote while at the Cato Institute, a Washington-based libertarian think tank. Doug Bandow, a Cato senior fellow, made a similar case in 2024.

In a 2015 paper, Charles L. Glaser, now a senior fellow at MIT’s security studies programme, proposed that Washington end its commitment to defend Taiwan in exchange for Beijing peacefully settling its maritime disputes and accepting a continued US military role in East Asia.

More recently, Kavanagh and Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow in the Carnegie Endowment’s American statecraft programme, argued in Foreign Affairs in February 2025 that Washington should prepare to stay out of a Taiwan conflict if the People’s Liberation Army did not attack US bases or warships.

In September 2025, Michael Swaine, a senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute, proposed a gradual transition to explicit non-intervention, emphasising the reassurance of allies and Beijing.

Swaine said that maintaining the possibility of the US intervening militarily would become increasingly dangerous and would risk a major war with China under a worsening strategic rivalry between the two powers.

He said there was an increasing tendency in Washington to regard Taiwan as a vital strategic location that, by implication, must be kept from Beijing. Alongside this, Beijing was steadily increasing its military capabilities regarding Taiwan.

“These two trends are increasing the likelihood of one or both sides taking what they view as deterrent actions that cross red lines, leading to a major crisis and possible conflict,” Swaine said.

“If these trends do not change, the US must consider just how vital Taiwan is to the US. Since I believe that it is in fact not a vital enough interest to justify risking a major war with China.”

Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University, said the basis of strategic ambiguity stemmed from the extremely strong US military capability and its deterrent power, but the policy had become meaningless with the rise of Chinese military power.

But he said it would be difficult for this argument, which was still proposed by a minority voice, to become a mainstream view due to policy inertia.

“They’re actively debating it and it’s no longer just a one-sided policy position that leaves no room for discussion. The fact that this is happening is a good thing in itself, regardless of whether it will ultimately succeed,” Xin said.

The argument for policy change comes as US foreign policy is in a period of flux, with US President Donald Trump’s administration pushing the boundaries of what has long been status quo foreign policy.

Taiwan was among the most closely watched issues at the two summits between presidents Trump and Xi Jinping this year. While former US president Joe Biden repeatedly said the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a potential conflict, Trump has declined to say whether he would do so.

After the first summit in May, the US paused a US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, which is still on hold. And the US is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Apec summit in Shenzhen, the SCMP reported last month.

While he was silent on the Taiwan issue during the second summit last month, Trump raised the question after the meeting in Beijing in May of whether it would make sense for US forces to travel 9,500 miles (15,300km) to fight a war.

.

item.title: [SCMP] Plan to live-stream US execution tests Southeast Asia’s content curbs
item.description:
The US government’s plan to live-stream the execution of a former Army member convicted in a deadly 2009 mass shooting is raising questions about how effectively Southeast Asian governments can restrict graphic online content.

Analysts say while authorities may have powers to restrict access to the live stream, containing clips and altered copies of the killing posted to social media could prove far more difficult.

The issue gained fresh urgency on Tuesday, after Australia’s Environment Minister Murray Watts condemned the proposed broadcast as “disgusting”.
item.content:encoded:
The US government’s plan to live-stream the execution of a former Army member convicted in a deadly 2009 mass shooting is raising questions about how effectively Southeast Asian governments can restrict graphic online content.

Analysts say while authorities may have powers to restrict access to the live stream, containing clips and altered copies of the killing posted to social media could prove far more difficult.

The issue gained fresh urgency on Tuesday, after Australia’s Environment Minister Murray Watts condemned the proposed broadcast as “disgusting”.

Australia’s online regulator, eSafety, told Agence France Presse it lacked the power to prevent the live stream, but stressed that online services had a responsibility to protect users from harmful content.

New Zealand’s Classification Office had earlier said it could not classify a live stream while it was taking place and lacked the authority to block access to such an event.

Nidal Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be live-streamed, and the Pentagon subsequently confirmed the plan.

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had not made a final decision on whether the execution would be live-streamed, despite his comments a day earlier approving the broadcast, leaving the plan’s current status uncertain.

Details of how the broadcast will be distributed also remain unclear.

In Southeast Asia, existing rules provide potential avenues for restricting access, but analysts say whether authorities invoke them depends on their assessment of the broadcast, how it is presented and where it appears.

Benjamin Ang, head of the Centre of Excellence for National Security at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said regulators would first need to determine whether the broadcast warranted restrictions.

“Regulators and platforms would then need to coordinate to pre-identify when and where the live stream will take place so they can effectively detect the live stream and block access to it in their countries,” he said.

Powers to restrict

In Singapore, the Internet Code of Practice requires licensed providers to comply with rules on prohibited material. For websites, internet access providers meet their obligations by denying access to sites notified by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) as containing such material.

The code considers whether content depicts “detailed or relished acts of extreme violence or cruelty”, alongside any intrinsic medical, scientific, artistic or educational value. These are assessment criteria, rather than an automatic requirement for blocking an execution broadcast.

Malaysia’s Online Safety Act provides for the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) to order licensed platforms or network providers to restrict access. This follows MCMC’s assessing a user report and determining on reasonable grounds that the content is harmful.

The law covers material that may incite violence or terrorism, promote public hostility or disturb public tranquillity, but does not specifically list execution live streams.

Indonesia’s Ministerial Regulation No. 5 of 2020 on Private Electronic-System Operators, amended in 2021, requires operators to prevent the distribution of prohibited material, including content that relevant authorities classify as unsettling the public and disrupting public order.

Operators must comply with takedown orders within 24 hours of receipt. In urgent cases, they must act without delay, and no later than four hours after receiving a warning. Failure to comply can lead to access blocking, including through internet service providers.

These deadlines, however, do not shield viewers from a short live event. This Week In Asia has reached out to IMDA, MCMC and Indonesia’s Communications and Digital Ministry for comment.

Beyond the original stream

Even if access to the original broadcast were restricted, recordings and excerpts could spread elsewhere, creating a separate challenge for regulators and platforms.

Drawing on lessons from Islamic State beheadings and the Christchurch terrorist massacre, Ang said regulators should work across platforms to limit resharing, while services should use machine learning to detect altered copies of the footage.

Platforms must also “downgrade related search terms, and de-monetise and disable offending accounts”, he said.

Benjamin Y.H. Loh, a communications and media scholar at Monash University Malaysia, said containing reposted footage could become “a cat-and-mouse game”, with social media users uploading clips of the event to spoof platforms’ detection efforts.

He also pointed to the Christchurch attack, where redistribution of footage on the massacre became a major content-moderation challenge. Clips were altered with music, sped up or mirrored before being uploaded in attempts to evade platform moderators and automated detection tools.

However, advance notice would allow platforms to prepare for the broadcast, Loh said. “You need to have a lot of human moderators on standby to handle the incoming reports.”

He said moderators could also monitor retransmission of footage, citing how illegal live streams of World Cup matches in June and July were quickly discovered and blocked or banned.
