“It’s not going to be instantaneous, of course,” he said. “There will definitely be a few that will go through the cracks.”

Loh also cautioned that a broadcast showing the execution directly versus an indirect account of proceedings would raise different questions.

“The platforms’ decisions really depend on the material and how they apply their own Terms of Service,” he said.

Propaganda tool

The risks of broadcasting or live-streaming Hasan’s execution could extend beyond exposure to graphic imagery, as experts warn the footage could also be used to promote extremist narratives.

“Some of the accounts that clip or repost the original live stream may do so to advocate violence or incite hate against certain races or religions,” Ang said, adding that community and religious leaders and educators could help raise public awareness of the dangers of such content.

But for political scientist Bilveer Singh, live-streaming the execution would simply reinforce anti-West or anti-American views among extremist actors and susceptible audiences in Southeast Asia.

“It will also complicate ongoing deradicalisation efforts that Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia have been pursuing, because if this execution goes through, it provides extremists with material to exploit,” he said.

Analysts warn that extremist sympathisers could also portray Hasan as a martyr, regardless of his crimes.

“Therein lies a radicalisation toolkit for these people,” Bilveer said.

For Ang, the practical objective is reducing harm rather than promising complete containment.

“It may be impossible to stop every instance of the livestream, but countries can do as much as they can to reduce the harm to their populations,” Ang said.

item.title: [SCMP] Systems to counter missiles and drones take centre stage at US defence expo
item.description:
As missiles and drones take a bigger role in modern warfare, major defence contractors gathered in Washington this week to showcase their latest advances in the technologies – and systems to counter them.

The three-day Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition, which opened on Monday, is one of the largest ground-based weapons shows in the US.

This year there was a strong emphasis on air and missile defence systems, reflecting growing concern about how to counter aerial threats as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East rage on, and following reports that the US military’s missile stockpiles have been badly depleted by its war on Iran.
item.content:encoded:
As missiles and drones take a bigger role in modern warfare, major defence contractors gathered in Washington this week to showcase their latest advances in the technologies – and systems to counter them.

The three-day Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition, which opened on Monday, is one of the largest ground-based weapons shows in the US.

This year there was a strong emphasis on air and missile defence systems, reflecting growing concern about how to counter aerial threats as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East rage on, and following reports that the US military’s missile stockpiles have been badly depleted by its war on Iran.

Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s largest defence contractors, had its latest advanced missile systems on show – the Extended-Range Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM), launched from its High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (Himars), a light multiple rocket launcher.

But the main focus was its air and missile defence systems, with the latest PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) and Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) on show – used for short- and long-range air defence, respectively.

The company also had its new PAC-3 Edge next-generation missile interceptor on show for the first time after it unveiled the programme on Friday.

The PAC-3 Edge is an upgrade of the PAC-3 MSE currently in operation in Ukraine, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific region.

It incorporates a new seeker, upgraded flight controls and a multi-pulse rocket motor supplied by Northrop Grumman, which Lockheed Martin says enhance the interceptor’s ability to counter advanced threats, including hypersonic missiles, ‌at ⁠longer ranges and higher altitudes.

During the ceremony at the AUSA expo on Monday, Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control for Lockheed Martin, said the PAC-3 Edge would “fly further, faster and higher” than its predecessor, with more manoeuvrability, thrust and sensitivity. It is expected to begin testing by 2027 to be ready for deployment in 2031.

“We’re looking forward. We’re asking ourselves, what are our adversaries going to be doing in three or four or five or 10 years from now? And we’re preparing for that,” Cahill said.

“We’re going to make sure that the adversaries have nowhere to hide. It doesn’t matter what they do. It doesn’t matter what they try. This missile is going to take them out.”

It comes as the ongoing war in Iran has exposed the importance of munitions stockpiles and defence against low-cost drone swarms in modern warfare.

According to an April report by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, the US military may have used more than half of its pre-war inventory for four key munitions – PrSM, SM-3, THAAD and Patriot missiles – and more than 1,000 rounds of Tomahawk and Joint Air-to-Surface Stand-off missiles during the first 39 days of its war with Iran, which began on February 28.

That situation could be “critical” for a potential western Pacific conflict, the report said, as it would take up to four years to return stockpiles to pre-war levels, which were already deemed insufficient for a war against a peer. “Building stockpiles to levels adequate for a war with China will take additional time,” it added.

In contrast, Iran has heavily relied on its low-cost, one-way attack drones – such as the Shahed-136 “kamikaze” drone – that were used to swarm and overwhelm the air defences of US military bases in the region.

The US and Gulf states have consumed and depleted multimillion-dollar air and missile defence rounds to combat the cheap drones, prompting calls for more efficient solutions.

These drone warfare tactics are also projected to be critical in the Indo-Pacific flashpoints – particularly the Taiwan Strait, where both the US and China have been building up their drone fleets in preparation for a potential armed conflict.

A satellite imagery analysis suggests that the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has stationed over 200 obsolete 1960s-era J-6 supersonic fighter jets – converted into attack and cruise-missile-like drones – across six airbases near the Taiwan Strait.

In response, the US has introduced the “hellscape” concept into its Taiwan Strait strategy, aimed at deploying a massive fleet of autonomous drone swarms, loitering munition systems and marine drones to disrupt PLA amphibious invasion forces in any contingencies. It also requested US$54 billion for “autonomous and remotely operated systems across air, land, and above and below the sea” in the 2027 budget request, according to the Pentagon’s budget overview book.

To counter short-range drone swarms and incoming missiles, General Dynamics, one of the largest American land-based arms contractors, showcased its two latest air defence systems – the Leonidas Ground Vehicle (GV) and the Manoeuvre-Short Range Air Defence (M-SHORAD) Increment 4.

The Leonidas GV is a mobile high-power microwave counter-drone defence system developed as a collaborative initiative by the defence tech company Epirus and General Dynamics.

Scott Taylor, director of US growth at General Dynamics, said the Leonidas GV was developed with “drone swarm defeat” in mind and aimed to solve the “prolific problem” of being unable to use electronic warfare interruption against fibre-optically controlled drones by using weaponised electromagnetic interference technology.

In this way, the Leonidas GV could overload the internal electronics, navigation and communication systems of multiple hostile drones at once, causing them to drop from the sky simultaneously.

“One of the things that’s been very clear in a lot of the studies that are publicly discussed out there, particularly in Southwest Asia, is that the enemy can start flying enough drones at you that it overwhelms an electronic warfare or a kinetic machine gun capability,” Taylor said.

“So the Epirus-based vehicle – the Leonidas over there – that one uses electromagnetic interference to weaponise, and it can drop 50 drones at one time, single pulse, no bullets, no fratricide risk.”

Also on display, the M-SHORAD anti-aircraft weapon system uses a self-loading equipment dock mounted on light, tactical and utility vehicles to provide air defence against short-range drone and missile threats for light infantry brigades.

Taylor said it had “powerful short-range air defence and counter-drone capability integrated in one”. It is equipped with Iron Wasp suicide drones that intercept incoming enemy drone attacks, as well as a 30-calibre machine gun.

“With what’s going on in Ukraine, what’s happening in the Persian Gulf in the Strait of Hormuz, there’s a lot of people talking about the challenges with drone defeat,” he said.

“Now they’re having US$30,000 drones destroying multimillion-dollar vehicles, and so trust me, we’re being approached all of the time by our allied nations as well.”

The need to counter drone attacks – and a desire to reduce American casualties on the battlefield – has accelerated the integration of autonomous systems into US Army operations.

At the expo, GM Defence showcased its prototype of a “commercially derived” Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) concept, with a design based on Chevrolet’s Silverado to demonstrate potential future drive-by-wire controls, camera-based sensing and modular payload capabilities for support missions like logistics and casualty evacuation.

Pete Johnson, vice-president of integrated vehicle solutions at GM Defence, said the UGV was a “direct reflection” of how his company listened to the US Army and paid attention to the changing character of warfare.

“We’re watching closely the developments in Ukraine and the Middle East, and how the army is organising the campaign in the Indo-Pacific,” Johnson said. “And all of those observations are pointing to a very clear need: more robotic and autonomous capability to deliver operational effect and to reduce risk for our soldiers.”

item.title: [SCMP] Can Singapore engineer love on dating apps? From public service to private romance
item.description:
For Singaporean civil servant Clare*, finding a suitable lifelong partner has been an uphill battle. Swiping on dating apps soon became a chore after multiple unsuccessful first dates, so when the government launched its own platform, the 32-year-old was all for it.

“It’s like: ‘Why not?’, and I think it does have a few screening procedures so it might save you some trouble like having to deal with impersonators or people who do not match with their advertised profiles,” she said.

Singapore launched dating platform FirstDate last month, as the city state grapples with a record-low fertility rate. While the platform has drawn some criticism online for its limited range of eligibility, observers also say it is a good way to encourage first meetings for potential couples.
item.content:encoded:
For Singaporean civil servant Clare*, finding a suitable lifelong partner has been an uphill battle. Swiping on dating apps soon became a chore after multiple unsuccessful first dates, so when the government launched its own platform, the 32-year-old was all for it.

“It’s like: ‘Why not?’, and I think it does have a few screening procedures so it might save you some trouble like having to deal with impersonators or people who do not match with their advertised profiles,” she said.

Singapore launched dating platform FirstDate last month, as the city state grapples with a record-low fertility rate. While the platform has drawn some criticism online for its limited range of eligibility, observers also say it is a good way to encourage first meetings for potential couples.

FirstDate is being piloted among government employees aged 21 to 35 by GovTech, which told local media there was no decision yet to expand the initiative beyond the public sector. The government agency has not provided figures on how many users in the sector meet its present criteria for the app.

Singapore’s public service workforce is about 158,000-strong as of March this year, according to the government job portal.

App users answer a survey about their interests and values, and the platform uses a Nobel Prize-winning algorithm to generate recommended pairings based on participants’ preferences and compatibility.

The first round of sign-ups closed on October 5 after emails on the platform were sent to public officers a week before. A matching cycle lasts about a month, according to local media reports.

Public reaction to the app has been mixed, with some online commentators arguing that limiting it to civil servants is elitist and that having an age limit implies an expiration date for relationships.

Many also pointed out that dating was not a top priority for young Singaporeans facing rising living costs.

If life was cheaper, people would “go out more often, go dating and have kids”, one social media user wrote.

The FirstDate platform, which matches participants to one partner at a time, can still be effective for those who are serious about finding love, according to Norman Li, a psychology professor at the Singapore Management University.

“Today, people are overwhelmed with perceived choices, many of which are not even real choices, which makes it psychologically hard to settle down and stay with any one person,” he said.

But he noted that the agency faced the challenge of getting enough sign-ups to broaden the dating pool and increase users’ chances of perceiving potential matches as suitable and attractive partners.

“A major problem today is that people’s standards are too high for the market to clear, due to constant exposure to celebrities, internet and movie stars and dating app choices,” Li said.

For Jean Liu, an associate professor of psychology at the Singapore Institute of Technology, restricting matches is a positive as it helps prevent dating fatigue and being overwhelmed by choices.

“You won’t have a few highly popular individuals flooded with attention, as you might on a typical app,” she said.

The platform launch comes amid the city state’s battle to raise its fertility rate, which sank to a low of 0.87 last year. The government has rolled out new measures, including increasing childcare leave and lowering childcare fees, and set up an inter-agency work group to tackle the trend.

Li said that FirstDate likely had similar goals of boosting marriage and fertility.

The platform – powered by an algorithm that earned one of its creators a Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences in 2012 – is the latest in a series of Singaporean initiatives aimed at matching singles.

In 1984, the government launched the Social Development Unit (SDU), which organised events for university graduates to meet up. In a speech a year earlier, Singapore’s founding father Lee Kuan Yew had warned that graduates were marrying late and having fewer children than the less educated.

A separate body, the Social Development Section (SDN), was created in 1985 for those with only secondary school qualifications. In 2009, both units were merged and renamed the Social Development Network to widen the dating pool and create more opportunities for singles to meet and eventually marry.

Li predicted FirstDate would be more successful than its predecessors. “The goals are the same as before, but SDU and SDN were event-based, which apparently didn’t attract too many people,” he said. “This time, a systematic dating app has been thoughtfully designed to create matches.”

Liu, however, said the initiatives were fundamentally different. FirstDate sprouted from a GovTech “hackathon”, she said, and should be best viewed as a government product trial that borrowed the agile and experimental approach of private tech.

She urged users to refrain from dismissing the platform because it was a government project.

“When others step in, whether the government or our own family members, it can feel orchestrated and ‘unromantic’,” she said. “However, if we look across history and in many parts of the world, relationships have often been arranged or brokered by families or communities.”

Daniel Goh, an associate professor of sociology at the National University of Singapore, agreed that it was premature to pass judgment on the platform since it was still in its pilot phase.

“I would be shocked if the government does not open the platform to citizens if it is proven successful,” he said. “The question is: what is the threshold for success?”

Other Asian countries, faced with a similarly dipping birth rate, have also tried to play Cupid. In 2024, Japan launched a government-backed dating app that required users to prove they were committed to marriage, verify their income and undergo an interview with the app operator.

As of June this year, 16,000 people had registered on the app, 760 couples were in “serious relationships” and 265 couples had tied the knot, according to Japanese government data.

Also in 2024, authorities in South Korea launched a dating programme for participants in Seoul to mingle through curated activities, such as outdoor dining by the Han River.

Some 126 couples were matched during that event, prompting the city government to roll-out the second edition last month, which was heavily oversubscribed with more than 2,300 singles aged 25 to 45 registering for just 100 slots.

According to a survey by pollster YouGov, one in four Singaporeans used dating apps in 2024, with Gen Zs and millennials more likely than older generations to have done so.

Out of those who have swiped for love online, 59 per cent used Tinder – making it the most popular platform – and 46 per cent took to Coffee Meets Bagel.

Civil servant Clare, meanwhile, is keeping her hopes up despite not finding a match after the first round of pairings concluded on FirstDate.

“I’m slightly bummed, but I’ll wait for the next cycle to start to try again.”

*Full name withheld at interviewee’s request

item.title: [SCMP] ‘A pack of lies’: Abby Choi’s mother rejects claims Kwong family repaid her debts
item.description:
The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has denied in court that she was repeatedly in debt because of gambling, calling her former son-in-law’s claim that he had financially supported her “a pack of lies”.

Cheung Yin-fa accused Alex Kwong Kong-chi on Monday of acting unscrupulously by demanding the return of HK$150,000 in shopping expenses she owed him, while failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million he had received from Choi for investment.

Wrapping up her five-day testimony in the High Court, Cheung also rejected the defence’s suggestion that she was so addicted to mahjong that Choi had to pledge a property she received as a wedding gift to secure a HK$4 million mortgage to repay her mother’s debts.
item.content:encoded:
The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has denied in court that she was repeatedly in debt because of gambling, calling her former son-in-law’s claim that he had financially supported her “a pack of lies”.

Cheung Yin-fa accused Alex Kwong Kong-chi on Monday of acting unscrupulously by demanding the return of HK$150,000 in shopping expenses she owed him, while failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million he had received from Choi for investment.

Wrapping up her five-day testimony in the High Court, Cheung also rejected the defence’s suggestion that she was so addicted to mahjong that Choi had to pledge a property she received as a wedding gift to secure a HK$4 million mortgage to repay her mother’s debts.

Cheung appeared emotional as she responded to the defence’s contention that Kwong, who said he had run a restaurant in mainland China and worked as a parallel betting agent in Macau, had helped repay her debts and supported her over the years.

“This Kwong family of brutes repaid my debts? Impossible,” she said. “How can he tell such a lie? Is he human? It’s all a pack of lies.”

She also denied ever receiving HK$7.5 million from Kwong through a luxury watch company, saying the money was simply a return of funds she had given him via a currency exchange shop.

Kwong, 31, is accused of conspiring with his father and elder brother to murder his ex-wife after parts of the 28-year-old’s dismembered remains, including her head and legs, were found at a flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village in February 2023.

He is standing trial on a joint murder charge alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35.

Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, has pleaded not guilty to preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body, while his two sons pleaded guilty to that charge before the trial.

Prosecutors argue the family feud stemmed from the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin. The father, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the luxury home and enlisted his two sons to help kill her so that he could keep it.

Under cross-examination, Alex Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, said his client did not oppose the sale and had been asked by Choi to persuade his father to sign a power of attorney allowing her to negotiate with prospective buyers.

Cheung reiterated that the entire Kwong family had been reluctant to sell the flat until she threatened legal action.

Raffell cited a series of text conversations that he said showed Alex Kwong had previously given his former mother-in-law more than HK$500,000.

Cheung rejected that interpretation, saying she owed Kwong only HK$150,000 for shopping expenses. She added that he had given her daughter HK$370,000 in profit from the sale of a car that his ex-wife had bought.

On her gambling habits, Cheung acknowledged that she occasionally visited mahjong parlours with friends and gambled up to HK$100,000 for “entertainment”, but stressed she had never run up debts so severe that debt collectors harassed her family.

Raffell suggested that Choi helped her mother clear her debts by taking out a second mortgage of up to HK$4 million from a high-rise property at the Manhattan Hill residential estate in Lai Chi Kok, which she received from the father of her partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, as a wedding gift.

The counsel noted that the white Toyota Alphard that Cheung had been using to travel to court in the present case was splashed with red paint in February this year, which he said was indicative of her financial difficulties.

Messaging records showed that Cheung complained to Detective Constable Ko Yan-ki, the chief investigating officer of the murder case, that she had been harassed by a woman she met in a mahjong parlour in Mong Kok over a monetary dispute she thought had been resolved seven years ago.

Raffell also highlighted text exchanges between Cheung and Choi, in which the witness acknowledged she would occasionally play mahjong “till daybreak” and that what she owed her daughter “cannot even be repaid in this life”.

Cheung dismissed Alex Kwong’s contention as smearing and stressed she did not have any outstanding debt. She also denied that her gratitude towards Choi was because she had repaid her gambling debts, saying she was simply thankful for her daughter’s support.

Raffell suggested that Alex Kwong had co-owned a restaurant in Guangzhou and knew an agent who sold Richard Mille watches in Macau.

Cheung admitted she had no direct knowledge of her former son-in-law’s income, apart from what Choi had told her about his failure to contribute to the support of their two children.

Separately, Raffell argued that his client had been angry with Cheung for calling police after Choi disappeared on February 21, 2023, despite knowing that he was wanted over his role in a HK$6.3 million theft case after jumping bail in 2015.

Cheung said she was unaware that authorities were still pursuing her former in-law. She reiterated that she believed the matter had been “settled” by Kwong Kau years before Choi’s killing.

During re-examination, prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC sought to counter the defence’s suggestion that Cheung’s family was not as wealthy as she had claimed. She asked Cheung to explain the jewellery and luxury items she had worn or brought to court during her week-long testimony.

They included a luxury watch set with diamonds and rubies, a pair of bracelets, a diamond necklace and a pair of earrings.

Cheung said the valuables – excluding the watch, which was a gift from Choi – were worth at least HK$1 million.

She added that the handbag she carried to court on Monday was worth about HK$50,000, while another Hermes Birkin bag she had previously brought to court had been bought by Alex Kwong for more than HK$100,000 using her money.

The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] From fishing boats to Michelin stars: Vietnam’s CoCo Dining turns the humble into haute cuisine
item.description:
“You know the phrase ‘fish out of water’? Well, that’s me in the city,” chef Vo Thanh Vuong laughs. “Now, I’m back on the water.”

It’s just past dawn; we’re on a fishing boat off the coast of Vung Tau, roughly 100km (62 miles) southeast of Vietnam’s largest city, Ho Chi Minh. Vung Tau is the port that supplies Ho Chi Minh City’s best restaurants, but by the fleet’s clock, it’s already late; most of the other vessels have already unloaded their catch. Vuong is showing me how to hold a fishing rod. His hands seem to know the motion better than his mind does.

Vuong grew up in Phan Thiet, about 160km (100 miles) north along the coast, where his family’s livelihood depended on what the South China Sea had to offer. Vung Tau is where his family’s boat went down in 2000, when he was 11 years old, 40km (25 miles) off its coast. Losing the watercraft cost them dearly, and suddenly, every pair of hands mattered – including his. Vuong was fishing full-time until he was 20, long enough to know the fishing life was not for him.
item.content:encoded:
“You know the phrase ‘fish out of water’? Well, that’s me in the city,” chef Vo Thanh Vuong laughs. “Now, I’m back on the water.”

It’s just past dawn; we’re on a fishing boat off the coast of Vung Tau, roughly 100km (62 miles) southeast of Vietnam’s largest city, Ho Chi Minh. Vung Tau is the port that supplies Ho Chi Minh City’s best restaurants, but by the fleet’s clock, it’s already late; most of the other vessels have already unloaded their catch. Vuong is showing me how to hold a fishing rod. His hands seem to know the motion better than his mind does.

Vuong grew up in Phan Thiet, about 160km (100 miles) north along the coast, where his family’s livelihood depended on what the South China Sea had to offer. Vung Tau is where his family’s boat went down in 2000, when he was 11 years old, 40km (25 miles) off its coast. Losing the watercraft cost them dearly, and suddenly, every pair of hands mattered – including his. Vuong was fishing full-time until he was 20, long enough to know the fishing life was not for him.

So, he left for Ho Chi Minh City, also known as Saigon.

Now, almost two decades later, he is back on the water – not because he has to be, but because he wants to be.

By mid-morning, we have caught almost nothing. Vuong shrugs. He tells me this is what most trips are like: long stretches of nothing punctuated by work. Because “the sea gave you very little entertainment, you learned to be comfortable with silence”.

Back on shore, we head to a local fish market in Vung Tau to pick up something for lunch. Everything is laid out at knee-height. Vuong moves through the displays like he’s reading a familiar book. He picks up a big fish with one hand and turns it over. He doesn’t wince or fidget the way many people do when handling something slippery and cold. He checks the gills, the eyes, the firmness and sets it back down – or keeps it, and moves on.

“When an ingredient is truly good, you don’t need to do much to it. Sometimes, the best thing a cook can do is step out of the way.”

In Vung Tau, he cooks a meal from the catch of the day. “Do you want to see the fisherman or the chef cook today,” he asks. He explains that the fisherman cooks fast, because at sea, speed is survival: you cook to eat and move on. But the chef cooks slower, because he has learned to enjoy the process – the prepping, the seasoning, the tasting, the small adjustments.

We tell him we want both. He laughs and gets to work.

His preparation is simple, and he hums as he cooks – the way he did as the youngest boy in his family, with two brothers and a sister. Several gas stoves are burning at once. He chops the garnishes with precision and seasons the braising liquid, gauging measurements by eye.

He steams a mix of flower crabs and three-spot swimming crabs with beer. He sets a hotpot going with tamarind, pineapple and tomato, and portions the cobia into chunks. He treats the oriental trumpeter whiting like a ceviche: sliced thin, cured in lime juice for 15 minutes, then tossed with a home-made sweet-spicy sauce, raw onion and herbs – the way he used to make it on the boats.

On those trips, food was whatever the sea and the hold allowed. Rice and instant noodles were the foundation, and they carried mam (fermented-seafood paste), nuoc mam (fish sauce), dried fish and squid, pickled vegetables, eggs and water. A good meal might be muc com – baby squid with its roe – with sour fish soup and pickles. “We would spend the whole day catching fish for other people,” he recalls. “At night, we’d sit together and argue about which fish was best for ourselves.”

Some nights, the swells were heavy enough that seawater splashed into their rice bowls; the rice would turn salty, but they would look at each other, laugh and keep eating. “You didn’t complain,” he says. “You were hungry, and you were at sea.”

And the night the power died and the charcoal got too wet to burn, they ate a freshly caught grouper raw on deck – bled, sliced thin, with wild lime and sea salt, similar to what he prepares for us.

He serves the food the way he always does: everyone else first, himself last. It’s what he calls a staff meal, the food he makes for his team at CoCo Dining – his one-Michelin-star Vietnamese restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City, opened in 2021 – after service.

What he has prepared for us today is not, by his own admission, the food that made his name – that food was French. When Vuong left fishing behind and enrolled in culinary school in Ho Chi Minh City, he didn’t go in with a plan. He had no kitchen training and no technique. He also had no language for what he was learning.

What he did have was nine years at sea. At the time, that felt like something to hide. “I didn’t want to expose my past,” he says, recalling his inexperience. “I had self-esteem issues.”

Vuong didn’t finish Grade 6 and, later, quit culinary school. He became a chef by observing the people around him, figuring things out along the way. He spent a decade training under French-Cambodian culinarian Sakal Phoeung and learned to cook in the French tradition.

In Vietnam, that still carries a particular weight: post-colonisation, French cuisine remains the benchmark for fine dining. For a Vietnamese chef with no pedigree, no formal training and a past aboard fishing boats, French haute cuisine was how Vuong proved he belonged.

“I simply didn’t see [Vietnamese cuisine] as something I needed to learn,” he recalls. “It was everyday food, so I didn’t think about it as a cuisine I could build a career around.”

So, Vuong learned to cook French, well enough to find success with it. For years, that was his identity in the kitchen. It even won him the first prize on the televised cooking competition Top Chef Vietnam in 2019. From 2021 to 2023, he was changing the menu at CoCo Dining twice a year, working mainly with modern gastronomy and fermentation. Eventually, he felt like he was running out of ideas.

One night, towards the end of 2023, he and Daniel Dang Hung Minh – CoCo Dining’s managing director – were drinking together, unwinding after another week of trying to solve a menu that wouldn’t come together. Vuong started cooking just for the two of them, preparing the kind of Vietnamese drinking food he would naturally make for himself. After tasting it, Dang said: “This tastes much more like you; this is where you’re strongest. Why don’t you just be honest with your cooking?”

Vuong resisted. He thought, “No, this can’t be the direction of a fine-dining restaurant.” He had spent years learning modern techniques and developing himself as a chef. Going back to familiar food almost felt like going backwards.

But what Dang had said stayed with him, so Vuong started experimenting secretly at home. “Maybe I had been trying too hard to become the chef I thought I was supposed to be,” he says, “instead of being honest about the chef I actually was.”

In 2024, CoCo Dining served a menu called Ra Khoi – meaning “to set sail” – but for Vuong, it signified “a return to the source”, as the first tasting menu he designed after deciding to lean into his fishing heritage. His first version of the menu pulled together fragments of memories: the mam muc (fermented-squid paste) he used to eat on the boat became stuffed baby squid with fermented-squid sauce. A wind-dried prawn reminded him of how his family preserved seafood, so he worked with tiger prawn. A simple crab salad became blue crab with mustard greens.

Never before had Vuong put his childhood on a plate on purpose. Last year, the restaurant earned its Michelin star. It turns out, the fisherman and the chef could coexist after all.

“I wasn’t sitting there thinking to myself, ‘I’m going to make a menu about my childhood.’ I was just following one memory into another, and suddenly, there was a menu,” he says.

Back in Ho Chi Minh City, Vuong brings out his oldest jar of mam chao (fermented fish) from the fermentation room at CoCo Dining. A whiff of it brings us back to the market of Vung Tau. The fermented fish is threadfin bream, sun-dried for five days in Phan Thiet by his family, who have been fishing and making mam for generations. At the restaurant, he and his team mix it with a starter made from sticky rice, layer it in a jar and seal it tightly. Usually, it’s ready after a month, but he lets his develop for at least two. “We learned not to waste anything,” he says. “Even the fish that wasn’t going to be sold had a purpose.”

Vuong believes his role is to bring the ingredients to life again: “In a museum, you put an artefact behind glass to stop it from changing. In my kitchen, the things I want to preserve are alive: they ferment, they age, they dry and they continue to change.”

It’s what makes his “archive” different from a museum’s. Recipes can be written down and “collected” and remain the same for generations, but his fermentations live and breathe. “You can’t treat each batch exactly the same,” he says. “You have to observe it, smell it, taste it and understand how it is developing.”

At CoCo Dining, Vuong balances the deep umami of his fermented seafood with ginger and other aromatics. In his signature dish, baby squid is stuffed with squid trimmings and pork, then glazed with a sauce made from squid ink and a spoonful of the mam muc. If diners are curious, he brings out a jar so they can taste the fermented-squid paste as it is.

“For me, that’s the heart of my ‘Living Archive’. If you put something in a box and never touch it, eventually, it becomes history. If you cook it, share it and pass it to someone else, it continues to live,” he explains.

His menu, Luu Tich (“Living Archive”), arrives at a moment when what deserves to be preserved and presented as part of Vietnamese culinary heritage is under debate. Vietnam is bidding to become the next global gastronomy hub, with a pitch built on “luxury” through authenticity rather than European-style fine dining. Vuong is cautious about the language. He has spent too long on the other side of the word “authentic” to trust it easily.

Real necessity informed those techniques, he says. “Coming from a fishing boat off Phan Thiet, the word ‘luxury’ felt very far from my life. But there was a lot of knowledge in those practices.”

“Vietnam doesn’t need to borrow someone else’s definition of luxury”

Vo Thanh Vuong

For him, that knowledge of salt, patience and time is its own form of wealth. “Vietnam doesn’t need to borrow someone else’s definition of luxury,” Vuong says. He thinks that luxury today can be the time and attention we give to something that was once simply part of daily life, “not taking something humble and making it expensive just because we put it on a fine-dining plate”.

But that doesn’t mean he cooks the same way his grandmother did. In Vuong’s eyes, French technique is merely another set of tools – just as sorting and scaling fish is part of a fisherman’s toolkit. Both, he says, come from the same place: trying to understand an ingredient and bring out the best in it.

But does that make a dish less Vietnamese?

“If authenticity means following a recipe strictly without any changes, maybe some will feel that what we do is not authentic enough,” he says. “I’m not trying to recreate the past exactly. A dish doesn’t become inauthentic because it evolves. It becomes inauthentic only when you lose sight of where it came from.”

If he were to curate a museum piece for people 100 years from now to understand where he came from, he would choose a thung leu, the wooden barrel used to make fish sauce in Phan Thiet. His grandfather used to make fish sauce at home, and the whole area of Phan Thiet, Vuong remembers, smelled like fish sauce. “Now, Phan Thiet is much more modern; that smell has mostly disappeared,” he says. “Not many households make fish sauce at home any more, so something that was once part of everyday life has become much less visible.”

In the museum, the label for the exhibit would read: “Thung Leu, Phan Thiet, Vietnam – a wooden vessel for making nuoc mam. For one boy from the coast, it was simply part of home. Inside it are fish, salt and time. Around it is the knowledge of generations who learned how to live with the sea.”

item.title: [SCMP] Kurt Campbell on US deterrence, the Quad, Aukus and Taiwan after Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
Kurt Campbell is a veteran US diplomat and strategist who has played a leading role in shaping Washington’s approach to China and the Indo-Pacific for more than a decade.

He served as the White House coordinator for Indo-Pacific affairs from 2021 to 2024 and as US deputy secretary of state from 2024 to 2025. Previously, he served as assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs from 2009 to 2013 and was a key architect of the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia”.

Often described as the Biden administration’s “Asia tsar”, Campbell also helped develop the Quad and the “small yard, high fence” approach to technology competition.
item.content:encoded:
Kurt Campbell is a veteran US diplomat and strategist who has played a leading role in shaping Washington’s approach to China and the Indo-Pacific for more than a decade.

He served as the White House coordinator for Indo-Pacific affairs from 2021 to 2024 and as US deputy secretary of state from 2024 to 2025. Previously, he served as assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs from 2009 to 2013 and was a key architect of the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia”.

Often described as the Biden administration’s “Asia tsar”, Campbell also helped develop the Quad and the “small yard, high fence” approach to technology competition.

A former US Navy officer, Harvard professor and co-founder of the Centre for a New American Security, he is now chairman and co-founder of The Asia Group, a Washington-based strategic advisory firm.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

You once argued that America’s enduring advantage over China was “allied scale” rather than unilateral dominance. But China’s strategy today looks different from the one Washington confronted in 2021. China now presents itself as a champion of sovereignty, non-interference and a more “multipolar” order while expanding its diplomatic and security presence. Is this a genuine strategic shift or a new form of competition expressed in different language? What is the realistic objective of US policy towards China today?

I think it is the determination of both leaders to take steps to stabilise a complex dynamic relationship between the two countries.

Both leaders understand that at the current moment, it is in the best interests of both countries to get along strategically. There are a variety of reasons for that. Some of them rest in a desire to improve competitive advantage. And some are motivated by a desire to genuinely work together.

My own sense is that the US is most effective as a global power when it works constructively with its allies and partners. President [Donald] Trump has taken more time and put more focus on building a stronger relationship with China than he has on working with some of his allies and partners. I very much support efforts to stabilise US-China relations. But I would like to see President Trump make more effort to stabilise relations with other partners. For instance, what we’re seeing in relations with Canada is quite shocking, suggesting that Canada is no longer one of the closest friends and partners to the US.

I find the fact that Canada is seeking to join the EU quite troubling. My general argument would be that US technology strategy, US efforts to sustain the global order are best achieved not just by trying to stabilise the US-China relationship, but by also seeking to maintain a strong posture with allies and partners.

So what is the realistic objective for US policy towards China?

There are a number of things that are necessary for US-China relations as we head into the next critical phase. I personally believe that the path to true cooperation between the United States and China on AI is very complicated, especially since President Trump said he seeks a dialogue with China but insists on dominance.

That message is a complicated one for Chinese friends to hear. It probably is a disincentive to seek true collaboration, because it suggests that the terms are implicitly or explicitly negative for China. What I think is important going forward is that both countries understand clearly the risks of frontier work, especially when researchers on both sides are increasingly voicing concerns about AI that we don’t fully understand or comprehend.

It is important that both the United States and China recognise that racing for advantage in a technological space that holds such potential risk – as well as promise – raises concerns. I would commend the work that the two countries have taken to date to at least find a degree of common ground for a continuing dialogue. But I will also say that this issue is developing rapidly, and both sides are going to need to adapt their position to establish a true dialogue around potential areas of collaboration, on safety reporting and mutual engagement.

The question for many of us is what is the appropriate metaphor when we think about AI. Is it nuclear weapons? Is it Covid? Is it climate change? Are there other experiences historically that we can utilise and apply to this new technology in the US-China context?

I think the one thing that is unique here is the role of the labs. These are not just technological capacities. They are the most powerful economic and commercial players of modern times. They are absolutely dominant. So they will want a voice in any deliberation between the United States and China. We don’t have as many experiences in the past in which it’s not just government to government, but the most powerful commercial and technological voices as well.

So are you particularly concerned about AI competition between China and the US?

In the larger context, I am worried about AI writ large. I believe that the politics of AI in the United States are becoming increasingly complicated. There is a bipartisan anxiety about data centres and their development. You’re seeing many states now questioning the buildout of these large entities. There are questions about capital use. There is an incredible level of investment in AI that has taken investment from other areas. In fact, many believe that to the extent that we have economic growth in the United States currently, it is largely because of the investment in AI. But I think more directly, it is undeniable when the most senior people in various companies are calling for government intervention and restraint that alerts us that there is a problem here.

Every week there is a new story of an AI entity that has escaped captivity and gone on an excursion, often creating havoc. There are also stories of engineers choosing to resign from these prestigious posts because they are worried not just about an incident but the status of humankind. Many very senior people have worried about human extinction.

It seems to me that if that is a truly serious matter and debated among engineers and designers of AI, it is incumbent on us to reflect, to think about guardrails, to consider safety and to understand that there are existential issues here that in many respects transcend simple competition.

Let’s talk about Taiwan and Japan. Does strategic ambiguity remain the best policy or have China’s military capabilities and pressure campaigns made greater clarity necessary?

I still believe that one of the great success stories of US-China relations – this is rarely discussed – is the complex maintenance of peace and stability between the two countries with respect to Taiwan.

There have been lots of tensions and disappointments, but the truth is the status quo has served the interests of the people of Taiwan. I would argue the framework that the United States and China have maintained for decades is being increasingly tested by military and political developments. But I still believe that this framework is in the best interests of all concerned. And so it is often said that we have a degree of strategic ambiguity but tactical clarity; I think that it is important for the United States to underscore our determination to maintain peace and stability.

But it is also the case that a dialogue over Taiwan is handled carefully between the two leaders. It’s undeniable that this issue has come up and that it is being actively discussed.

If Beijing imposed a quarantine or blockade without launching a conventional attack, would that trigger a US response?

I’m out of government now. I’m not really in the business of offering views on particular scenarios. My own sense is that the more we discuss openly potential scenarios, the less it might be stabilising to the situation. If anything, they tend to draw sharp contours in a complex environment. And, in many respects, create even greater distrust.

My own sense is that the United States should maintain a strong unofficial relationship with Taiwan, recognise how critical this issue is in a larger US-China relationship and manage this with care and dexterity.

Despite the ups and downs, history reflects that it is possible to take the necessary steps to maintain peace and stability. And I fully expect that this can continue.

On Taiwan, what is the strategic cost of treating arms sales to Taiwan as negotiable within the broader US-China relationship? Is there any practical form of Taiwan-related cooperation that Washington and Beijing could undertake? What would a credible cross-strait dialogue look like if Beijing continues to reject engagement with Taiwan’s current government?

The strategic risk of treating arms sales to Taiwan as negotiable is that it can inject doubt into the credibility that has helped preserve cross-strait stability for decades. While there are deep differences over Taiwan, both Washington and Beijing have a common interest in crisis management, military-to-military communications and reducing the risk of unintended escalation.

Given the tensions between China and Japan, what responsibility does Washington have to ensure that the US-Japan alliance remains a mechanism for deterrence rather than escalation? Is Japan primarily becoming a frontline deterrent, an industrial and technological partner or a military coequal?

I would simply say that Japan is an important partner of the United States. It has a relatively small military and its defence investments are quite modest. I believe that one of the most critical paths of diplomacy in Asia is to make sure that lines of communication between Beijing and Tokyo are open.

My own sense is that the Japanese would prefer to have a more open dialogue with Beijing. I think one of the issues occasionally challenging is that the historical issues still animate Beijing’s thinking about Japan.

One of the things that I’ve noted is the effectiveness of Chinese diplomacy generally, their ability to reach out to countries in which they have a complex history. In particular, what we’ve seen is renewed diplomacy between China and India. I think it would be in China’s interests to open up more lines of communication with Tokyo. I do not believe that Japan is somehow an American cat’s paw. The people of Japan are deeply peace-loving. Efforts to revise the constitution or to move Japan in a more assertive direction have actually met with substantial domestic opposition.

I think some of the military modernisation in Japan is indeed modest. It is designed to reflect increasing challenges in the Indo-Pacific. And remember, those do not come exclusively in the US or in the Japan-China relationship.

What Japan is confronting is an increasingly hostile North Korea that is well armed and has nuclear capabilities. So Japan is seeking to play a larger role in Asia. I support that. But at the same time, I do believe there have been periods in the past where the lines of communication between Tokyo and Beijing have been much stronger. I do know that the Japanese are troubled by how difficult it has been to establish communication with Beijing. And I think just as President Trump and President Xi [Jinping] have found some common purpose and would meet in a complex time, I think President Xi and Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi can find the political courage to sit down as well.

China increasingly portrays this sort of alliance – whether it’s with Japan, or trilateral cooperation with South Korea and Japan, or quadrilateral with India, Australia and Japan – as an instrument of containment. Given China’s thinking, how should Washington support their expanded security role while assuring China that these alliances are defensive?

The US seeking closer relations between Japan and South Korea has more to do with their own histories than it does with China. I would simply remind Chinese friends that not every development in Asia is about China: South Korea and Japan have profound historical tensions, but they are close allies of the United States. It is only natural that the United States would seek the two countries to coordinate more closely. Each country has its own unique relationship with China. It is also the case that closer coordination among the three could have a stabilising impact across the Indo-Pacific. The Quad has not met at the leader level under President Trump, but its first incarnation in the early 2000s was a result of the tragedy that struck Indonesia and Malaysia. The terrible tsunami.

I myself had been actively engaged in the Quad. Much of what the Quad was involved with in its most recent incarnation was Covid vaccine development and South Pacific issues related to education and training.

I would say that the Quad was primarily about delivering well-being to underserved groups and creating more capacity. I don’t believe that any country in the Quad would support the institution becoming an alliance aimed at any one country. I see it mostly as developing common approaches to complex societal and security problems. These are four maritime democracies and each again has its own set of relationships.

With Beijing, more recently, we are seeing India and China edging closer to a more substantial dialogue. I think the Quad can exist with a range of diplomatic formations in Asia. As much as anything, it helps anchor the United States in the Indo-Pacific, which is in the strategic interests of Washington.

Should the Quad become more institutionalised? Or would that make it less flexible and more threatening to China? How vulnerable is it to domestic political changes in these four member states?

I cannot speak to what’s expected next in the Trump administration, but there has been no discussion recently of reconvening the Quad at the leader level. I think without that, it’s difficult to sustain active forward momentum. I do not know what President Trump’s ambitions are for the Quad besides the foreign ministry meetings and a variety of other assessments. But I think at this juncture, there is no push or intention towards institutionalisation. If anything, the focus continues to be on areas which are primarily about the well-being, for instance, of Pacific island nations. One of the areas of cooperation in the past, for instance, was on dealing with illegal fishing in the Pacific, which is an issue that Pacific island nations care deeply about and do not have the capacity to address.

So I do not see the institution emerging as a direct vehicle for somehow containing China. And I just think that framework is outmoded. China is a great, powerful country with deep interests across the world. It’s not possible to contain China and the most recent work towards this coming summit between the United States and China brings that point home. China is a country that needs to be engaged actively. It is not possible to think about China in the context of containment.

Would a reduced US-China rivalry lessen the importance of security partnerships such as the Quad, Aukus and other minilateral groupings? If so, what implications would that have for the balance of power, deterrence and Indo-Pacific stability?

Partnerships like the Quad and Aukus are valuable because countries across the Indo-Pacific recognise that many of the region’s challenges, from maritime security and technological change to supply chain resilience and disaster response, require closer cooperation. The value of these partnerships does not depend on the status of the US-China relationship.

Even in a period of more stable US-China relations, these partnerships would continue to play a critical role in strengthening deterrence, building collective capacity and fostering a regional balance that supports peace and prosperity. In many respects, the greatest contribution of a grouping like the Quad is the creation of habits of cooperation, strategic trust and practical capabilities.

What would the durable regional security architecture look like if it included China rather than being organised against China? Is it possible to have such a thing?

We’ve had a number of efforts at regional security or regional dialogue, such as the East Asia Summit, the Asean Regional Forum, which have been established for decades.

One of the challenges has been the uneven participation of the United States. We don’t attend all of the meetings. In fact, I think you’ve seen, particularly in the Trump administration, an ambivalence about regional institutions. We’ve long sought to create capacities for more dialogue and cooperation among Indo-Pacific actors. We’ve seen that at Apec. We’ve seen that at the Asean Regional Forum and in the East Asia Summit. I would go as far as to say that, by some measurements, nine of the 20 members in G20 are Indo-Pacific nations. In many respects that institutional innovation was designed to reflect the increasing importance, not just of China but of other rising nations in the Indo-Pacific.

I would like to see the United States more actively engaged in that multilateral diplomacy. I do not think it is a secret that the United States is less interested and focused on that diplomacy and seeks, in many respects, to act unilaterally without constraints with other countries. I do not believe that is in America’s strategic interests. I think investing in regional architecture is important and a critical dimension of our national power.

What’s your take on the US changing the name of INDOPACOM to USPACOM?

It was Trump’s first administration that originally changed it to Indo-Pacific. And now they’re changing it back. I don’t know if that is a desire to return to an earlier period framework. At first, the Indo-Pacific framework was adopted by Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, and that framework was accepted by parts of the Trump administration. When President [Joe] Biden came to power, the Japanese asked for that framework to be continued. We supported that. I do not know if this is a request from President Xi to President Trump, or whether this is a rethinking by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. There are too many things that have happened in terms of Pentagon policy to speculate about why they move in one direction or another.

How can Washington reassure its Asian allies and Southeast Asian countries that its partnerships do not force them to choose between the US and China? Is the current alliance-centred strategy sufficiently attentive to Asean priorities?

The most important dimension here is for the United States to invest actively in regional institutions and bilateral engagements. Most of the frameworks of engagement that we have seen most recently have been around highly difficult trade relations with a variety of countries in Southeast Asia. I increasingly hear from a variety of Southeast Asian countries that they are adopting policies that allow them to maintain a degree of flexibility in engagement with both Washington and Beijing.

The most effective US policy does not demand countries to make some sort of overt choice between the two.

And there is a deep recognition that commercial and political ties between Beijing and Southeast Asia are only natural, as is the United States maintaining close ties in Southeast Asia. These are not zero-sum relationships. They can be mutually beneficial.

What do you think is Hong Kong’s role in Sino-US relations? And how should the city move forward?

It’s a complex city. It’s undeniable. It is, in many respects, a financial launching point for China’s relations with the world. It still has some characteristics of its past, but it is increasingly a Chinese city that has an extraordinarily critical and important role in the global economy.

And as far as I can tell, it appears to continue to play a very dynamic role in the global financial economy. And it is continuing to be a meeting place between East and West and the financial centre of activities across the Indo-Pacific. There are other capitals that are emerging in that equation: Singapore, Tokyo and the like. But Hong Kong continues to play a vital role.

item.title: [SCMP] From Abby Choi to the ‘Hello Kitty’ killing: Hong Kong’s most shocking crimes
item.description:
The alleged murder and dismemberment of Abby Choi Tin-fung in 2023, which prosecutors say was linked to a dispute over a luxury flat, has once again gripped Hong Kong as the trial over the 28-year-old socialite’s death entered its second week.

Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, have pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of her body. Their father, Kwong Kau, 68, has pleaded not guilty to the same charge. All three men deny murdering Choi.

While Hong Kong has a reputation as one of the world’s safest cities, it has seen its share of sensational and gruesome crimes.
item.content:encoded:
The alleged murder and dismemberment of Abby Choi Tin-fung in 2023, which prosecutors say was linked to a dispute over a luxury flat, has once again gripped Hong Kong as the trial over the 28-year-old socialite’s death entered its second week.

Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, have pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of her body. Their father, Kwong Kau, 68, has pleaded not guilty to the same charge. All three men deny murdering Choi.

While Hong Kong has a reputation as one of the world’s safest cities, it has seen its share of sensational and gruesome crimes.

1. Plaza Hollywood stabbings (2023)

Just months after Choi’s alleged murder, two women were stabbed to death in a frenzied knife attack at the Plaza Hollywood shopping centre in Diamond Hill by a man suffering from severe mental illness.

News of the unprovoked attack, captured on CCTV, spread widely online and heightened safety concerns at a time when the city was still recovering from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Szeto Sing-kwong, 43, a former warehouse worker, wandered through the shopping centre with an unsheathed knife he had just bought before encountering Fong Hiu-tung, 26, and Lau Kai-hei, 22, outside a Sasa cosmetics shop.

CCTV footage showed Szeto repeatedly stabbing one of the women in an attack lasting nearly a minute. The second woman tried repeatedly to intervene but was herself slashed and stabbed.

Fong sustained 27 knife wounds and Lau eight, according to medical evidence. Both died from blood loss and respiratory failure.

Szeto later pleaded guilty to two counts of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility, after prosecutors accepted that an acute relapse of paranoid schizophrenia meant he should not be held liable for murder.

Last month, the High Court ordered him to receive indefinite mandatory psychiatric treatment and supervision at Siu Lam Psychiatric Centre in Tuen Mun, noting that he continued to show limited insight into his condition.

2. British banker turned double murderer (2014)

British banker Rurik Jutting tortured and killed two Indonesian women in his Wan Chai flat between October and November 2014.

Jutting tortured 23-year-old Sumarti Ningsih for three days, subjecting her to what the court described as increasingly cruel violence using a belt, sex toys, pliers and his fists, before slitting her throat on or about October 27. Her body was later found in a large black suitcase.

Five days later, he took 26-year-old Seneng Mujiasih, also known as Jesse Lorena Ruri, back to his flat and cut her throat.

It was reported that his murder spree was triggered by the break-up with his fiancée.

Jutting was sentenced to life imprisonment for two counts of murder in 2016. He later appealed to the Court of Final Appeal, which dismissed his final attempt after just eight minutes.

3. Son’s gruesome slaughter of parents (2013)

Henry Chau Hoi-leung, then 29, killed his parents in a rented flat in Tai Kok Tsui and placed their dismembered heads in a refrigerator.

Chau had planned to murder his father, Chau Wing-ki, 65, and mother, Siu Yuet-yee, 63, for six months. He told the court he hated his parents and blamed them for his failures in life and love.

He killed and dismembered the couple at a flat belonging to his friend, Angus Tse Chun-kei. Tse said Chau had threatened to harm his own mother, prompting him to help pack and dispose of some body parts at sea.

Chau was caught after sending text messages confessing to the killings, having earlier filed a missing persons report and made an online appeal for help finding his parents.

Forensic officers believed some of the couple’s body parts had been cooked, microwaved and salted. Others were decomposing when found.

In 2015, Chau was convicted of two counts of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. Tse was sentenced to one year in prison for preventing the lawful burial of bodies.

The case inspired the 2022 film The Sparring Partner.

4. The ‘Hello Kitty’ case (1999)

In one of Hong Kong’s most horrifying cases, 23-year-old nightclub hostess Fan Man-yee was kidnapped and tortured by three triad members before her death. Her head was later placed inside a Hello Kitty doll.

Fan was abducted and held in a flat in Granville Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, after the men accused her of stealing HK$4,000 (US$510) from one of their wallets.

She was held for nearly a month in the flat, which was filled with Hello Kitty toys. The attackers, believed to have been under the influence of drugs, were suspected of torturing her in the days before her death.

After she died, the men dismembered her body, boiled the flesh to conceal the smell of decomposition and discarded other remains. They kept her skull and sewed it into the head of a large Hello Kitty toy.

The case came to light when a 13-year-old girl told police she had been having nightmares and felt “haunted” by a ghost. She was the girlfriend of one of the three killers and had occasionally joined them in assaulting Fan.

In exchange for immunity, she testified against the men, who were convicted of manslaughter. Because only Fan’s skull, a tooth and some internal organs were recovered, the court heard there was insufficient evidence to determine whether she had been murdered or died from another cause, such as a drug overdose.

The three men were sentenced in 2000 to life imprisonment for manslaughter, false imprisonment and preventing Fan’s lawful burial. One had his sentence reduced to 18 years after a retrial.

5. The ‘Rainy Night Butcher’ serial killings (1982)

Perhaps Hong Kong’s most infamous serial killer, night-shift taxi driver Lam Kor-wan murdered four women in the 1980s after picking them up as passengers on rainy evenings.

He drove them to secluded locations, strangled them with wires, photographed their bodies, dismembered them and preserved body parts in containers at his home.

Lam was arrested in 1982 after attempting to develop photographs of his victims at a Kodak shop in Mong Kok. The shop manager alerted police, who ambushed Lam when he returned to collect the pictures.

Although the photographs suggested there may have been more victims, Lam was ultimately charged with the murders of four women police were able to identify.

The court heard that he had eaten part of one victim’s intestine and, according to evidence, including photographs and videos, engaged in necrophilia.

Lam was sentenced to death, but the sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment.

item.title: [SCMP] A fortune, a HK$72m flat and a family feud: inside the Abby Choi murder trial
item.description:
A bitter family dispute over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat allegedly led a retired police officer and his two sons to murder socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung three years ago, a Hong Kong court has heard.

The trial over the 28-year-old model’s killing, which shocked Hong Kong and attracted international attention, started after a one-week delay caused by unresolved preliminary issues and jury selection.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, told the High Court how her relationship with her daughter’s former in-laws deteriorated, accusing them of clinging to her family’s fortune and having “bitten the hand that fed them”.
item.content:encoded:
A bitter family dispute over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat allegedly led a retired police officer and his two sons to murder socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung three years ago, a Hong Kong court has heard.

The trial over the 28-year-old model’s killing, which shocked Hong Kong and attracted international attention, started after a one-week delay caused by unresolved preliminary issues and jury selection.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, told the High Court how her relationship with her daughter’s former in-laws deteriorated, accusing them of clinging to her family’s fortune and having “bitten the hand that fed them”.

Giving evidence for the prosecution, Cheung became emotional at times as she accused Choi’s former in-laws of living in luxury without contributing to the upbringing of the two children her daughter had with her ex-husband.

She wept in the witness box while watching footage of her daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat on February 21, 2023, the day she was last seen alive.

“My daughter was a really good daughter, a really filial daughter,” Cheung said tearfully. “She trusted and gave her kindness to the wrong people. This family really bit the hand that fed them.”

Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial after pleading not guilty to murdering her.

Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial.

The killing came to light after some of Choi’s dismembered remains were discovered in a 600 square foot flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village on February 24, 2023.

Inside, police found a hammer – the alleged murder weapon – a meat mincer, two cooking pots containing Choi’s remains, and multiple saws and knives.

The prosecution alleges that the killing stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s attempts to sell it and enlisted his sons to help kill her so he could keep it.

Prosecutors have described the alleged murder as a carefully crafted plot in which each defendant played a role. It allegedly involved renting the village flat, driving Choi to the remote location on the pretext of collecting her daughter from school, and striking her with a hammer during the journey.

Prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC suggested that money was the motive and highlighted the significant wealth gap between the two families.

Choi’s stepfather, Choi Cho-san, was described as a wealthy businessman who provided a monthly allowance of more than HK$1 million to support his wife, Cheung, Choi and the model’s two stepsisters in Hong Kong.

The court heard that Choi received a HK$41 million flat as a wedding gift from the father of her partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, who also came from a wealthy family, although the couple never formally registered their marriage. She was also said to have received more than HK$300 million from the Tam family over the years.

The Kwong family, according to the prosecution, was far less affluent. Kwong Kau’s wife, Jenny Li Sui-heung, and their two sons were said to be unemployed, while he relied on an annual pension of HK$145,000 after retiring from the police force in 2006.

The court also heard that Kwong Kau had worked as a taxi driver, although his lawyer disputed this.

Cheung testified that her daughter had registered the Kadooria flat in Kwong Kau’s name to avoid HK$9 million in double stamp duty, with the understanding that he would hold it on trust for the two children she had with Alex Kwong.

But when Choi indicated in June 2022 that she wanted to sell the flat and move the children closer to their school in Tuen Mun, Kwong Kau allegedly attacked her and threatened to kill her and her entire family if she went ahead.

In a series of audio messages to her mother in October and November 2022, Choi complained that her former in-laws were ungrateful despite her having supported their lavish lifestyle for years. She also expressed regret at having registered a property in Hainan province and a Rolls-Royce in her former father-in-law’s name.

Cheung said she and her daughter had supported the Kwong family for years but received nothing in return.

She told the court that Alex Kwong had obtained more than HK$70 million from his ex-wife after saying he would invest the money in luxury watches. He also persuaded Choi to lend him her credit card to pay his living expenses in mainland China while he was evading justice over his involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case, Cheung said.

Anthony Kwong received HK$2 million from Choi to run an egg waffle shop in Sham Shui Po, according to Cheung. He became Choi’s stand-in chauffeur in early 2023 after he and his mother repeatedly urged her to give him a job, the witness added.

The court also heard that Choi gave Kwong Kau a monthly allowance of HK$20,000 and paid more than HK$200,000 towards his medical expenses when he was seriously ill.

During cross-examination, defence lawyers challenged Cheung’s account of their clients’ financial dependence on Choi.

Anthony Kwong’s lawyer, Trevor Beel, said his client had never received substantial financial support from Choi. He said the egg waffle shop had been set up at her request because her two children loved the snack.

Oliver Davies, representing Kwong Kau, described his client as a businessman with considerable savings who had contributed half of the Kadooria flat’s HK$60 million purchase price in 2019.

He challenged Cheung’s account of her husband’s wealth, arguing that Choi Cho-san was “constantly in debt” and could not have afforded to give her HK$1 million a month.

Davies also pointed to the limited assets Choi left behind, suggesting that she was not particularly wealthy either.

Cheung will face further cross-examination by Alex Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, when the trial resumes on Monday.

item.title: [SCMP] China agrees to slash EU hybrid car exports in half, putting brake on trade war
item.description:
The European Union and China have “reached an understanding” that will cut Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc by “more than a half”, in a temporary salve to trade tensions that have threatened to boil over into a full-blown trade war.

Speaking after marathon trade talks in Beijing, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said the deal would see China slash its hybrid car exports “by several million cars” over a four-year period.

“This is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tensions, and I very much appreciate that,” Sefcovic told reporters in the Chinese capital.
item.content:encoded:
The European Union and China have “reached an understanding” that will cut Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc by “more than a half”, in a temporary salve to trade tensions that have threatened to boil over into a full-blown trade war.

Speaking after marathon trade talks in Beijing, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said the deal would see China slash its hybrid car exports “by several million cars” over a four-year period.

“This is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tensions, and I very much appreciate that,” Sefcovic told reporters in the Chinese capital.

The sides also agreed to expedite EU applications for rare earth mineral export licences and improve market access for goods including car parts, olive oil and textiles, which Sefcovic said could be worth “almost €4 billion” (US$4.5 billion) in current export value.

Beijing said it had received assurances that the EU and its members would “facilitate specific priority licences to China among dual-use sectors”, without naming the industries in question.

The parties agreed to give advance warning of export controls, “improve the transparency of listing and delisting procedures” and work towards delisting companies that have been named.

The latter is significant as powerful EU members are considering a new weapon that could instantly exclude firms from the single market.

Brussels said its incoming inverter ban was not aimed at any particular country, despite EU officials confirming it was intended to wind down a heavy dependence on China.

The Chinese commerce ministry described the talks as “equal, professional and constructive”, but Commerce Minister Wang Wentao made it clear that he was not happy with the EU’s newly assertive stance, expressing “concern over the recent trade and economic restrictions imposed by the EU”.

He added that “China is not the root cause of the EU’s problems, but rather a partner in resolving them”.

The ministry added that Wang had “urged the EU to work with China to properly handle frictions and differences through dialogue and consultation”.

For Beijing, however, the big prize could be preserving the status quo as far as possible, given the economic importance of exports and the closure of the US market to many Chinese goods.

“Judging from the details released by the EU, China appears to have made significant concessions on several issues. Whether these concessions will lead to corresponding adjustments by the EU on trade restrictions and market access remains to be seen over the coming months,” a commentary published by Geopolitechs, a website specialising in Chinese policymaking, said.

Sefcovic, meanwhile, said EU national leaders would decide next week whether China’s concessions were enough, but downplayed the likelihood of an all-out tariff war.

“It’s very easy to declare a trade war or any war, but it’s very difficult to stop it,” he said. “So therefore, I put so much emphasis on negotiations, and I’m glad that today I can present to you the outcome.”

Sefcovic declined to share further detail on the arrangement on hybrid cars – shipments of which have ballooned in recent months – but hinted that it could follow a recent import curb the bloc placed on Chinese steel.

“There are different techniques,” he said. “If you look in recent couple of months, I think you would find the answer.”

A source briefed on the talks suggested that it would be a safeguard measure, by which the EU is able to place quotas and tariffs to urgently curb import surges.

This is far from the end. It is a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing

Maros Sefcovic, European commissioner for trade

Earlier in the week, EU sources had explained that the bloc was seeking a “proof of concept” deal in a single sector – hybrid cars – which would be seen as a test of whether Beijing was negotiating in good faith.

A joint statement by the two sides, published following two days of negotiations, said that talks would continue over reducing tariffs and creating minimum price deals that would allow Chinese electric vehicles to enter the EU market at a lower duty rate.

The 16-point agreement listed a series of deliverables from the latest round of talks, with the two sides set to meet for further discussions in March next year. Most of these centred on further talks over long-standing trade disputes, including over medical equipment and power inverters.

Sefcovic – who met with Wang and Vice-Premier He Lifeng – had been pressing Beijing to cap exports of hybrid vehicles, as a recent surge in shipments to Europe had led to fears within the bloc that its car industry could be hollowed out.

“We never had the level of intensity of our exchanges and contacts as we have [had] over the last three to four months with our Chinese counterparts,” Sefcovic said. “I want to say that this was done in good faith, and this is the result of very intense work.”
