But he cautioned that the outcomes laid out in the joint statement would not be enough by themselves to reduce tensions between the two sides.

“I often say that genuine negotiations deserve a real try. Therefore, I appreciate my counterparts’ engagement. Having said that, this is far from the end. It is a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing,” Sefcovic said.

“As President von der Leyen has said, dialogue needs results, and where the dialogue cannot deliver, the EU will use its tools to ensure rebalancing.”

The latest talks came amid rising tensions between China and the EU over a range of trade issues, with calls growing in Europe for Brussels to take firmer action to curtail a surge in Chinese exports to the bloc.

Next week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will brief EU national leaders on the results of the talks with Beijing, as the European Commission seeks instruction on how to respond to what is now widely described in Europe as a “China shock 2.0”.

Member states have been coalescing around a tougher approach, shown by a joint paper from the governments of France and Germany – leaked on Monday – which called for a weapon to cut countries or firms perceived to be cheating on trade out of the EU market almost instantly.

The commission is then likely to present a series of new trade tools before the end of the year. It was also expected to launch a flurry of investigations aimed at quickly curbing Chinese imports in sectors including chemicals, plastics and automotive, though it remained unclear on Friday whether the progress in Beijing would alter those plans.

Businesses responded positively to the Beijing talks.

The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU (CCCEU) welcomed the “pragmatic outcomes”, saying they showed both sides’ “willingness to handle trade frictions and stabilise bilateral trade relations through dialogue”.

The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association said “this announcement is a positive step in easing trade tensions between the two” sides.

Pascal Canfin, a lawmaker who manages the China file in the European Parliament’s trade committee, told the South China Morning Post that the hybrid deal was “a very first step towards rebalancing our trade relationship”.

“But while dialogue has delivered a first result today, we are under no illusion: the imbalance is systemic,” Canfin said. “We will therefore have to go further, and we must of course not give up on using our trade defence instruments to safeguard our economic security.”

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese brokers work to crack the final code: win clients on global stage
item.description:
China’s investment banks spent decades trying to emulate Goldman Sachs, the Wall Street powerhouse that became a benchmark for the country’s financial ambitions and whose alumni included senior US policymakers like former Treasury secretary Henry Paulson.

Today, Beijing’s goal has evolved beyond building a Chinese version of Goldman.

At the Central Financial Work Conference in 2023, President Xi Jinping called for cultivating first-class investment institutions as part of China’s ambition to become a financial superpower with distinct Chinese characteristics.
item.content:encoded:
China’s investment banks spent decades trying to emulate Goldman Sachs, the Wall Street powerhouse that became a benchmark for the country’s financial ambitions and whose alumni included senior US policymakers like former Treasury secretary Henry Paulson.

Today, Beijing’s goal has evolved beyond building a Chinese version of Goldman.

At the Central Financial Work Conference in 2023, President Xi Jinping called for cultivating first-class investment institutions as part of China’s ambition to become a financial superpower with distinct Chinese characteristics.

Many analysts and industry players believe the foundations are already in place. China now operates the world’s second-largest capital market after the US, while direct financing through stocks and bonds for the first time surpassed bank lending in 2025, ushering in a golden era for securities firms, they said.

The next challenge lies beyond mainland China. As Hong Kong’s role in China’s capital markets expands and mainland companies invest more aggressively overseas, Chinese brokerages are increasingly pushing into international markets.

“Overseas business, particularly in Hong Kong, is one of the key growth drivers for Chinese securities companies as they expand beyond their home market,” said Franco Lam, a director at Fitch Ratings.

From apprentice to contender

Compared with Wall Street and the City of London, China’s capital markets have a relatively short history.

When China International Capital Corporation (CICC) was established in 1995 as the country’s first Sino-foreign joint-venture investment bank, its ambitions were global from the outset. Yet its bankers had little experience to draw on.

Fang Fenglei, one of CICC’s founding executives, in an article published in 2018 in China Securities Journal, recalled how Morgan Stanley, one of the venture’s founding shareholders, arranged study visits for him to New York and London to learn the operations of Western financial markets, as part of what he described as a journey to “learn from the West”.

The learning curve was steep. Paulson said in his book, Dealing with China, that Goldman Sachs bankers gave CICC executives and Chinese officials what amounted to a crash course in taking companies public as they prepared China Mobile’s predecessor for its Hong Kong and New York listing in 1997.

The deal raised US$4.2 billion, offering an early glimpse of how quickly the gap between Chinese and Western investment banks could narrow.

At the time, the relationship between Chinese and foreign investment banks was heavily tilted in favour of Wall Street, whose firms brought technical expertise and access to international institutional investors that Chinese brokerages lacked.

Over the following two decades, Chinese securities firms moved beyond simply learning the mechanics of international investment banking to acquiring the networks and capabilities needed to compete overseas.

A first-class investment bank should not merely be large, but should have a voice in global capital allocation and asset pricing while attracting top financial talent

Wu Qing, China Securities Regulatory Commission

Citic Securities took a major step in 2013 by acquiring brokerage CLSA from French bank Credit Agricole, gaining an established research, sales and trading platform spanning major global financial centres. More than a decade later, the group is increasingly adopting the Citic Securities International, or CSI, identity across its global operations as it gradually phases out the CLSA brand.

Industry veterans liken the transition to one from apprentice to competitor.

Wang Junhong, deputy CEO of Guotai Junan International, where he has worked since 2012, said Chinese brokerages spent their early overseas years as “apprentices”, often playing secondary roles on deals led by foreign banks.

But as Chinese bankers accumulated experience and recruited internationally trained talent, they progressed from taking part in underwriting syndicates to leading them, Wang said.

“You go from being a participant in the underwriting syndicate to becoming the lead underwriter,” Wang said in a recent interview with the South China Morning Post. “The apprentice graduates. You become capable of standing on your own, and in some businesses you may even do better.”

Today, Chinese investment banks were “at least on an equal footing” with their Western rivals in much of Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market, and led in some areas, Wang said.

The rise of Chinese companies had also changed the equation, he said. As mainland businesses grew larger and more familiar to global investors, Chinese brokerages’ understanding of their home market became increasingly valuable. At the same time, the growth of mainland institutional investors and private wealth had created a much deeper pool of Chinese capital to support offshore transactions, Wang added.

Beijing’s push for global champions

Beijing is giving new momentum to a decades-old ambition as it pursues its broader goal of becoming a financial superpower.

China’s securities regulator has set a goal of having two to three investment banks and financial institutions with international competitiveness and market leadership by 2035.

Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), said in December that a first-class investment bank should “not merely be large”, but should have a voice in global capital allocation and asset pricing while attracting top financial talent.

The renewed policy push has been accompanied by a wave of fresh capital. At least nine mainland Chinese securities firms had announced or completed plans to inject a combined 51.7 billion yuan (US$7.7 billion) into their Hong Kong operations as of the end of August, according to a calculation by the SCMP.

Among the largest commitments, Citic Securities raised 16 billion yuan to support its international business, while Guotai Haitong Securities and Huatai Securities announced plans to inject 9 billion yuan and up to HK$9 billion (US$1.1 billion), respectively, into their offshore units to support overseas expansion.

By the end of 2025, 34 Chinese securities firms had established 36 international subsidiaries with combined assets of HK$1.94 trillion, up nearly 32 per cent from a year earlier, according to data from the Securities Association of China.

But Wang said the industry’s recent capital injections should not be viewed simply as compliance with Beijing’s policy directives.

“When you have a good business foundation and want to do more business, you need more capital to support it,” he said, describing much of the fundraising as “proactive” expansion rather than a sign of weak overseas operations.

The timing has also been favourable. A revival in Hong Kong’s IPO market and growing demand from mainland clients for offshore diversification had created new growth opportunities, especially as the recovery in mainland capital market activity remained gradual, Fitch’s Lam said.

Hong Kong: the proving ground

For most Chinese securities firms, internationalisation has started in the same place: Hong Kong.

Wang described the city as both a “bridgehead” and a “core hub” for the industry’s overseas expansion. Its proximity to the mainland, bilingual business environment, and status as the principal offshore financing centre for mainland companies made it the natural first stop, he added.

Hong Kong also provided Chinese investment banks with a market where their biggest competitive advantage – deep knowledge of Chinese companies and investors – mattered most. Mainland companies now accounted for about 78 per cent of Hong Kong’s stock market capitalisation and 90 per cent of trading turnover, according to Fitch Ratings.

While mainland markets had stabilised in the first half of 2026, profitability growth across the securities sector could moderate in the second half because of a high comparison base and softer market sentiment, according to Fitch.

IPO activity on the mainland also remained below levels seen in 2022 and 2023, Lam said. Hong Kong, by contrast, offered access to mainland clients through cross-border links, a broader range of investment products, a diverse international institutional-investor base and global market reach, he said. Changes to listing rules had also enhanced the city’s appeal as a listing venue, Lam added.

Those advantages have translated into stronger balance sheets and a growing pipeline of capital-market business.

Citic Securities generated 15.86 billion yuan in revenue outside mainland China in the first half of 2026, up 45.5 per cent from a year earlier, while net profit at its international arm more than doubled to US$829 million, according to its interim report.

CICC’s overseas revenue rose 45 per cent to 9.19 billion yuan over the same period, accounting for about 35 per cent of its total revenue.

Hong Kong subsidiaries of Chinese securities firms accounted for 50.6 per cent of IPO business among the city’s top 30 brokers in the first eight months of 2026, up from 35.3 per cent in 2022, according to Fitch data. The share held by foreign securities firms fell to 26.5 per cent from 29.3 per cent over the same period.

Chinese brokerages were also seeking to diversify beyond the more volatile investment banking and trading businesses by expanding wealth and asset management operations, while cross-border investment schemes were creating additional opportunities over the medium term, Lam said.

“If you see more opportunities coming ahead, definitely they want to put more capital into areas where there is more growth potential,” he added.

Their success in Hong Kong also points to the next challenge: whether advantages built around Chinese companies, Chinese capital and a China-linked financial centre can be replicated in markets where those advantages are less pronounced.

There is still a long way to go. The 2.0 version has yet to arrive

Chen Zhiwu, University of Hong Kong

Charting a new path

The next experiment is already under way. Chinese securities firms are extending their reach beyond their traditional Hong Kong base, with Southeast Asia and the Middle East emerging as key growth markets.

China Securities established a regional office in the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) in late September to pursue opportunities in equity and debt capital markets, investment banking, asset management and institutional business.

CICC opened its own DIFC branch a year earlier, positioning Dubai as a gateway between China and the Gulf region.

Southeast Asia has become another testing ground. China Galaxy Securities has built one of the industry’s broadest regional networks, spanning Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

However, the expansion abroad has also exposed firms to the risks of operating beyond familiar markets.

Everbright Securities’ investment in European sports-rights agency MP & Silva and Haitong International’s heavy losses during the offshore bond market downturn offered costly lessons. Haitong International lost a combined US$1.7 billion in 2022 and 2023 after defaults swept through the high-yield debt market, where it had become a major player.

Winning local trust

“There is still a long way to go. The 2.0 version has yet to arrive,” said Chen Zhiwu, a finance professor at the University of Hong Kong, referring to the next stage of internationalisation in which Chinese securities firms build substantial businesses among local, non-Chinese clients.

“Internationalisation is not just about setting up an office in New York or London. That is relatively easy,” Chen said.

The harder test, he said, was whether a company in Europe, Southeast Asia or Latin America, presented with a choice between a local bank, a Wall Street institution and a Chinese broker, would choose the Chinese firm to lead its IPO or advise on an acquisition.

The same question applied to wealth management: would a wealthy local family be willing to “entrust millions of dollars to a Chinese institution”? Chen asked. “It means that you can make them feel you are one of us or you can be one of us.”

Guotai Junan’s experience in Vietnam illustrates the challenge. Its local brokerage, acquired in 2019, ranked about 40th among roughly 80 securities firms in the country and was aiming to break into the top tier over the longer term, according to Guotai Junan’s Wang.

“We want to accelerate our growth, and given our client base, capital scale and market expertise, we could become much bigger very quickly. But there are still some constraints,” Wang said.

The veteran banker, who also chairs Guotai Junan’s operations in Vietnam and Macau, said an outsized presence by Chinese companies could stir local sensitivities in some overseas markets such as Vietnam.

“If a Chinese company became one of the dominant players, they might feel some pressure,” he said.

For Wang, Chinese investment banks would only become “truly global” when they could occupy a position in London or New York similar to the one Goldman Sachs and other global banks enjoyed in Hong Kong, and when their client base was no longer predominantly Chinese.

“Ultimately, you need to serve local companies with global presence,” he said. “Can you serve an American company like Apple? Can you serve Google?”

If that was the case, Wang said, “then I think you could say you have truly become global”.

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
item.description:
Indonesia officially barred under-16s from using “high-risk” social media earlier this year. But that hasn’t stopped the son of one Jakarta-based writer from using it.

Aged 14, he already had accounts on Instagram and TikTok – among the platforms Jakarta said children would be banned from using – as well as popular video game Minecraft and gaming platform Roblox. To register, he simply lied about his age.

“He can access everything,” Inne Abidin said of her son. “His friends use everything too.”
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia officially barred under-16s from using “high-risk” social media earlier this year. But that hasn’t stopped the son of one Jakarta-based writer from using it.

Aged 14, he already had accounts on Instagram and TikTok – among the platforms Jakarta said children would be banned from using – as well as popular video game Minecraft and gaming platform Roblox. To register, he simply lied about his age.

“He can access everything,” Inne Abidin said of her son. “His friends use everything too.”

Since March, Indonesia has had some of Southeast Asia’s strictest rules governing children’s social media use.

Yet like elsewhere in the region, such restrictions are only as effective as the systems Big Tech platforms put in place to identify underage users – and keep them out.

From Malaysia to Vietnam, the Philippines and Singapore, governments that once merely urged platforms to protect children are now imposing rules designed to force social media companies to take responsibility.

Patchy compliance

Indonesia’s child protection regulations have already had an effect on how social media companies operate.

In April, Meta Platforms raised the minimum age for a Facebook, Instagram or Threads account from 13 to 16 in Indonesia, with YouTube following suit later that month. Both said they would begin a phased deactivation of accounts belonging to underage users.

TikTok, which was the first platform to comply with the new rules, raised its minimum platform age to 16 on March 28. By October, it had deactivated 9 million underage accounts, Indonesia’s digital affairs minister announced on Wednesday.

And online gaming platform Roblox now scans Indonesian users’ faces to estimate their age, restricts some communication features for children and has added age-based account limitations.

Yet youngsters seemingly still find ways to skirt the rules. To combat this, Indonesia’s government has given tech companies until the end of the year to complete comprehensive self-assessments detailing how their algorithms, age-verification and ad-targeting systems protect children.

If the platforms fail to comply, the Communications and Digital Affairs Ministry has finalised a sanctions mechanism that – once codified into law – would allow Indonesia to levy fines of up to 6 per cent of tech firms’ global revenue. Applied to Meta’s reported revenue for 2025, that would amount to roughly US$12 billion.

Such a fine would not be without precedent. In August, Meta agreed to pay a coalition of US states up to US$18 billion to settle lawsuits alleging Facebook and Instagram were deliberately designed to make children addicted and caused them harm.

The settlement also forced sweeping changes to how teens experience the platforms, including daily usage limits, overnight usage blocks and strengthened age-verification controls.

Meta has reportedly migrated some 22.5 million Indonesian platform users across to these “teen accounts”, but for the country’s government this does not go far enough.

“While we see this as progress, we still do not consider Instagram and Facebook teen accounts to be low-risk,” Communication and Digital Affairs Minister Meutya Hafid told reporters in Jakarta on Wednesday. “They remain categorised as high-risk.”

Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost

Unggul Sagena, digital rights advocate

For Southeast Asia, the unavoidable question now being asked is whether governments can turn the threat of penalties into real change.

“In my view, the level of cooperation comes down to a few factors: how valuable the market is, how credible the government’s enforcement is, whether the rule threatens the platform’s global business model, how closely it aligns with obligations they already meet elsewhere and whether it carries legitimacy,” said Unggul Sagena, head of internet access at the Southeast Asia Freedom of Expression Network, an Indonesian digital rights organisation that advocates for internet freedom and user safety.

As the region’s largest economy, the sheer size of Indonesia’s consumer market – as well as its risk-based approach to online child protection – lent its arguments and regulations weight that smaller countries lacked, Unggul said.

“Global platforms are complying,” he said. “Even if not yet fully.”

Part of the reason for the changes is the legal machinery Indonesia already has in place, including a regulation passed in 2020 that obliges platforms to act on government takedown orders within tight deadlines, as short as four hours in urgent cases.

“The government has also taken the issue directly to headquarters,” Unggul said, noting that the communications minister met representatives from Meta’s global public policy and safety leadership team in New York last month to push for faster deactivation of underage accounts.

“Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost,” he added.

Still, Indonesia’s proposed fine framework has yet to be legally codified and many question marks remain over how it will ultimately be implemented.

Unresolved issues include how to collect fines from companies with no local assets, how to accurately verify global revenue “and what due process exists when the same ministry writes the rules, judges compliance and imposes the sanction”, Unggul said.

Blocking sites, meanwhile, “hurts Indonesian users more than the companies”, he said. “And the government can order [content] removals, but it still has little visibility into how the platforms are actually designed.”

The threat of high fines could push platforms to invest more in safety-by-design and high-privacy defaults for children, said Indriyatno Banyumurti, executive director of ICT Watch, an Indonesian civil society organisation focused on digital literacy.

But he warned that legal clarity and consistent enforcement were key, stressing that child safety “should not depend solely on voluntary corporate commitments”.

Indriyatno said much would depend on how violations were defined, how compliance was monitored, how evidence was assessed and whether sanctions could be applied fairly and consistently.

Regional rules

Indonesia’s social media ban may have been Southeast Asia’s first, but it is far from alone in trying to make Big Tech take responsibility for children’s safety online.

In Malaysia, rules in force since June now bar under-16s from opening or maintaining social media accounts and require platforms to verify users’ ages. Companies that fail to comply face fines of up to 10 million ringgit (US$2.5 million), with further penalties for ignoring regulatory directives.

Vietnam is considering a draft decree that would limit under-16s to a view-only mode of social media, preventing them from posting content, commenting, sharing or reacting to other posts. Accounts would have to be registered using a parent or guardian’s details under the proposed rules, with platforms compelled to block age-inappropriate material and place caps on children’s online gaming time.

The Philippines’ approach has been more piecemeal. It already legally forces internet providers to block child sexual abuse material or face heavy penalties and has used regulatory pressure to squeeze direct concessions from platforms. Lawmakers are also considering introducing age limits and other measures.

In August, Meta and Roblox agreed to strengthen age checks, parental controls and content takedowns following talks with Philippine authorities over child safety and online radicalisation. A spate of school shootings this year also spurred officials in Manila to order Reddit and Discord to appoint local representatives to coordinate on online threats. Discord was briefly blocked before agreeing to cooperate.

Singapore requires social media giants to shield users, including children, from harmful material under its Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act that came into effect in 2023, with non-compliance carrying a financial penalty of up to S$1 million (US$781,500).

App stores have been legally required to verify the ages of users who want to download age-restricted material in the city state since April this year. And an Online Safety Commission, launched in June under legislation passed last year, has the power to order the immediate removal of harmful content and restrict offending accounts.

While these efforts have helped effect some change, analysts say the results have been uneven.

“Platforms do respond, but market size is a factor they consider,” said regional tech policy adviser Paco Pangalangan, a technology and human rights fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School in the US. “A large market might get more attention, while a smaller one might get a slower, more minimal version. Whether there’s a law matters too.”

By his count, most of the big social media companies do not even have in-country representatives in five of Asean’s 11 member states.

“So there’s often no real channel for regulators or civil society to raise problems,” Pangalangan said.

Strength in numbers

Individual governments, especially those that represent sizeable markets with credible enforcement mechanisms, may be able to force social media platforms to comply with their rules.

But global technology companies can also opt to deal with countries one by one, which analysts and advocates say makes it harder for smaller markets to exert sustained pressure. One solution could be to present a more united front.

“A regional coalition can push Big Tech to create child-friendly ecosystems in ways no single country can,” Unggul said. “Individually, each Asean country is a market platforms can afford to deprioritise. Together, the region is not.”

Pangalangan said that, taken as a whole, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations could leverage the region’s more than 400 million social media users to strengthen its hand in negotiations..

“Collectively, we have a market that platforms can’t afford to simply deprioritise,” he said.

“If we can agree on common standards, including requirements around how platforms are designed, there’s less room for platforms to play one country off against another or just wait things out.”

Allan Cabanlong, Asean regional director for cybersecurity and cloud services provider CyberCX’s regional cyber advisers programme and a former assistant secretary at the Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology, agreed that collective action could hand regional governments greater bargaining power.

“A broom with one strand cannot sweep,” he said. “We have hundreds of millions of users in Asean. If the Philippines were to stand alone, it would not be listened to.”

As this year’s Asean chair, the Philippines could push the protection of children online higher up the regional agenda, Cabanlong said, while the bloc could also work to strengthen its existing mechanisms for digital regulation.

Asean would not be starting from scratch. Its declaration on the protection of children from online exploitation and abuse, adopted in 2019, and associated regional plans of action already recognise online harm to children as a cross-bogrder issue.

Other frameworks on personal data protection – and a declaration on safe and responsible social media use, adopted last October – widen that scope to include online radicalisation and AI-related risks.

But few observers expect a single, regional law on children’s social media use to be the end result.

“Asean does not necessarily have to start by creating one identical social media law for all member states,” said Ysrael Diloy, executive director of Stairway Foundation, a non-profit children’s rights organisation in the Philippines.

“Given differences in national legal systems, regulatory structures and capacities, that may not be the most realistic starting point.”

Indriyatno agreed that a more realistic approach would be for Asean to agree on common expectations for factors such as risk assessments, minimum standards of platform accountability, privacy defaults for children and cooperation on cross-border cases.

“Regulators could also develop more compatible requirements for platform transparency and information sharing,” he said.

Alejandro Reyes, chief strategic officer of non-profit organisation AI Safety Asia, said national regulators would also need to share information and cooperate more closely.

“If Singapore identifies a serious failure in a platform’s child-safety systems, its counterparts in Malaysia, the Philippines and elsewhere should have access to those findings,” he said.

“Joint investigations, shared technical expertise and coordinated enforcement would make it harder for companies to exploit differences between national regulatory regimes.”

Such a baseline would not demand identical laws, but it would provide common ground in dealing with companies that straddle borders.

It would also carry risks. “The concern here is that child protection is part of a much broader framework of government control over online content and expression,” Reyes said, urging caution given the differences in countries’ legal systems, political priorities and enforcement capacity.

Other issues, according to Unggul, include the fact that Asean members currently compete for technology investment, have very different track records when it comes to free expression and make decisions as a bloc by consensus.

“Collective leverage only works if it is credible and rights-based, and that is where civil society across the region must make sure the coalition strengthens accountability rather than state control over content,” he said.

“Child safety must not become cover for censorship. Bargaining power comes not only from penalties but from legitimacy.”

Limits of laws

Governments can restrict access, require age verification and impose penalties on platforms, but they cannot regulate the behaviour of children and families, online child safety experts say.

Fandy Zulmi, programme manager at the Centre for Child Study and Protection in Indonesia, pointed to recent Communications Ministry data showing that three out of five Indonesian children had falsified their age to access restricted platforms.

Without stronger digital literacy, parental involvement and robust reporting mechanisms, Indonesia’s social media ban for children might simply move the risks “somewhere else”, he said.

“It is still too early to conclude that the policy has effectively deterred children from going online,” Fandy said.

Indonesia’s implementation challenge begins with the fact that there are between 60 million and 80 million children in the country whose circumstances differ enormously, according to Diena Haryana, founder of the Sejiwa Foundation, a Jakarta-based child welfare organisation.

“Where they live, what education their parents have, what digital parenting awareness the parents have, whether the parents themselves have digital skills – all of that varies massively, especially between somewhere like Jakarta and rural areas,” she said.

Some parents used social media platforms to keep children occupied while they worked, Diena said, while others were more aware of the risks involved with giving their children unfettered access.

“We all need to work much harder to make sure children understand what the regulation is, why it exists and how implementation should actually work,” she said.

But ultimately, it is the platforms themselves that bear the brunt of the responsibility for child safety, according to Pangalangan.

“They already know where many of the harms are,” he said. “They don’t need a law to fix things they control in their own products.”

item.title: [SCMP] Dr Ron Roukema on education, leadership and life at Hong Kong International School
item.description:
I WAS BORN in October 1972, in New Jersey, in the United States. My parents were both immigrants – young adults who migrated during World War II, in the early 1940s. My father is Dutch and my mother is Italian, from Sicily. As children, we were always told that if we worked for the state, we’d be well taken care of.

MY MUM WAS a nurse and she met my father in New York. She worked in a hospital, and he was a police officer. My father retired when he was in his 40s after he broke his back. We then moved to North Carolina, which we chose because it was the exact halfway point between my two sets of grandparents (in New Jersey and Florida).

MY FAMILY IS made up of educators. I’m the youngest of five siblings. I have three older sisters, and my parents adopted the son of my father’s friend, when I was about 12. My eldest sister is a university professor and runs a business that does training with government departments. My middle sister retired in one state, moved to another and continues to teach in public schools. My youngest sister is a psychologist and also runs a business working with the government. My brother’s birth father was also in the police force; they were having problems at home, so he lived with us until he was 20. It was just like having a bigger brother, but also a friend who was a role model in some ways. I know he’s a firefighter now in the mountains, but I haven’t seen him in 15 or 20 years.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in October 1972, in New Jersey, in the United States. My parents were both immigrants – young adults who migrated during World War II, in the early 1940s. My father is Dutch and my mother is Italian, from Sicily. As children, we were always told that if we worked for the state, we’d be well taken care of.

MY MUM WAS a nurse and she met my father in New York. She worked in a hospital, and he was a police officer. My father retired when he was in his 40s after he broke his back. We then moved to North Carolina, which we chose because it was the exact halfway point between my two sets of grandparents (in New Jersey and Florida).

MY FAMILY IS made up of educators. I’m the youngest of five siblings. I have three older sisters, and my parents adopted the son of my father’s friend, when I was about 12. My eldest sister is a university professor and runs a business that does training with government departments. My middle sister retired in one state, moved to another and continues to teach in public schools. My youngest sister is a psychologist and also runs a business working with the government. My brother’s birth father was also in the police force; they were having problems at home, so he lived with us until he was 20. It was just like having a bigger brother, but also a friend who was a role model in some ways. I know he’s a firefighter now in the mountains, but I haven’t seen him in 15 or 20 years.

I LOVE SCHOOLS in general. I grew up in a family where everybody enjoyed going to school. I was in about 20 organisations and clubs in secondary school, playing sports and joining activities to make friends. I was voted “Most Involved” and I was also the lead in the school musical, captain of the wrestling and baseball teams, and field conductor for the marching band. Every now and then, I’d choose classes to be with friends, only to regret it when the classroom turned into more play than study.

GROWING UP, WE didn’t really have the funds to pay for university. I got a full scholarship as a teaching fellow, to teach in the state of North Carolina for four years after graduation, in exchange for tuition. During university (at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill), I continued to play baseball and also did cheerleading. I got my master’s at East Carolina University and my doctorate at North Carolina State University.

MY WIFE AND I went to the same secondary school, but we didn’t meet until university – which is good, because I grew up a lot between the time that I met her and the time that I graduated. I was a fourth-year student, and she was a first-year student. She’s an accomplished photographer and has taught photography at different levels. We’ve been married for 28 years.

MY FIRST JOB was as a fill-in teacher of kindergarten classes at Southern Pines Elementary; that lasted about three months before I realised that was the wrong age group for me. I had kids tell me, “I have to go to the bathroom.” I’d reply, “Well, just go down the hall and go to the bathroom.” But they were like, “No, no, no. We have to walk as a class.” Learning to teach kindergarten was very different. After that, I went back to Pinecrest High School to teach secondary-school history.

MY FIRST ADMINISTRATIVE job was the last year that Southern Pines Middle School existed (2000). I was tasked with converting the academic framework into an International Baccalaureate Primary Years Programme and helping my former colleagues transition, either to other schools or to different areas of education.

ACTUALLY, I NEVER wanted to go into administration. I love teaching. But Joyce Edwards, my associate principal at the time, wanted me to go along with her because she thought I asked good questions. Joyce gave me two options: be the middle-school principal at the new school we’d just built, or move to Durham, in North Carolina, and get a doctorate and go to work at this new school out there.

SO, I MOVED to Durham, in 2000. I helped introduce technology programmes at Eno Valley Elementary School as an administrator, where they told me it would take three to five years to build a technology programme. We built it in seven months.

IN 2007, AROUND the time that my wife and I were expecting our first child, I was offered a job at an international school in Beijing. But instead of going there, we headed to Shanghai American School, where I served as the founding principal of the middle school at the Pudong campus. I worked there for several years before taking my first headship, reporting directly to the board, at Marymount International School, in Paris, France.

WE WERE HAPPY in Paris. We stayed for four years. It was a great school that aligned with my beliefs and philosophies. When our second daughter was born, we started thinking about moving back to Asia. One of the things that drew me towards Hong Kong International School (HKIS) is my Christian faith and the way the school embraces Christianity.

WHAT’S THE PURPOSE of knowledge? I think that’s why religion is important to me, because to understand and to learn – it has to be for a greater purpose, and that greater purpose, in the end, is understanding God’s word and what he hopes for us. In the meantime, it’s also about using your knowledge to serve others and develop a culture that people want to be part of, and to understand that everything we do and everything that happens is for a greater purpose.

MY FIRST IMPRESSION of Hong Kong was in 2007 – right here in this very office, purely by chance. HKIS was hosting a meeting for middle-school principals, and this office I’m in was previously a boardroom. I joined HKIS as the upper-primary principal in 2014. About a year later, they asked me to move into a larger role, as the associate head of school, or what they called the provost at the time, because of my background in education and the knowledge that I had built up over 20-plus years of experience, which was what the school was hoping for and needing at the time. So, I supported them in that role.

DURING THAT FIRST visit, we brought Eva, our oldest, and went to Hong Kong Disneyland. On a trip to Stanley, I ran into the then-head of school, Richard Mueller. We were having lunch at Pizza Express with my wife’s cousins when Richard and his wife walked by and we started chatting. That brief encounter showed me how close and open people in Hong Kong are across both the expat and local communities. It made me feel that I would be happy here, both on an academic and personal level.

I AM HORRIBLE with raising my own children, in the sense of being a parent and an educator at the same school where they go and I work. My oldest graduated two years ago, my youngest is in Year Five and my second daughter is in Year Seven. Whenever I go to an open house or a play to support my kids, I usually get pulled away. It’s hard to just be a dad there, because other parents don’t see me for my kids – they see me for them.

STILL, FOR THE most part, my kids have loved having me around. I walk my son to school every day, and he’s very happy to do it. Whenever my oldest saw me in secondary school, she’d run over, give me a hug and make sure her friends got to say hello.

I WORK IN Hong Kong, but I live in North Carolina. Every summer and Christmas, we go home and see family and friends that we went to school and university with. We have a nice home there – the kind of place people want to be. No dates, no deadlines, but we know that’s eventually what we’ll go back to. It’s just exciting to be around people who have the same origins that I have.

I’M PART OF what we call the “US Gourmet Eating Club”, where we go eat fast food in Hong Kong. It’s just a bunch of people; some are associated with the school, some are not. We get together for new restaurant openings. We’re looking forward to the opening of (American fast-food restaurant) Dairy Queen here in Hong Kong – we joke around and call it “gourmet”.

MY JOY OF working in schools started before I had kids, and it will continue after they have grown up. I feel like I’ve made an impact in each role I’ve held. When I was a teacher, it was daily conversations to help people make decisions that were impactful. Most of my conversations today are about helping students develop lifelong skills, so that they can be successful in the future. I’m interested in seeing how communities come together and grow.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

This story was made possible with support from Hong Kong International School

item.title: [SCMP] This womb for rent: why are some Chinese cities hubs for illegal surrogacy services?
item.description:
It was like something out of a movie: blindfolded, her cellphone confiscated, Miranda was being driven in a van carrying only other women. When she attempted to strike up a conversation with the passenger next to her, the driver made her move to another seat.

The silence stretched for 45 minutes before the blindfolds were removed and the vehicle pulled up at what appeared to be a resort-style compound.

“I only knew the site lay on the city’s outskirts, nothing more,” said Miranda, who declined to give her full name. “They did not want me to learn the precise location. That was standard procedure every single time I was taken there.”
item.content:encoded:
It was like something out of a movie: blindfolded, her cellphone confiscated, Miranda was being driven in a van carrying only other women. When she attempted to strike up a conversation with the passenger next to her, the driver made her move to another seat.

The silence stretched for 45 minutes before the blindfolds were removed and the vehicle pulled up at what appeared to be a resort-style compound.

“I only knew the site lay on the city’s outskirts, nothing more,” said Miranda, who declined to give her full name. “They did not want me to learn the precise location. That was standard procedure every single time I was taken there.”

The facility was a surrogacy house in Wuhan, capital of central China’s Hubei province and Miranda’s hometown.

Chinese law says assisted reproductive technologies can only be performed by permitted medical institutions for married couples dealing with infertility, and only for medical purposes. Those using such technologies for surrogacy can be fined or face criminal charges.

‘Professional’ services

“I knew it was illegal, of course, but surrogacy was a forced choice for me, and it was my last hope of having my own baby,” Miranda said. She opted for it following two second-trimester miscarriages caused by moderate intrauterine adhesions, which complicate pregnancy by damaging the uterine lining and shrinking the space required for a fertilised egg to develop.

About five years ago, she learned about the Wuhan surrogacy agency from a friend in Shenzhen.

Her first impression was that the facility was clean and well-equipped. She described the agency as “professional”, while noting the irony of applying that term to an illegal operation.

“The doctors they arranged came from top local hospitals,” Miranda said. “For egg retrieval, a doctor and anaesthetist would come to the house, and nurses would make home visits for the ovulation-induction injections. But for key examinations, they would drive me to hospitals.”

Two years later, her son was born in a Wuhan hospital. The baby’s birth certificate listed the names of her husband and the surrogate mother. After obtaining her son’s household registration document, Miranda asked the surrogate mother to sign a contract waiving her parental rights.

She paid more than 600,000 yuan (US$89,454) to the Wuhan facility, with roughly a third going to the surrogate mother.

Miranda said the agency told her that most of its clients turned to surrogacy for the same reason: their uteruses were no longer medically viable to carry a pregnancy. Others were seeking to avoid exhausting rounds of hospital treatment.

China’s restrictive stance on surrogacy is consistent with concerns expressed by many policymakers and ethicists

Olivia Ngan, University of Hong Kong

Government concerns

An analysis released in March by Frost & Sullivan, a consultancy firm, said the number of infertile couples in China had risen from 54.8 million in 2020 to 60.6 million last year, and was projected to climb to 74.4 million by 2035.

While surrogacy may appear to be the solution for women like Miranda, Chinese policymakers consider it a practice carrying far more risks than benefits, and the authorities are adamant that surrogacy activities – in any form – are prohibited.

In 2021, when deputies to the National People’s Congress – the country’s top legislature – suggested allowing legal surrogacy to prevent repeated illegal operations, the National Health Commission replied that “surrogacy severely harms women’s health rights and interests”.

The practice “objectifies women and gives rise to a string of grave social problems, including human trafficking, and can cause ethical crises within the family and society”, it said.

The authorities renewed a clampdown on underground surrogacy networks last month.

Two laboratories, one in Wuhan and the other in Changsha, the capital of neighbouring Hunan province, were shut down for offering surrogacy services. Wuhan’s municipal health commission said eight people had been detained, police were investigating and “any illegal activities” would be severely punished.

This month, the health commission in Taicang, part of Suzhou bordering Shanghai, said it had carried out inspections together with police at an alleged surrogacy facility following online tip‑offs. It has yet to release its findings.

They were not the first crackdowns by national and local regulators targeting surrogacy operators.

In the second half of 2023, a 14-department task force headed by the National Health Commission rolled out a targeted nationwide campaign. It sought to root out crimes stemming from the unauthorised use of assisted reproductive technology, including commercial surrogacy and illegal egg harvesting.

“China’s restrictive stance on surrogacy is consistent with concerns expressed by many policymakers and ethicists,” said Olivia Ngan, research assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong’s school of clinical medicine. “The central ethical concern is that commercial surrogacy may lead to the commodification of women, reproduction and children.”

She said critics argued that “when pregnancy becomes a paid service, there is a risk that economically vulnerable women may be pressured into acting as surrogates, raising concerns about exploitation, coercion and unequal power relationships”.

‘One-stop service’

“Demand for surrogacy does not arise in a vacuum,” Ngan said, noting that those who had experienced infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss or related medical conditions could have a profound desire for genetically related children.

Propelled by such desires, China’s underground surrogacy industry now provided “one-stop service”, said Karen, a Shanghai resident who also declined to give her full name.

She married late and struggled with infertility for over five years. By the time she turned 45, her diminished egg quality meant scant prospects for wholly natural conception.

That was when Karen began exploring alternative options outside hospital care and was surprised to discover that the underground industry offered everything she needed. She opted for the same agency used by Miranda.

“The eggs I bought were relatively affordable,” she said. “I paid around 10,000 yuan because the donor – a woman in her twenties – did not have a top-tier educational background.

“The surrogate mothers were typically in their thirties. The agency told me that all of them had previously given birth, and it only recruited women from southwestern China’s Yunnan or Guizhou provinces because they tended to come from relatively low-income backgrounds.”

After the eggs were successfully fertilised with her husband’s sperm, the agency matched Karen with a surrogate mother.

Industry insiders said Wuhan and Guangzhou, the capital of southern China’s Guangdong province, were the two major Chinese hubs for surrogacy agencies, drawn by convenient transport links and relatively lower living costs, which helped keep overall expenses down.

China recorded a crude birth rate of 5.63 per thousand people last year, less than half the 12.95 per thousand in 2016, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

Block or channel?

Ngan said that as China’s population aged and fertility rates remained low, “reproductive aspirations and reproductive health needs may become even more prominent social issues”.

To address infertility, China provides assisted reproductive technology services, with more than 600 medical institutions having been approved to deliver them or serve as human sperm banks by June last year.

At a news conference in June this year, the National Health Commission said the success rates for assisted reproductive technology services in China had reached internationally advanced levels. “Following comprehensive interventions, 80 per cent to 90 per cent of couples experiencing fertility difficulties are able to conceive naturally,” a commission official said.

However, that means multiple fertility treatments fail for 10 per cent to 20 per cent of women who are unable to carry a pregnancy.

Professor Kirsty Horsey, from the school of social sciences and humanities at Loughborough University in the United Kingdom, said: “Prohibition [of surrogacy] tends to make people seek alternatives, like going overseas or entering into more dangerous clandestine and potentially unethical arrangements. It is not unknown for trafficking and surrogacy to be connected, but ‘feeding’ this market by prohibitions really does not help.”

Chinese media have reported that because legal surrogacy services were unavailable, some people had sought them out overseas, with the US serving as one of the top destinations. Several high-profile Chinese actresses have been caught up in overseas surrogacy controversies in recent years, leading to some of them being effectively banned from the entertainment industry.

Beyond the United States, the UK, Canada and New Zealand also permit altruistic surrogacy, while banning the commercial arrangements allowed in America. Australia is conducting a review of its laws related to surrogacy.

Ngan said many countries that permitted surrogacy only allowed altruistic arrangements, where surrogates were reimbursed for expenses but received no payment for carrying a pregnancy. “This approach seeks to reduce commercial incentives and the risk of exploitation,” she said.

Horsey said overseas experience in jurisdictions with regulated surrogacy showed that “having a regulated and safe form of surrogacy available to infertile couples – with involvement of legitimate clinics, counsellors, lawyers, et cetera to give their respective advice and guidance – would legitimise a particular form of or route through surrogacy, meaning people would not have to resort to dangerous underground arrangements which are also likely to be less ethical”.

Miranda said that without surrogacy, “women like me” who were basically incapable of conceiving babies, even with modern medical help, “might never have children”.

“So I don’t believe this government-led clampdown will fully stamp out the business,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] From kitchen waste to sky-high costs: inside Hong Kong’s quest for green jet fuel
item.description:
China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold.

The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area.

EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity.
item.content:encoded:
China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold.

The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area.

EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity.

“I can recall that the gutter oil we collected was basically free 10 years ago, and authorities even offered subsidies [to collectors], but now the unit cost is even more expensive than fuel,” he said.

Gutter oil is among a selection of feedstocks, such as animal fat and agricultural waste, that can be used to produce renewable jet fuel, an alternative that will reduce life-cycle carbon emissions by up to 80 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel.

SAF, a “drop-in” substitute, can be safely blended with jet fuel and used in aircraft engines without modification, but the challenge is the price.

The Hong Kong government has set a 2030 target for the use of SAF, but has yet to clarify who will pay for it.

“Producers need confidence that demand will be there. Airlines need fuel that is available and affordable. Investors need clarity on the direction of policy. A well-designed policy can connect these needs,” the CEO of Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways, Ronald Lam Siu-por, said at a clean jet fuel conference in September.

A ‘cautious’ target

The city government initially set a goal for SAF to account for between 1 and 2 per cent of all fuel consumed by flights departing from Hong Kong International Airport by 2030.

But in the city’s first five-year plan released in September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu revised the target to 1 to 3 per cent. He also said the city would aim to develop an internationally competitive SAF value chain in the bay area.

Niki Wang Yangwen, Asia-Pacific associate director of biofuels at S&P Global Energy, said Hong Kong’s aim was considered achievable, with Asian economies generally setting targets of 1 to 5 per cent for 2030.

“From our conversations with the market, the general feeling is that 1 to 3 per cent is a fairly cautious target, and people do not have much concern about it,” she said of the city’s goal.

Some industry players expected the city to be a trial site for mainland China to gauge market reactions and, if things worked out, gradually roll out similar measures, she explained.

Hong Kong, like Singapore, is a key aviation hub in Asia, with a dominant home carrier and mostly international traffic, Wang said.

Hong Kong’s airport is one of the busiest in the world, last year recording 61 million passenger trips and a sector-leading 5.07 million tonnes of cargo throughput.

According to the Civil Aviation Department, the number of flights departing from Hong Kong, including cargo and passenger services, jumped by 8.6 per cent to 197,374 in 2025 from a year earlier, while the number in 2024 was 181,663, up by 31.6 per cent from 138,056 in 2023.

In addition, 197,325 flights arrived in 2025, representing an 8.7 per cent increase from the previous year.

Hong Kong is not alone in setting green fuel targets. Elsewhere, demand for SAF is being driven more by mandates than pledges by airlines.

The International Civil Aviation Organisation has adopted a collective goal to cut global aviation emissions by 5 per cent by 2030 on the path to net zero by 2050.

The European Union requires fuel suppliers at its airports to use SAF, starting at 2 per cent of overall fuel in 2025, rising to 6 per cent in 2030 and to 70 per cent by 2050.

Singapore has confirmed a goal of SAF accounting for 1 per cent of overall fuel by 2027 and 3 to 5 per cent by 2030, subject to global developments and SAF availability, while other Asian countries, including Thailand, Japan and South Korea, have also set targets.

How can Hong Kong achieve its goal?

In its latest policy address, the government committed to studying a mandatory consumption mechanism, and launching targeted publicity and educational campaigns by 2028. It will also develop a local blending facility to mix neat SAF with conventional jet fuel into a ready-to-use supply to support uptake.

Separately, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing’s Core Climate carbon marketplace will explore offering green energy and other environmental equity products to the market, including SAF certificates and green hydrogen certificates.

In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the Transport and Logistics Bureau and the Environment and Ecology Bureau said the local blending facility was expected to begin operations by 2030.

“This will complete an end-to-end regional value chain, streamline logistics and enhance SAF price competitiveness,” the bureaus said.

As part of the broader value chain in the bay area, the government has also spearheaded the establishment of EcoCeres’ SAF production base in Dongguan, which will begin production by 2030, producing 450,000 tonnes of SAF and renewable diesel per year at full capacity.

EcoCeres’ Chan said the company’s current production of about 770,000 to 800,000 tonnes, well above the 3 per cent requirement of around 200,000 tonnes, was manageable.

“I also believe we will not be the sole supplier. There will be other suppliers in a fair market, so I don’t think there will be any pressure on the overall supply, even at 3 per cent or up to 10 per cent,” he said.

EcoCeres, a clean energy unicorn backed by the family office of Henderson Land Development co-chairman Peter Lee Ka-kit, is the world’s second-biggest producer of SAF, after Finland’s Neste.

Chan said the supply chain was end-to-end, with Dongguan as its starting point. Used cooking oil is collected from nearby bay area cities and pre-processed in the area, while Hong Kong handles blending, research and development, and financing.

Who pays the extra cost?

Chan said the government should have a longer-term plan beyond 2030 and provide details of its mandatory mechanism, noting that the EU had set goals for 2050.

Merlin Lao Man-chi, the head of policy and research at the Business Environment Council, said the government’s mandatory mechanism was crucial, as it would determine market confidence and who would ultimately bear the cost.

“It is important to determine the cost allocation and who will be in charge of the cost as it could scale up the whole industry,” he said.

According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), global SAF production is expected to reach 2.4 million tonnes in 2026, representing just 0.8 per cent of aviation fuel use, at a cost of US$4.3 billion to airlines.

The South China Morning Post contacted four Hong Kong-based airlines – Cathay, its budget arm HK Express, Hong Kong Airlines and Greater Bay Airlines – but none offered any comment.

Singapore introduced the world’s first green levy, with passengers bearing the cost, while the EU holds suppliers responsible through penalties.

Lao said the government should offer short-term subsidies, but it would also need to determine how to allocate costs in the longer run.

He said the levy mechanism in Singapore helped encourage acceptance among consumers, but such a move would be “a long shot” in Hong Kong and the government would need to work to garner broad public support.

Lao used Hong Kong’s ill-fated waste-charging scheme in 2024 as an example. Officials and lawmakers initially had good thoughts initially and all agreed on the proposal. But when it came to implementation, residents opposed the measure and the scheme was eventually scrapped.

Asked whether imposing a levy would threaten the city’s status as an international aviation hub, Lao said the fee could be imposed only on passengers or cargo departing from Hong Kong, not those in transit.

Hong Kong’s airport currently charges a HK$200 (US$25) departure tax. In the past few months, airlines have added fuel surcharges on the back of price hikes caused by the Middle East war.

“The mechanism will ensure that we do it first and decide the transshipment and transition later, as they are very price sensitive,” Lao said, noting that a green levy would also hedge against future price volatility.

Lawmaker Chan Siu-hung said he was not worried that the aviation industry would lose customers, as the city’s airport should fight for its own “target customers”.

“Everyone has to understand that protecting the environment comes at a cost. If we do not pay it today, our children and grandchildren will have to pay it in the future,” he said.

However, Chan argued that the government should not offer subsidies because Hong Kong relied on both local and international airlines. Subsidising local airlines could be regarded as unfair competition, while taxpayers’ money should not be used to fund foreign airlines, he said.

Alan Chan of EcoCeres said the extra cost of SAF should be seen as “green value” rather than a “green premium” as each tonne of its fuel would cut life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by up to 94.4 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel depending on feedstock composition. This was a benefit that everyone would enjoy, he argued.

“If you do not realise it is a value, the product itself will have no value,” he said. “Why would you pay more for the same thing?”

How to lower the price of SAF?

The IATA estimated that the price of SAF would surge to US$2,872 per tonne in 2026, about 2.5 times the price of jet fuel, while S&P Global Energy’s data showed that the SAF price in China was US$2,340 per tonne on October 6.

Lawmaker Chan said scaling operations was essential to bringing down SAF costs.

“Hong Kong is a small market without the scale or critical mass, but the Greater Bay Area has many airports, and their combined demand can reach critical mass,” he said.

If there was a clear demand for SAF, the region’s many facilities and suppliers would naturally be willing to invest in scaling, he added.

The legislator said the next step was developing a carbon trading market that could help bring down costs as the industry scaled up.

One example, he said, was the SAF certificate mentioned in the policy address: airlines could trade the certificates in the market, while companies short of carbon credits could buy them.

Samuel Wong, Asia-Pacific vice-president for sales at PAC LP, a technology supplier in the United States, said used cooking oil alone would not be sufficient to produce SAF on the scale the aviation industry would eventually require.

“Used cooking oil can be turned into SAF, but it can also be used to produce biodiesel and other renewable fuels, so different sectors are competing for the same limited supply,” Wong said. “That competition has pushed prices above US$1,000 per tonne in some markets.”

He said the supply of used cooking oil was inherently limited, meaning the industry would have to develop alternative feedstocks and production technologies as SAF demand increased.

“There are fundamental constraints on both supply and cost,” Wong said. “The amount of used cooking oil that can be sustainably collected is finite, so used cooking oil alone cannot provide all the feedstock needed to scale SAF globally.”

HEFA, or hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids, is currently the main commercial pathway used for producing SAF and uses feedstocks including used cooking oil, vegetable oils and animal fats.

But Wong said achieving much larger SAF volumes would require the industry to diversify beyond HEFA.

“HEFA is essential for scaling SAF today, but it cannot be the only solution,” he said. “The industry needs a portfolio of pathways.”

Lawmaker Chan said Hong Kong needed a detailed action plan beyond 2030.

“[The government] needs a mandatory target by 2030, and then have a clear direction in 2035 to raise the target along the way,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
item.description:
While walking alongside Victoria Harbour or riding the Star Ferry, luck might have allowed you a glimpse of Way Foong motoring by. Its old-fashioned appearance is a sign that the boat is obviously from an era long past but, because it is not a traditional junk, you may not have realised you were looking at an authentic piece of Hong Kong history: a wooden motoryacht constructed locally almost 100 years ago.

Commissioned by the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (now HSBC) – “Way Foong” being a transliteration of the bank’s name in Cantonese – and built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, the vessel was used by the bank as a ferry, a tugboat and a pleasure craft for employees for more than seven decades before passing into private ownership. In the late 2010s, it was acquired by a patron of the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF) – an organisation officially founded earlier this year by individuals passionate about preserving the city’s maritime legacy.

When hired for parties or other events, Way Foong can often be seen cruising side by side with Java, another 1930s-era wooden vessel built by the same shipyard. Java entered service in 1935 and served for decades in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1. It transported VIPs and port officials, conducted anti-piracy patrols, towed and positioned mooring buoys and even corralled the odd swimming water buffalo. Its Burmese-teak construction, with deck planks measuring almost 4.5cm thick, earned the boat a reputation for being “almost unsinkable” and invulnerable to typhoons.
item.content:encoded:
While walking alongside Victoria Harbour or riding the Star Ferry, luck might have allowed you a glimpse of Way Foong motoring by. Its old-fashioned appearance is a sign that the boat is obviously from an era long past but, because it is not a traditional junk, you may not have realised you were looking at an authentic piece of Hong Kong history: a wooden motoryacht constructed locally almost 100 years ago.

Commissioned by the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (now HSBC) – “Way Foong” being a transliteration of the bank’s name in Cantonese – and built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, the vessel was used by the bank as a ferry, a tugboat and a pleasure craft for employees for more than seven decades before passing into private ownership. In the late 2010s, it was acquired by a patron of the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF) – an organisation officially founded earlier this year by individuals passionate about preserving the city’s maritime legacy.

When hired for parties or other events, Way Foong can often be seen cruising side by side with Java, another 1930s-era wooden vessel built by the same shipyard. Java entered service in 1935 and served for decades in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1. It transported VIPs and port officials, conducted anti-piracy patrols, towed and positioned mooring buoys and even corralled the odd swimming water buffalo. Its Burmese-teak construction, with deck planks measuring almost 4.5cm thick, earned the boat a reputation for being “almost unsinkable” and invulnerable to typhoons.

Way Foong and Java are two of five vessels now owned and maintained by the HKHVF. “By restoring and preserving such examples of the world-class craftsmanship that Hong Kong shipyards were capable of, we aim not only to encourage Hongkongers to discover the city’s commercial, governmental and recreational maritime heritage, but also to nurture the region’s next generation of boaters and ocean-lovers,” says CEO Philip Giannecchini.

Java, the first vessel in the collection, was found by chance. One of the avid sailors who would later establish the HKHVF noticed Java moored in Tai Tam Harbour, on the south side of Hong Kong Island, when taking out his own boat, and wanted to learn more about the 56-foot wooden launch. He ended up meeting the then-owner, and bought Java in the early 2000s. At the time, the rationale behind the purchase was simply to have such a historical pleasure craft in one’s possession. Eventually, the desire to safeguard Hong Kong’s maritime history took hold, setting in motion other acquisitions and the founding of the HKHVF.

A years-long search for extant, pre-50s boats built in the city followed. Nine, in various states of repair, have been identified by the organisation’s historians – some now in the HKHVF collection, others happily and privately owned, and one, Mon Lei, whose whereabouts are unknown.

Given Hong Kong’s coastal geography, boats have, and will always be, an integral part of the city. Yet, while today’s harbours and inlets are teeming with craft of various shapes and sizes, most are built elsewhere, the city’s shipbuilding days having long passed.

However, in the early 20th century, two giants of the industry, the Taikoo Dockyard and the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, were firmly in their prime, and a number of small and medium-sized shipbuilders, such as Hung Hom’s Hop Kee Shipyard, Ah King Slipway and Cheoy Lee Shipyard, also produced wooden vessels for global clients.

Teresa Mak Hiu-see, one of the in-house researchers at the HKHVF, notes that “the 30s were one of the high points in Hong Kong’s shipbuilding tradition for all types of vessels, from cargo liners to pleasure craft, and the industry steamed ahead until Japan invaded Hong Kong in December 1941. Until the end of World War II, all dockyards were under Japanese control”.

Rare survivors such as Way Foong and Java escaped the scrapyard, but many other Hong Kong-built vessels from the 20s and 40s were not so lucky. Says Mak, “With the 40s being a time of war and post-war recovery, that might be a factor in the small number of surviving pleasure craft from that decade.”

In 1972, the Taikoo Dockyard and the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company were merged to form the Hongkong United Dockyards. In 1980, the Whampoa site was shut down and the land was redeveloped into the Whampoa Garden housing estate, now easily identified by its superyacht-shaped shopping centre, a 110-metre-long concrete landmark “moored” amid the residential blocks.

When the Cheoy Lee Shipyard at Penny’s Bay was reclaimed by the Hong Kong government in 1999 to provide a location for Hong Kong Disneyland, it signalled the end of an era: shipbuilding operations in the city were coming to an end. But the final straw came when Ah King’s Causeway Bay shipyard closed, in 2002.

With shipbuilding essentially a thing of the past, the preservation of Hong Kong-made boats has become ever more important, Giannecchini explains, as these examples are “more than just beautiful old vessels – they tell the story of Hong Kong’s craftsmanship, ingenuity and connection to the sea, and that’s a story we want future generations to be able to experience”.

James Barker, captain of the HKHVF fleet, who coordinates the repairs, maintenance and operation of the boats and can often be seen piloting them, adds, “Caring for nearly century-old boats is not easy. Every project you take on turns out to be much larger, more complicated and more expensive than you first envision. For example, the Gardner engine on Way Foong needed to be replaced, but that [British] company went out of business in the 90s, so we had to source everything we needed from other places.”

It is not just hardware that is difficult to secure. Experts who have the technical knowledge to carry out such repairs are dwindling in number as well, he says. “Everyone who used to do these specialised jobs has either retired or passed away. In the absence of all other options, we are forced to research, plan and take on the task ourselves,” says Barker.

“We recently had to pull the propeller shaft from So Fong and replace the rotten timber around the stern, which meant drilling a new hole through the replacement wood,” he continues. “We’re looking at the bones of these boats, not just making sure they look beautiful on the surface. Significant work is needed to ensure these vessels can last for another 100 years.”

As Giannecchini notes, preservation in its finest form means not only maintaining the physical aspect, but also the histories of these vessels. In an effort to share the stories behind the fleet, the HKHVF website has detailed introductions to each boat.

Some have lived lives rich with adventure and drama. Way Foong transported gold and silver bullion to and from ships anchored in Victoria Harbour, as well as chests of banknotes to HSBC branches on Hong Kong’s outlying islands. It was even used for “burning picnics”: junior staff from the bank’s note-cancellation department would burn sacks of old bills in the boiler room, back when Way Foong had its original steam engine, converting the to-be-disposed-of cash into fuel.

According to one account, Way Foong was taken up the Pearl River at the outbreak of World War II and scuppered to prevent it from falling into Japanese hands. After the war, its skipper reportedly returned to the bank to ask for his job back. He was told that it was his if he could find the missing launch. He did – Way Foong was recovered in 1945 and returned to service after a major refit.

Another HKHVF vessel, Tai Mo Shan, served as a film prop in Mamma Mia! (2008), appearing as the sailing boat that transports the three male co-leads – Pierce Brosnan, Colin Firth and Stellan Skarsgård – to the fictional Greek island of Kalokairi, where the wedding in the plot takes place. Tai Mo Shan had been domiciled in Athens at the time of filming and a broker linked the producers to its owner. While the boat was not in great condition, this suited the filmmakers, who wanted to show the fictional owner, played by Skarsgård, as a “scruffy” character; they even exaggerated its run-down look to drive the point home.

Tai Mo Shan was undergoing restoration work at a shipyard in Greece when the HKHVF became aware of it, in the summer of 2025, through a yacht broker’s flier. Arrangements were made to buy the boat, and it was delivered in October 2025.

Tai Mo Shan was built by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, in 1933, and left the city on a 16,000-plus-mile transpacific and then transatlantic voyage to Dartmouth, in Britain, which, by some accounts, included an attempt to spy on Japanese naval installations in the Kuril Islands.

Another vessel, Typhoon, was discovered by the HKHVF through research on Facebook. Built in 1934 at the Hop Kee Shipyard to a design by Harold S. Rouse, for the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, the boat enjoyed a successful racing career up until the relocation of its owner, back to his native Britain. Typhoon was in Scotland when it was acquired, also in 2025.

Late last year, Tracy Van Buskirk, a retired banker who enjoys exploring coastal Maine, in the United States, aboard a 30-foot retrofitted lobster boat, shared her recollections with the HKHVF after having googled the name “So Fong” out of curiosity and found out that the schooner, on which she had sailed in the 70s, from Stamford, Connecticut, to Singapore, was still afloat.

So Fong, a gaff-rigged schooner measuring 82 feet, was built on an Ah King slipway, on commission for American yachtsman A. Thornton Baker. It took around 250 artisans more than seven months to complete the boat. Following its launch in March 1937, So Fong sailed for about 30,000 miles, travelling through the Philippines, the South Seas, the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean and the South Atlantic before reaching San Juan, Puerto Rico, in April 1938. During World War II, the US Coast Guard requisitioned So Fong, according to a commemorative plaque aboard the vessel. After the war, it returned to the Pacific and was used for racing.

Van Buskirk recalls that, at the age of 21, in 1978, she had recently graduated from university after spending a year studying Mandarin in Taiwan.

“I had every intention of returning to Asia, but decided to spend the summer in my hometown of Fairfield to get a job. By early October, I had started planning my flights back to Taipei. One weekend, my mother invited me to go sailing with a family friend, on his 28-foot sloop. He asked me about my plans and volunteered that his son had been hired as first mate for a delivery job of a large schooner that was scheduled to leave Stamford soon and sail to Singapore. William Mathers, the new owner, had bought So Fong earlier that year and hired the captain, Don Kuhn, to take her on this 14,000-mile journey.

“I was intrigued and immediately drove to the Stamford Yacht Club to introduce myself and see about a berth. Kuhn was busy with last-minute arrangements but took a moment for a brief interview. After determining that I was healthy, held a current passport and had some savings, he said I was hired. We left two days later [on October 18, 1978].”

Van Buskirk and So Fong would reach Singapore on March 21 of the following year.
