If I had to choose one, I would probably choose mapo tofu.

The reason is that it’s a really good example of a recipe that uses a little bit of meat and very delicious fermented bean spices to give an amazing flavour to a plant food. For me, it’s a really good example of how Chinese food offers ways to eat healthily and sustainably but without sacrificing pleasure, because this dish is utterly delicious.

Do you have any ongoing projects?

At the moment I’m writing another cookbook, and it’s not just about one region. It’s more of a simple homestyle Chinese cookbook, a bit like my previous book Every Grain of Rice.

So it’s designed to give readers the tools of some traditional Chinese techniques to cook wonderful food at home, not always with Chinese ingredients, but to cook food that’s really delicious and quite healthy and exciting.

item.title: [SCMP] 80 years on from WWII, China’s interests lie in peaceful Asia-Pacific: Rana Mitter
item.description:
Rana Mitter is a leading historian whose research focuses on the impact of Japan’s invasion of China during the second world war on the development of Chinese politics, society and culture. He is S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School and previously taught at Oxford University on the politics of modern China. He was also director of Oxford’s China Centre.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

As China prepares to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II, what are your thoughts on the role of the conflict in shaping contemporary China?
item.content:encoded:
Rana Mitter is a leading historian whose research focuses on the impact of Japan’s invasion of China during the second world war on the development of Chinese politics, society and culture. He is S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School and previously taught at Oxford University on the politics of modern China. He was also director of Oxford’s China Centre.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

As China prepares to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II, what are your thoughts on the role of the conflict in shaping contemporary China?

World War II is one of the most important factors in the shaping of modern China, but it’s often underestimated, both in China and the West.

This was the greatest political and economic trauma of the 20th century. The invasion of China by Japan led to many millions of deaths. Many Chinese became refugees within their own country.

The infrastructure and the communications built in the 1920s and 1930s were largely smashed into pieces, so that was a huge influence in terms of having to start again after the war.

The war made it more likely that China would have a revolution rather than just reform after it ended, because economic and social conditions became so devastatingly bad that it opened up space for the Chinese Communist Party to really develop the revolution in the countryside.

Beyond that, many aspects of modern China that we think of as part of the revolution actually emerged during the war – such as the system of work units for example, that existed for a long time in socialist China under Mao Zedong and even beyond.

The role of women became more prominent in Chinese life during the war years. Many younger women also became involved in national defence, health and nutrition, trying to make society after the war better for families and more stable.

During the 1920s and 1930s, China was heavily split between rival military leaders. At the end of the war, China was much closer to becoming unified as a country, as many of those warlords were eliminated during the wartime period.

Although it would finally be the 1949 revolution under Mao that provided a solid unification of the country, the process began in the wartime years.

World War II continues to be very important in terms of remembering a time when different factions and parties, nationalists, communists and others came together against an outside enemy and were able to find a sense of national purpose.

How could Beijing use the 80th World War II anniversary commemoration as an opportunity to improve people-to-people exchanges with the West?

The problem is that China still isn’t very good at seizing diplomatic opportunities because it tends to fall back on language that is mainly about China’s complaints, rather than about opportunities that could really open up.

The opportunities tend to be expressed in very broad, positive but vague terms, and the complaints tend to be very specific. And the problem is, it’s quite hard to get people on your side if you don’t actually engage in a dialogue that seems as if both sides are genuinely talking to each other.

An example is cutting down the EU-China summit from two days to one. Beijing also insisted that the Europeans should come to Beijing, when actually it was China’s turn to come to Europe.

So Europeans have done these things – they’re diplomatic people. They say OK, but it’s not the easiest start in terms of suggesting that China is opening up a new conversation, where China is willing to actually be expansive and creative in its thinking.

So maybe a sort of reset of Chinese diplomacy is an opportunity to do that. So far, there aren’t many signs of that. China has, in the past couple of years, withdrawn from the famous Wolf Warrior diplomacy, but it hasn’t yet worked out what sits in its place.

Do you think Chinese officials understand how their diplomacy is viewed from an outside perspective?

Very smart Chinese diplomats are aware that China has a PR problem. Just because people now find the US much less predictable doesn’t mean that they think China is a safe bet.

So, finding ways to essentially define China – not just in words, but in actions and in patterns of behaviour – as a reliable partner, that’s the really key challenge for Chinese diplomacy in the next few years.

The language is sometimes there – not always, but sometimes – but the actions involve a lot of quite difficult and long-term effort. And so far, if that’s happening, it’s only at a very early stage of that process.

A lot of Chinese diplomats, publicly and privately, have said they thought the previous Wolf Warrior effort was a mistake, asking what comes next and how China actually takes advantage of the changing world order.

That will involve more than just hoping that people will feel alienated from America and automatically seek out China. They won’t. Well, that will not be enough on its own.

World War II ended in the Pacific theatre with two atomic bombs dropped on Japan. Now, 80 years later, Britain and France have announced joint cooperation on nuclear weapons and the US has once again deployed nuclear forces in the UK. What does this say about the future of nuclear weapons?

Nuclear non-proliferation is definitely much weaker than it has been. Many of the Cold War-era treaties between the Soviet Union and the US seem to be essentially falling away. Britain and France are primarily concerned with their own major security vulnerability as the future American position on Russia remains uncertain.

A lot of different actors are looking at new threats in the world and trying to work out whether their current nuclear stance is sustainable. Ukraine gave up nuclear weapons in 1994, which made it vulnerable to the Russian invasion. Many countries will be looking at Ukraine’s experience and trying to avoid that.

The US has engaged directly with Russia to end the Ukraine war but those warmer ties now seem to have cooled off. What is your view of the changing dynamic between them?

Right now, the person who is probably having to think most carefully about changing the US position is Russian President Vladimir Putin.

For much of the first part of the year, the Donald Trump administration tried to find ways to bring Moscow back into the negotiations about Ukraine.

But in the past few weeks, it’s become clear that President Trump thinks Putin has no intention of coming to a peace agreement. It’s possible that he may take a much more confrontational attitude with Russia.

The world was very surprised when Trump actually made the decision to bomb Iran. His general doctrine is that getting into wars is a bad idea, but when he considers it necessary he is prepared to use force – and that’s something Putin might now have to think about.

How could this changing dynamic in Russia-US ties affect China?

Maybe several months ago, there were some people in Washington who thought that it might be possible to detach Russia from China in a “reverse Nixon”, or “reverse Kissinger” play, but that is not a very widely held idea any more, for two reasons.

First, people realise that there is a very close relationship between Russia and China. This was made clear by Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi when meeting his European Union counterparts. For the first time, it was much more explicit that China would not wish to see Russia lose.

The other factor is the American idea that they could detach Russia from China and bring it close to the US has fallen away. People have seen that Putin has not changed his policy towards Ukraine at all and is bombing it more fiercely than before.

We’re likely to see a scenario in which the US tries to neutralise Russia as much as possible while still looking for a negotiation on Ukraine, but essentially there probably will be more concentration on pushing back against China alone.

What conditions could bring about the end of the war?

We don’t know what conditions it will take to come to an end, but we do know that, at least in the past few weeks, President Trump has reauthorised the supply of weaponry to Ukraine to fight back against Russia, which at one point he was holding back on.

Now it’s clear that weaponry is going to Ukraine and the war may last longer than would have seemed the case just a few weeks ago, when it seemed Ukraine might run out of ammunition.

The question becomes whether Russia can maintain its all-out war-based economy and conscription of soldiers, while keeping inflation – which is very, very high – under control.

The longer the Ukraine war continues, the less likely it is that Russia can do that, and the more weapons that are supplied by the Americans, along with the Europeans, the longer the Ukrainians can keep fighting.

Under former president Joe Biden, Washington and other Western capitals formed a united stance on a wide range of China-related issues. How will Trump’s presidency change that alliance on China?

Europeans are looking to negotiate on their own issues with the US, such as tariffs. The question of China has been put a bit on the back shelf but essentially, the issue is that China provides useful supply chains.

There is also a problem, in particular for Europe, of whether it can draw on China’s markets but not be overwhelmed by Chinese exports, particularly in areas like autos and electric batteries. Those problems are not really changed by the relationship with the US.

The EU has a whole variety of fundamental issues it needs to solve – about how it creates a new industrial model, where it cooperates with China and where it needs to restrict its market.

And in some ways, it’s learning from China, because China has heavily restricted its own market in some areas, such as online service provision. So the Europeans will also pick and choose where they feel vulnerable, opening up in certain areas and closing in others.

The Trump administration is still figuring out its policy on China. There are different strands of thinking that you can see from the outside, but how important they are in relation to each other, and how they will balance out in the end, is still unclear.

For instance, there are some traditional hawks, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and others, who take a view on China that in some ways would not have been that different from Republicans seven or 10 years ago.

But you also have the whole technology world – Silicon Valley and beyond. A lot of them are still very interested in making sure that the relationship with China is smooth.

Apple is one of the most profitable and innovative companies in the United States, but huge amounts of its production and connection still take place in China. Of course, some production has moved to India, but China is still really important to a company like Apple.

There has been a growing interest in moving more production and intellectual property back to the US but there’s no sense yet that this is a complete disconnection from China, and that points in a different direction from the hawks.

Then there is the question of what Trump himself thinks. It’s interesting to look at the tariff policy, because tariffs have been put on China but also on other countries, including traditional US allies.

Also, when Trump says “I like to talk to my good friend Xi Jinping. We can talk about things” – what does he want to talk about? Not clear.

Compared with other presidents, Trump seems to really like personal diplomacy. In other words, he believes that his personal relationships with leaders are the important thing.

Speaking of leadership diplomacy, what conditions do you think will be needed for Trump and Xi to meet?

I think a meeting between the two leaders is quite likely. Trump is announcing that the deal has been done with China. He would only want to go to China if the deal is kind of there, so he can mark it in a big ceremony and have a prominent meeting with Xi.

I don’t think he would want to go to China to negotiate. We’re moving into a phase where the US wants to get most of its tariff deals done within the next couple of months.

During his first term, Trump had a very grand welcoming ceremony provided by Xi in Beijing. I think he would like to do that again – a big, grand meeting that Trump will think of as a historic event, that showcases he’s able to do negotiations and deals with China in a way that other presidents haven’t been able to do. I think he would want to push quite hard in that direction. That’s my guess.

Are the two presidents likely to get along?

I think that’s perfectly possible. You might remember that when Trump invited Xi to Mar-a-Lago, he said that he gave Xi a big piece of chocolate cake. He never talked about giving chocolate cake to German chancellor Angela Merkel.

That’s a sign that he feels there’s some sort of ability to speak leader to leader in that sense. Xi has said less about Trump, but he hasn’t said any very publicly hostile things personally about him.

Will it stop competition? No. Will it stop conflict? Maybe. In some areas – I would single out technology – I think the US and China are going to be increasingly in competition and there will be less sharing of intellectual property or scientific development.

That would mean other countries could benefit from both, or they may have to choose a side. This will not change because of a meeting.

But can the two leaders talk about lowering the temperature and avoiding misunderstandings that could lead to military confrontation? That might be more possible.

Turning to China’s security environment, how might Beijing’s relations with its neighbours change, given the uncertainties of Washington’s policies during the Trump administration?

My guess is that China will be assessing how solid and secure American security guarantees are in Asia. There’s some evidence that the United States might want to maintain and maybe deepen its relationship with standing allies Japan, Australia and South Korea.

We know that Trump is interested in the Korean peninsula. In his first term, he wanted to do personal diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. But even when South Korea is going through political change and a lot of turmoil, there’s no sense that I’ve seen that the United States is stepping back from its relationship.

I would say that if you are looking from Beijing, the conclusion to draw at the moment is that things will change much less in Asia than in Europe.

Supposing American security guarantees, naval presence and alliances were withdrawn from Asia – the first thing that would be likely to happen is that Japan and South Korea would think hard about getting their own nuclear weapons. They have the capacity, science and the technology. They could do it, but they won’t do it at the moment.

in a strange way, Beijing’s best bet for keeping the region relatively nuclear-free is to encourage the Americans to stay. And most of its neighbours would share that analysis.

They want the Chinese market, but they also want American security. They don’t want either one to disappear. I think that’s what makes the calculation different in Asia and that will affect the way that China and the US deal with other countries in the region.

What about the South China Sea?

The South China Sea is probably one of the most potentially dangerous flashpoints, along with Taiwan.

The South China Sea has more of a chance of running out of control because it’s not just between two or three entities – seven or eight are involved. The US is not so directly involved in that.

But I would say that China is missing a big soft power opportunity, which it could take up at a time of uncertainty about American security intentions, of being able to provide reassurance to regional neighbours like the Philippines.

If China is not looking to increase its maritime and territorial claims, it could create a much better basis of trust in the region. But right now there’s much more military activity from China, not just near the Philippines but also off the coast of Australia, and that’s heightening tensions in the region.

How is the importance of Taiwan to Beijing shaping the security environment?

One of the most interesting things is that after repeatedly trying to take the island, Mao Zedong basically said to then-US president Richard Nixon, when they met in Beijing in 1972, that the Taiwan problem could be left to the side for 100 years.

That’s a reminder that actually the Taiwan question has not been a constant one at the forefront of China’s relationship with the world.

Right now, there are a whole variety of reasons that China needs to think about its changing place in the world. It has an opportunity to influence the world order at a time when the United States is changing its role.

It also has significant economic problems at home, in terms of creating new forms of employment, dealing with the way technology has changed labour markets, and stimulating domestic consumption, which the party has repeatedly said is a really important domestic priority.

In that context, you could say that with all those important problems, Taiwan doesn’t appear as a major solution or issue that will help to resolve any of them.

If you look at Chinese policy priorities, it’s very clear that the single most important task for the government is the economy.

China needs the Asia-Pacific region to be economically productive to get its economy going again. That means the attention has to be on the domestic economy and how it relates to a peaceful, calm Asia that does not have any sort of confrontation.

In five to 10 years, if current trends continue, the Asia-Pacific region could be even more of a driver of the global economy than it is now. It can become the most economically dynamic region in the world, with lots of foreign direct investment and expansion.

However, for that vision of Asia to emerge, the region needs to stay peaceful and stable and absolutely avoid wars. Any regional confrontations could put that economic future in danger and that would be very bad for China and its neighbours.

Alongside the nationalism that comes with the promise of building a powerful China, there is also a revival of traditional Chinese culture in both society and the official narrative. How do you think this will shape China’s governance and foreign policy?

This is one of the most interesting and important elements of what’s going on in thought and ideology in China today.

First of all, there is a real interest in what some people call traditional thought, or pre-modern thought, which includes the Confucian tradition but also lots of other areas, such as Taoism.

The Chinese government has been sponsoring publication of China’s canon of official writings, with the parts that suit contemporary politics tending to be stressed.

For instance, Confucian thinking does have an interest in proper hierarchy and this is something that is obviously very attractive to the Communist Party, because it wants people, essentially, to be stable and ordered.

But there are other ideas – such as individual self-development or self-cultivation, which could lead more to the idea that people should have individual rights – that are less popular with the party.

China’s political culture since 1949 has been heavily shaped by the Marxism and Leninism that underpins the Chinese Communist Party.

Many of the ideas are still there and you can hear them in the language of Xi and other top leaders. Even while they are praising traditional Chinese culture and wisdom, they are also pointing out that Marxism and Leninism still have significance.

How are these two things compatible? Actually, it’s not easy.

There was a TV show broadcast in Hunan province that got a lot of criticism on Chinese social media. It was called When Marx Met Confucius and was a way of trying to talk about the difficulties in combining these ideas.

There is actually quite an interesting and difficult tension in the way that these two thought systems operate in China today, but I think that they are both very much part of the debate.

How has the Chinese intellectual landscape changed in the past 10 years? Do you share the view that it can be summarised as a rise in nationalism, Sinification of ideas and declining critical voices? What other trends are you seeing and what are their effects?

In some ways, China’s intellectual sphere has narrowed, at least in public, but in other important ways, it has expanded.

The narrowing is real, and probably the biggest obstacle that China places in its own path to developing new ideas at home and being able to exert influence abroad. It’s difficult to persuade the wider world that you’re a force for new thinking if new thinking at home is heavily restricted.

In terms of subjects, including history, most people would say that the room for publication and discussion is much more limited than it was 10, 15 or 20 years ago. Many aspects of modern history are harder to research and write about in China today than in the past.

The most productive recent time intellectually in China was the late 1990s and early 2000s, when there was the most capacity to be able to speak more freely. That time will need to come again as China comes to grips with its new role in the world. It’s not possible to have a very narrowed intellectual sphere and a very wide influence.

But there are some areas where I think things are broader, and I’m particularly thinking about social media and the way it has expanded and grown so significantly in China in the past decade.

Lots of ideas actually are discussed at a popular level, even when there’s censorship a lot of ideas still get out there – not about top-level politics as that’s too sensitive to permit – but if you think about things like concerns about economic change, people’s concerns about their own financial situation, ideas about the position of women, society, feminism, those are quite visible in Chinese social media.

That is not the same thing as two or three scholars sitting in a think tank writing some big paper, but in terms of understanding social trends and how they are shaping China today, social media has been very valuable to reflect those changes.

How has the China studies community been affected by the changes of recent years? What will the subject look like, with a growing percentage of scholars outside the country unable to conduct interviews and on-the-ground research in China?

You have put your finger on one of the most problematic issues – the number of students studying Chinese languages and doing higher-level research in the West on China is going down significantly. It was never very high, but it was going up, and now the numbers are shrinking.

One reason is the sense that doing serious research in China – particularly for social scientists but also for researchers who need to use archives and libraries – is much more difficult than it used to be.

What real China researchers need is to be able to travel and set up their own agendas, to be able to do interviews at the local level that enable them to understand how local government works, or to collect large amounts of data that enables them to see how effective or ineffective particular policies are.

This is the work of real social science, and it involves transparency and openness on data and a willingness to welcome the gathering of data, rather than assuming that it has to be banned for security reasons.

So, although more scholars are coming back to China, opening up more capacity to be able to do real research in China is the next barrier that needs to be overcome.

There are a lot of brilliant Chinese students in many countries in the West who are doing significant social science and humanities research. But their Western equivalents who study China can’t do that kind of work in China, so it becomes very unbalanced.

What about your own experience with the Asia studies and Chinese history students you taught at Oxford and now Harvard?

When it comes to postgraduate students doing PhDs, a significant number are Chinese. We do still have some Westerners, but the problem is that they have to be enthusiastic about China, willing to learn its language and culture, and then be able to find a meaningful project to research.

It’s harder now to assure students that they can find a pathway to doing really good social science research inside China, so a lot of students just leave China out. If people say China is a very difficult place to do research and South Korea is easy, maybe people just decide they want to learn Korean instead.

The sense among Western researchers that it’s hard to do serious research in China has transmitted to students finding it difficult to find a career path if they do study China. I think that’s a great shame.

item.title: [SCMP] How Japan’s innovative Nakagin Capsule Tower is finding new life
item.description:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.
item.content:encoded:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.

Nakagin’s scattered course would have pleased its avant-garde architect Kisho Kurokawa (1934-2007), who conceived the design to emancipate what he called Homo movens (mobile humans). Many fans still demonstrate their unbridled enthusiasm for the building by donning zany get-ups inspired by its form – often described as a stack of front-loading washing machines.

In my mind’s eye, however, Nakagin had always been a colony of barnacles. That analogy borrows from the free movement of these crustaceans before anchoring themselves in place. But unfortunately, it was the unexpected immobility of Kurokawa’s capsules during their first phase of life that ultimately thwarted his vision that they be modular, interchangeable and recyclable.

That idea of impermanent permanence remains irresistible, however – at least in Japan. Which was one reason Metabolism captured the imagination of many during the country’s buoyant post-war expansion, making its name and ethos heard at the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo. Adaptable buildings and cities – with renewable nodes fed by circulation systems – sparked interest. Adding excitement was the promise of Expo ’70, whose theme was “progress and harmony for mankind”.

At that landmark event in Osaka, futuristic pavilions, including several by Kurokawa, allowed the forward-thinking to see for themselves the biomimetic potential of a movement whose proponents included other eminent architects, Kenzo Tange and Fumihiko Maki among them.

Nakagin, however, earned the kind of cult status accorded few other buildings in Japan. One reason was the charisma of Kurokawa, also a media personality and, towards the end of his career, a politician. His building was among the few examples of Metabolist architecture ever realised.

In late 2022, Ikko Yokoyama visited a warehouse in Chiba, near Tokyo, where salvaged Nakagin capsules, resembling pet Cyclops, awaited adoption. As lead curator of design and architecture at M+, she was there to see one of 23 pods that had been saved by the Nakagin Capsule Tower Preservation and Restoration Project, founded by former resident Tatsuyuki Maeda.

Hong Kong’s museum of contemporary visual culture was prepared for this inevitable moment, according to Yokoyama. Debate had raged for years about whether to preserve Nakagin whole, with Kurokawa himself shifting from yes to no. Ultimately, land value outweighed legacy, says Dytham, who had tried without success to persuade developers and hospitality groups to turn Nakagin into a boutique hotel. “It wasn’t sustainable to keep it there,” he says.

The decision to tear it down was made despite its uniqueness. Unlike anything the West had produced – except, perhaps, in the minds of Britain’s Archigram group of architects – Nakagin consisted of capsules “plugged” into the building’s towers, or cores, one 11 storeys high, the other two floors taller. Tight spaces between each pod impeded access and meant that repairs were difficult because “you couldn’t get in”, says Dytham. Worse, owners were unwilling to pay the high cost of detaching their capsules for upkeep every 25 years, as Kurokawa had warned they must. Decay set in, leaks appeared and damage from Japan’s frequent earthquakes saw the building’s exterior netted for safety. Additionally, the presence of asbestos complicated matters.

But M+’s capsule speaks volumes about their enduring appeal. A806 now stands beside another of the museum’s inspired acquisitions, Kiyotomo (1988), the sushi bar designed by Shiro Kuramata. Unlike that 656 sq ft restaurant – which was disassembled in Japan, shipped to Hong Kong and later put together again by the original contractors and an M+ team of restorers – Kurokawa’s capsule was purchased fully reconditioned.

The 2.78 metre x 2.69 metre x 4.21 metre capsule in the East Galleries is one of six standard units, complete with their famous round window at one end accommodating a circular blind that folds open like a hand fan. Also included within the 121.9 sq ft space are mod cons and a dinky unit bath, those tiny waterproof rooms sold as a single product in Japan.

“Like organ donation”, as Yokoyama puts it, parts for the capsule were harvested from others in the building because none of the pods survived with all of its original fittings intact. Kiyotomo’s neighbour now also boasts a new blue carpet and mattress, in addition to a fold-down desk, television and reel-to-reel tape deck, among other integrated features. Combine the service and payload modules of a spaceship and you get the idea.

Of the capsules plucked to safety by Maeda’s group, 14 have been sold to companies and museums, including M+ and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which purchased Kurokawa’s prized personal unit. Of the nine remaining, he says, four are to stay in Japan while five will head abroad.

Some have already been turned into display modules and mobile units and, next year, hotel-room conversions are expected, which should come as no surprise: in 1979, Kurokawa’s ideas also gave birth to the world’s first capsule hotel. New Japan Umeda continues to offer budget accommodation in Osaka.

Maeda’s is not the only group intent on giving the (in) famous corner building a second life. The Nakagin Capsule Tower A606 Project is named after the pod that another ex-resident helped restore several years before the building came down. This group, which owns seven units, has even more ambitious, albeit firmly parochial, aims.

“We plan to reconstruct a mini-tower using several capsules we own,” the group reveals via core member, architect Akiko Ishimaru.

“We aim to keep the reconstructed ones for 50 years [100 years after their completion] by continuing to use them ourselves. We want to utilise the capsules that were born in Japan and rebuild them in Japan.”

Crowdfunding has helped pay for the work so far. “The cost of asbestos control and investigation during the survey and dismantling, transportation and storage of seven capsules, storage of original parts, printing of a book with records, restoration of the interior of capsule A606, crowdfunding gifts [such as the aforementioned book], and fees consumed most of the total 8,673,000 yen [HK$443,000],” the group says.

Ishimaru’s efforts to keep Nakagin from history’s scrapheap underscores the passion in the project. But that’s not to say she fully enjoyed her year living in the building (and seven more working in two other capsules).

“One of my fond memories is drawing the actual survey plan for Nakagin Capsule Tower on my laptop at the original desk of Capsule A606 in August 2021,” she recalls, adding, “The 1.3-metre-diameter round window meant that the small room didn’t feel cramped.”

Having been designed as “hotel-like second homes” – or crash pads for salarymen – none of the capsules came with a kitchen. It was “very quiet”, Ishimaru recalls. The prefabricated steel modules didn’t share walls and, by 2013, when she moved in, there were only a few residents left. “Since it was so old and there was no hot water, I couldn’t even take a shower inside the capsule, so I stopped living there and used it as a shared office.”

Other assessments were bleaker. “From outside, the tower looked like a dying animal, sweating and greasy in the heat, trapped inside its wire netting,” reads an account by The Paris Review of Nakagin’s condition in 2016. “Looking up, you could see that some capsules had been half-filled with rotting garbage, a rippling line of trash drawn across their single windows. Inside, panels peel from the ceilings and mold crawls underneath; grime and seepage scorches the concrete with strange, bubbling forms.”

The reviewer added: “Kurokawa’s masterpiece was an utter, unsalvageable failure.”

And there’s the rub.

On whether Metabolism remains relevant in the 21st century, few can deny the importance of urban development that hews closely to principles of sustainability and flexibility. “The idea that buildings can change, grow and regenerate over time within a city may be increasingly needed to adapt to urban population growth and environmental issues,” the A606 group argue.

But how to label Kurokawa’s achievement remains as polarising as the fractious debates about whether the building should have been protected for posterity.

“It was an amazing success because he made it happen,” says Yokoyama, referring to how Kurokawa turned theory into reality and created a prototype. “It wasn’t just imagination.”

Dytham also believes Kurokawa got it “pretty right”, explaining that Nakagin was an early model. “If you’re building 10 of them, you get it. That was the first one.”

He adds that, for him, the building’s success had much to do with a design so simple that even a child could read and recognise it. “That would be a totally protected building if it was in the UK,” he posits. “Traditionally, here [in Japan], things are built in a temporary way.”

However, the recent wide dispersal of Nakagin capsules underscores the fact that Kurokawa’s vision has come to fruition. As Dytham says, “How many buildings have been taken apart and put all around the world?

“Taking [Nakagin] to the rest of the world is as important as just being all in one place.”

Metabolism was simply operating at its own pace.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Inconvenient truth’: Man City case spotlights realities of UK-UAE ties
item.description:
When Liverpool fans greeted Manchester City at Anfield on Sunday with jeers and banners demanding the Abu Dhabi-owned football club be relegated, they took aim at what critics have long dubbed “sportswashing” – the practice of using high-profile sports investments to launder a tarnished international reputation.

Focusing solely on public relations, however, obscures a much deeper network of high-stakes diplomacy and geopolitical economics between London and Abu Dhabi.

The reality behind the United Arab Emirates’ acquisition of the club is an “inconvenient truth” rather than a mere branding exercise, according to Simon Chadwick, a leading sports business expert and co-editor of The Geopolitical Economy of Football: Where Power Meets Politics and Business.
item.content:encoded:
When Liverpool fans greeted Manchester City at Anfield on Sunday with jeers and banners demanding the Abu Dhabi-owned football club be relegated, they took aim at what critics have long dubbed “sportswashing” – the practice of using high-profile sports investments to launder a tarnished international reputation.

Focusing solely on public relations, however, obscures a much deeper network of high-stakes diplomacy and geopolitical economics between London and Abu Dhabi.

The reality behind the United Arab Emirates’ acquisition of the club is an “inconvenient truth” rather than a mere branding exercise, according to Simon Chadwick, a leading sports business expert and co-editor of The Geopolitical Economy of Football: Where Power Meets Politics and Business.

Rather than buying influence through sport, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan’s 2008 takeover was the result of “intense diplomacy” that subsequently helped London navigate the global financial crisis that struck later that year, Chadwick said.

An emergency £7 billion bailout of Barclays Bank organised by Sheikh Mansour, involving Emirati and Qatari sovereign wealth funds, spared cash-strapped British taxpayers from footing the bill.

However, it later transpired that Barclays misled shareholders about the mechanism of the UAE’s £3.25 billion share of the bailout. They were given the impression that Sheikh Mansour had invested in his personal capacity, rather than through Abu Dhabi’s International Petroleum Investment Company, triggering a lengthy legal battle with British firm PCP Capital Group.

It ended in 2021 with a British court finding Barclays guilty of “serious deceit”.

Nevertheless, the City acquisition remained “part of a diplomatic landscape that saw Britain and the UAE drawing closer together”, said Chadwick, a professor of Afro-Eurasian Sport at the Emlyon Business School in France.

This was evident during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Britain in 2015. Rather than touring Anfield or Old Trafford, home of Manchester United, Xi went to City, where he was prominently photographed alongside then British prime minister David Cameron and Chancellor of the Exchequer George Osborne.

Chadwick, himself a generational fan of Championship team Middlesbrough, said it was “inappropriate” to describe the City case as sportswashing.

“This is not sportswashing, it’s sport diplomacy,” he said.

“The British government was part of this and now, of course, through this diplomatic activity, we’ve got a level of interconnectedness between the UAE and Britain the realities of which are proving to be unpalatable to a lot of people.”

These realities are reflected by the £30 billion of investments in Britain made by UAE sovereign wealth funds and state-owned enterprises over the last five years.

Alongside the much-vaunted urban renewal of Manchester as part of Sheikh Mansour’s strategic investment in the Blues, these injections into Britain’s defence, technology, life sciences and connectivity infrastructure have been a welcome boost after the Covid pandemic wreaked economic havoc – much like the Barclays bailout in 2008.

As mayor of Manchester during the Emirati-funded renewal of Britain’s second biggest city, Prime Minister Andy Burnham now finds himself trying to pull off a diplomatic rescue act to avert retaliation by the UAE.

Downing Street has made no secret of its worries that action by independent football regulators against City’s Emirati owners could have serious economic consequences.

Burnham, therefore, appears prepared to weather the domestic political storm, telling the BBC in an October 1 interview that he would be “really concerned to lose them” given that the UAE had been “such a huge partner” in building modern Manchester and turning City into a global force.

The prime minister’s initial response to the independent commission’s verdicts – which found the club’s leadership deliberately obstructive and evasive – was thus “tone deaf”, according to Guy Burton, a Brussels-based international relations researcher and co-host of The FootPol Podcast, a sports show focusing on the intersection of football and politics.

British newspapers have also noted that the Prime Minister’s Office, when approached for comment, has not disputed their reports that the UAE could freeze its investments in the country if independent regulators deem Sheikh Mansour’s ownership of City not “fit and proper”.

Shortly after taking office in July, Burnham called four Gulf leaders, including Mansour’s elder brother UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, to reiterate British support for their defence against Iranian air strikes being carried out in response to attacks by the US and Israel.

Their discussion further included ideas to “step up collaboration on technology and AI”, a Downing Street spokesman said in a statement.

The UAE is investing tens of billions of dollars in data centres, AI and other collaborations with US and European firms as part of a strategic drive to become a global leader in the field.

In addition to Burnham’s experience as Manchester mayor, his expectations of further UAE investment were fuelled by the free-trade pact Britain agreed with the six Gulf Cooperation Council states – the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman – in May.

London hopes the deal, the first free-trade agreement between the GCC and a G7 country, could boost the UK economy by an estimated £3.7 billion (US$4.9 billion) a year and increase wages by £1.9 billion annually in the long run.

The UAE is Britain’s biggest economic partner in the GCC, accounting for £25 billion of the £53 billion in bilateral trade in 2025.

It is home to about two-thirds of the roughly 300,000 British nationals living in the Gulf monarchies, with most clustered in Dubai, the country’s commercial centre, and more than 5,000 British-owned businesses.

With City’s appeal against the verdicts and further deliberations pending, any Premier League sanctions are unlikely to be unveiled until after the end of the season in May.

Burton also predicted additional fallout from other clubs “who feel they missed out on financial opportunities because of City’s financial doping”, much of which would play out during and after May, and “for years to come”.

“There are a lot of twists and turns still to come in this story, much as there are in the wider instability in the region,” Burton said.

With so much at stake, Burnham’s vow not to politically interfere in the case may ultimately prove to be hollow.

City’s case, the governance and application of rules within the Premier League, and the thriving relationship between Britain and the UAE “are embedded within a very dense network of interconnections between the two countries”, Chadwick said.

That means “it is an inconvenient truth for many people” that the City case might not result in the strict application and enforcement of rules through a “set of draconian sanctions”.

Instead, the outcome could be a “negotiated diplomatic settlement”, Chadwick said.

“But it’s not sportswashing,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] AI fuelling growth while putting Asia’s young workers at risk, IMF meeting hears
item.description:
An investment surge into artificial intelligence may be helping prop up a global economy battered by energy supply shocks, but the technology’s potential to cull jobs requires swift mitigation if Asia’s youth are to secure a place in the future workforce, delegates were warned at the IMF–World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Monday.

Soaring energy prices, persistent inflation and mounting debt framed the opening of the week-long summit, which was last hosted in the Thai capital in 1991.

Unusually, the US has not sent its Treasury Secretary to attend the gathering, despite triggering the energy crunch following its war against Iran, taken alongside Israel, in February.
item.content:encoded:
An investment surge into artificial intelligence may be helping prop up a global economy battered by energy supply shocks, but the technology’s potential to cull jobs requires swift mitigation if Asia’s youth are to secure a place in the future workforce, delegates were warned at the IMF–World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Monday.

Soaring energy prices, persistent inflation and mounting debt framed the opening of the week-long summit, which was last hosted in the Thai capital in 1991.

Unusually, the US has not sent its Treasury Secretary to attend the gathering, despite triggering the energy crunch following its war against Iran, taken alongside Israel, in February.

Since then, oil prices have oscillated around US$100 a barrel thanks to the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz, driving up inflation and forcing governments to drain reserves or borrow heavily to cushion consumers from high costs.

Yet the multi-trillion-dollar global plunge into AI and its supporting infrastructure – from data centres to printed circuit boards – had given a 3 per cent boost to a global economy bruised by successive crises, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

“AI – love it, hate it or fear it – it is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact,” said IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, citing the US, China and India as the main drivers of growth in the technology.

“That shift in [to a] higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at 3 per cent, despite the fact we’re being dragged down by the energy shock,” she told delegates, including finance ministers from across the world.

But the same technology serving as a sticking plaster for a wounded global economy risks undermining its workforce over the longer term unless policymakers act quickly to prepare their populations for the changes taking place.

“It is a slow-moving tsunami,” Georgieva said of the impact on employment. “We estimate 40 per cent of jobs will be augmented, downgraded or eliminated. In advanced economies, [that figure is] 60 per cent. [In] low income countries, [around] 23 per cent.”

“We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now … but we can be disciplined, draw lessons and act on them.”

Highlighting the upside of a technology whose capabilities and speed have thrilled and horrified people in equal measure, Georgieva said Asia’s ageing societies could offset shrinking workforces and declining tax bases with AI-driven productivity gains.

Advanced Asian economies could see an annualised growth increase of up to 1 percentage point from AI adoption, she said, while slower-adopting countries could gain between 0.2 and 0.8 percentage points.

To realise those gains, governments were warned to take a long-term view – especially in reforming education systems to equip graduates with skills needed to survive and thrive in the coming years.

“This is a whole new era,” Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam told the same panel on how smaller countries might also gain from scaled AI adoption.

“We should start with the recognition that growth is going to be critical to secure good jobs, but growth is not itself going to be sufficient. There is already a divergence between growth and job creation, and AI is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive.”

Global AI development remains heavily concentrated in the US and China, where leading foundation models are trained, hoovering up talent and capital as tech giants expand.

The resource-intensive infrastructure like data centres is frequently outsourced to developing nations, which often lack access to the higher-paid roles and training opportunities created by the technology.

To narrow that gap, Shanmugaratnam said Asian governments and private businesses must collaborate to ensure students acquire adaptable skill sets that can be continually upgraded.

Education systems would have to be retooled urgently to ensure young people entered the workforce with relevant skills, he added.

“The silver lining in job displacement is it’s going to happen task by task,” Shanmugaratnam said. “That gives us time to adapt, learn new skills and stay agile.”

Host country aspirations

The IMF was set up after World War II to stabilise the international monetary system, provide policy guidance and emergency loans to nations in crisis.

But critics say its bailouts have sometimes pushed borrowing countries deeper into hardship by imposing tough spending rules. Others condemn the organisation for maintaining Western economic dominance, noting that the US retains effective veto power over core decisions.

The IMF–World Bank annual meetings are held in Washington for two consecutive years before rotating to one of the institution’s roughly 190 member states every third year.

Thailand, which spent nearly US$35 million to host this year’s summit, is using the event as a showcase for its own economic ambitions.

The kingdom’s economy has logged growth of 1.5 to 2.5 per cent in recent years, struggling to overcome the lasting shock of the Covid-19 pandemic and trailing its regional peers such as Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam.

Host officials are framing the summit as an opportunity to position Thailand as a stable investment destination in Southeast Asia, highlighting its regional connectivity, regulatory streamlining and readiness to attract foreign direct investment – especially in data centres and core AI supply chains.

Thailand relied on billions of dollars in IMF emergency funding during the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis to pull it back from the brink. The lifeline came attached to structural reform requirements that eventually helped Thailand, alongside Indonesia and South Korea, stabilise and rebound.

Yet the country faces stark challenges, notably an education system that currently struggles to produce enough technical graduates to meet the demands of expanding AI firms.

Similar challenges face countries across the world as an estimated 1.2 billion young people turn 18 over the next 10 to 15 years. Across Asia, vast disparities in income, education, digital literacy and internet infrastructure persist.

These divides separate developed and developing nations, as well as cities and rural areas, leaving tens of millions of young people vulnerable to white-collar job displacement and linguistic isolation from English-dominated large language models.

“The most important thing is to remove the gap between youth and the system that shapes their future,” Sarah Rauzana, Chairwoman of the Asean Youth Organisation, told a separate panel. “We need to make sure youth are included in all of the policymaking process … from design to monitoring [and] implementation.”

Other panellists urged governments to keep pace with innovation by cutting bureaucracy and updating regulations to support young entrepreneurs launching start-ups.

“We see a lot of companies able to go regional [or] global from day one,” said Mei Chel Tan, global managing partner at the venture capital firm 500 Global. “Companies and entrepreneurs that grow with that global vision are the ones going on to create new jobs and new segments of the economy.”

But government leadership was critical to ensure the benefits of AI were widely shared, she added. “In Southeast Asia, we see incredible talent … but it has to be harnessed.”

item.title: [SCMP] US turns to low-cost Blackbeard hypersonic missiles to overwhelm Chinese defences
item.description:
The US Navy aims to field a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile on its carrier-based fighters, a weapon that could pose a new challenge to the air defences protecting Chinese warships and coastal military installations, experts said.

California-based defence company Castelion’s Blackbeard is designed to fly at more than five times the speed of sound and strike ships and land targets. Unlike more expensive hypersonic weapons, it is being developed with an emphasis on affordability and mass production.

In May, the Pentagon sought congressional authorisation and funding to buy more than 12,000 Blackbeard missiles for deployment across the armed services over five years. US Navy projections put the average gross unit cost at about US$385,000 in the financial years 2028-31.
item.content:encoded:
The US Navy aims to field a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile on its carrier-based fighters, a weapon that could pose a new challenge to the air defences protecting Chinese warships and coastal military installations, experts said.

California-based defence company Castelion’s Blackbeard is designed to fly at more than five times the speed of sound and strike ships and land targets. Unlike more expensive hypersonic weapons, it is being developed with an emphasis on affordability and mass production.

In May, the Pentagon sought congressional authorisation and funding to buy more than 12,000 Blackbeard missiles for deployment across the armed services over five years. US Navy projections put the average gross unit cost at about US$385,000 in the financial years 2028-31.

In contrast, the cost of Lockheed Martin’s larger Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) is estimated in US Air Force budget figures for the 2024 financial year to be about US$3.25 million.

The price difference could allow US forces to build much larger stockpiles and launch repeated attacks against Chinese warships, forcing them to expend defensive interceptors and potentially making it easier for larger, more powerful anti-ship missiles to hit their targets, experts say.

The Blackbeard could also threaten Chinese coastal anti-ship missile batteries and air-defence systems, although experts differed over whether American carrier-based aircraft could get close enough to strike such targets.

According to the US Naval Institute (USNI), the navy ordered 50 pre-production missiles in June and a further 444 in September and is seeking early operational capability this year – though budget projections and a Castelion announcement in April pointed to 2027.

USNI News reported that an F/A-18E/F Super Hornet showed in September that it could carry two Blackbeard missiles. The US Navy is planning to equip each Super Hornet to carry up to four missiles, it said.

The push for larger inventories reflects concerns about how quickly American forces could run short of long-range precision weapons in a conflict involving Taiwan, a continuing point of friction between Beijing and Washington.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

In war games published in 2023, the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US forces exhausted their simulated LRASM stocks within the first week in every iteration of a hypothetical attack on the island.

Meanwhile, Chinese military researchers have examined the various ways they could counter potential large-scale US precision strikes, according to Christopher Sharman, director of the US Naval War College’s China Maritime Studies Institute (CMSI).

Sharman pointed to a 2023 article published by the People’s Liberation Army journal Air Force Military Studies that examined more than a dozen conflicts involving US and allied long-range strikes. CMSI published an English translation in August.

The PLA authors recommended attacking US forces before they launched their weapons, jamming satellite navigation signals and coordinating drones, fighters and air-defence systems, Sharman said.

However, publicly available information did not establish whether the PLA had adopted those recommendations, he added.

The bigger question was not just “whether individual warships can intercept incoming missiles”, but whether the Chinese navy could “maintain an effective, integrated defence across the fleet” during a coordinated attack.

Sharman stressed that he was speaking in a personal capacity and his comments did not necessarily reflect the views of the US government, Defence Department or the Naval War College.

Peter Jones, a retired Australian vice-admiral and adjunct professor at UNSW Canberra, said hypersonic missiles forced defending forces to “detect, track, assign weapons about five or more times quicker” than against conventional subsonic anti-ship missiles.

A “layered defence” that would draw on the networked capabilities of ships and aircraft in a task group offered the best chance of countering such attacks, according to Jones. “Whether the latest Chinese destroyers can engage these missiles is unclear,” he noted.

Much would depend on the Blackbeard’s flight path and radar signature, as well as the effectiveness of Chinese radars, defensive weapons and electronic warfare systems, Jones said.

Another uncertainty is how much damage a Blackbeard strike could cause. The US Navy’s requirements specified a desired payload of about 34kg (75lb), although the missile’s actual warhead weight remains unconfirmed.

Timothy Heath, China expert and founder of security research firm Perceptum, said Blackbeard could be useful for “striking sensors such as radars that support anti-air missiles”.

Damaging those radars could make it easier for larger, more powerful anti-ship missiles used alongside Blackbeard to hit their targets, he suggested.

While Heath emphasises the missile’s supporting role, Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia Programme at Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, sees greater potential for Blackbeard to disable a warship on its own.

Calling it “a significant leap in US Navy capability”, Goldstein argued that the force of a high-speed impact could be “just as or more important than the warhead”.

Even one strike could cause “mission kill”, leaving a ship unable to fight and forcing it to return for repairs, he said.

Goldstein also argued that combining lighter and heavier missiles with long-range attack drones could make defending warships “especially challenging”.

Yet both Goldstein and Heath identified a major obstacle to employing the Blackbeard near Taiwan: the vulnerability of US carriers and carrier-based aircraft.

“The main limitation is the launch platform,” Heath said, noting that manned carrier-based strike aircraft were “expensive and vulnerable”. Beijing’s attacks could force US carriers farther from Taiwan, potentially beyond the missile’s effective range, he added.

Goldstein was more cautious, expecting US carriers to “operate on the margins of any conflict in the western Pacific”, potentially putting mainland Chinese targets beyond the reach of the Blackbeard.

But he predicted a possible role for the missile against PLA Navy warships operating farther into the Pacific Ocean and potentially threatening American logistics around Guam.

In contrast, Heath saw greater potential for attacks on Chinese coastal missile and air-defence systems, arguing that launching Blackbeard from carrier-based aircraft would “dramatically expand the flexibility and range with which the missile can be used”.

The Blackbeard’s effective range and ability to strike moving warships have yet to be publicly shown.

item.title: [SCMP] From laser shields to iPhone detectors: inside China’s booming secrecy industry
item.description:
A group of Chinese officials are in the middle of a highly sensitive meeting involving critical decisions yet to be made behind closed doors, with documents stamped “classified” spread across the table.

Suddenly, an invisible laser beams into the room, sweeping across a glass window and allowing the contents of the meeting to be transmitted elsewhere.

China’s Ministry of State Security laid out this seemingly futuristic scenario six months ago, warning government departments and other entities against a new form of laser-based eavesdropping potentially conducted by foreign spies.
item.content:encoded:
A group of Chinese officials are in the middle of a highly sensitive meeting involving critical decisions yet to be made behind closed doors, with documents stamped “classified” spread across the table.

Suddenly, an invisible laser beams into the room, sweeping across a glass window and allowing the contents of the meeting to be transmitted elsewhere.

China’s Ministry of State Security laid out this seemingly futuristic scenario six months ago, warning government departments and other entities against a new form of laser-based eavesdropping potentially conducted by foreign spies.

Sophisticated contactless surveillance technology like this relies on detecting vibrations in glass windows caused by sound waves inside a room. By directing an invisible laser beam at a window, receiving the reflected signal and analysing it, an operator can reconstruct speech from within the room, according to the ministry.

Dramatic and distant as that scenario may seem, solutions to these risks exist. Amid heightened fears of foreign espionage and data leaks, Chinese manufacturers are paying keen attention to client needs and racing to capture the skyrocketing market.

To fulfil the need to protect official secrets, they offer devices designed specifically to detect such laser eavesdropping tactics, as well as a growing list of devices and training to meet the mounting national security requirements in one of the world’s largest bureaucratic systems.

The boom coincides with technological advances, rising espionage fears and Beijing’s tightening national security requirements, creating new opportunities for manufacturers of secrecy-protection equipment.

As demand spreads from national authorities to local governments, companies are diversifying their products and services while seeking growth overseas, particularly in countries with close security ties to Beijing.

Lasers, curtains and Apple products

Any outsider would be surprised at the immense range of devices and technologies to maintain information secrecy available in the Chinese market.

Product catalogues from several secrecy-protection equipment companies obtained by the South China Morning Post showcase diverse products meant to address a host of espionage threats.

In the laser intrusion example, a monitoring system is capable of detecting and issuing alerts over incoming laser beams while identifying the direction from which the laser originates.

Another product uses laser-protection film that absorbs lasers of particular wavelengths while maintaining window transparency.

Then there are specialised curtains made from electromagnetic-shielding fabric that can block electronic signals and electromagnetic interference while providing protection against infrared thermal-imaging surveillance.

An insider said the products currently seeing the strongest demand were systems capable of detecting and blocking unidentified signals, including Wi-fi and Bluetooth signals from devices that are not on China’s approved whitelist for official use.

“Many advanced eavesdropping or covert surveillance systems are capable of wireless control via Wi-fi or Bluetooth from distances exceeding 100 metres (328 feet) – a range that may well extend beyond the defensive perimeter of physical security measures like on-site security scanners,” the insider said.

“As a result, systems designed to counter unidentified Bluetooth, Wi-fi and other signals have become a popular requirement.”

Among these unidentified-signal detection systems is another notable category: equipment that searches for signals emitted by foreign-made devices, particularly Apple devices, according to the catalogues.

Citing national security concerns, some Chinese government ministries and agencies have since 2023 required employees to stop using iPhones in the workplace.

Beijing has long restricted the use of foreign-made electronic devices and vehicles in certain areas of government compounds on national security grounds.

In 2021, Beijing barred vehicles made by US electric car manufacturer Tesla from entering government facilities and military compounds because of concerns about espionage.

The insider said covert anti-recording equipment was another growth area as companies updated and developed their products, with such devices mainly used when setting up secure meeting rooms and during overseas activities involving Chinese personnel.

While most devices sold by these Chinese companies are made domestically – product catalogues show that at least one also imports Russian-made anti-recording jammers to sell to Chinese customers.

Skyrocketing demand

According to an employee at a Chinese counter-espionage equipment manufacturer, the industry has existed for years but demand for its products surged around 2023.

“The company has been making secrecy-protection equipment for 20 years, and business had been neither particularly strong nor weak,” the employee said. “But since [2023], the value of orders has increased substantially year after year, and customers have become much easier to find.”

The company now has an annual output value of about 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million), according to the employee, who requested anonymity citing the sensitivity of the matter.

With brighter prospects for the sector, the company had also become more willing to invest in the development of more advanced secrecy-protection equipment designed to respond to emerging technologies, the employee added.

It is not entirely clear what drove the jump in demand in 2023, but it coincided with a series of major counter-espionage and data security developments in China.

In August that year, the Ministry of State Security set up an official account on WeChat, the country’s largest social media platform, churning out daily posts about espionage risks to the public.

Set up just one month after a new counter-espionage law came into effect, the account publishes weekly updates on typical cases of espionage and information theft to warn the public and officials of threats.

The ministry has also called for society as a whole to “jointly build a line of defence for secrecy protection and engage those in counter-espionage”.

Also in 2023, China passed major amendments to its 2014 anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage activities and the investigative powers of national security law enforcement agencies.

The ministry has repeatedly warned Chinese officials, students and tourists against recruitment traps and foreign intelligence operatives. The message comes against a backdrop of intense competition between Beijing and Washington, alongside its Western partners.

In July 2023, in a rare public comment, then-CIA director William Burns said the American agency was making “progress” in rebuilding its spy network in China after severe setbacks a decade earlier.

Beijing responded by declaring it would take “all necessary” countermeasures.

A year later, in 2024, China updated its Law on Guarding State Secrets, the first major change to the law since 2010.

Explaining the amendments, state news agency Xinhua said the revised law “makes clear that the state encourages and supports research and application of science and technology for secrecy protection … and fosters the secrecy-protection technology industry”.

The law also explicitly places secrecy protection within President Xi Jinping’s “holistic approach to national security”.

As a retired official from a local government secrecy-protection department noted: “Over the past decade, national security has gradually evolved from a relatively narrow and specialised field into a key principle within China’s economic, administrative and social governance.”

“China has made a series of adjustments to its policies, regulations and the way government departments operate to promote this shift,” said the retired official, who also requested anonymity citing the sensitivity of the matter.

Since 2024, the US Central Intelligence Agency has released Chinese-language online videos that explicitly seek to recruit informants from within China’s government and military.

Dennis Wilder, a former senior US intelligence official and policymaker, said the rapid growth of China’s counter-espionage industry stemmed “in part [from the fact] that both offensive and defensive intelligence collected remotely is growing in sophistication as AI comes into play”.

“China’s security system has always been massive,” Wilder said. “The technology of espionage and counter-espionage is advancing. It’s a predictable reaction to have new tools.”

Who buys the equipment and what they want

The industry insider said China had about 10 sizeable companies specialising in secrecy-protection equipment, many of which had some degree of connection to the defence industry.

The main clients of Chinese secrecy-protection equipment are military units, government departments at the provincial level or above, and state-owned enterprises dealing with state secrets, according to the insider, who noted particularly strong demand from companies in the defence sector.

The insider told the SCMP that the business was expanding into some local government departments where “construction of their secrecy-protection systems is still only at an early stage”.

Such ventures could already be accelerating.

The 2024 revision to the state secrets law stipulated that “governments at or above the county level shall strengthen secrecy-protection infrastructure and support the development and application of key secrecy-protection technical products”.

The law further required governments at or above the county level to include secrecy-protection work in their budgets.

According to the former official, “As secrecy protection develops into a mature industry backed by government regulations and procurement budgets, this is expected to create a self-reinforcing cycle in which security requirements and the market for protective technologies continue to expand.”

Anti-espionage training support

Besides the sales of devices, some secrecy-protection equipment companies help train officials travelling overseas in counter-surveillance and anti-eavesdropping techniques, according to another source familiar with the matter.

The source said companies were required to set up a room containing concealed surveillance devices, allowing officials to practise counter-surveillance skills and ultimately locate the hidden equipment.

“We teach the trainees how to use different types of portable counter-surveillance equipment, as well as the possible types and locations of eavesdropping devices. The training normally lasts one or two weeks and involves several rounds of assessment.”

“Sometimes the surveillance device they need to find is a stone inside a flowerpot. Sometimes it’s a piece of decoration attached to a dome light. They can be very well concealed,” the source added.

In January, China’s National Administration of State Secrets Protection published an article calling for stronger supervision, management and security-awareness training for personnel sent overseas on official assignments.

Eyeing growth overseas

Counting successes within China’s own borders, these secrecy-protection equipment companies are looking to expand their business overseas.

“Overseas sales of secrecy-protection equipment mainly involve government departments in Central Asian and African countries, particularly countries in those regions participating in the Belt and Road Initiative, including Tajikistan and Kazakhstan,” the source said.

Secrecy-protection equipment was generally not expensive, the source added, with a complete system typically priced at between 100,000 and 200,000 yuan (about US$15,000 to US$30,000), making it easily affordable for government agencies in developing countries.

A secrecy-protection equipment firm, which asked not to be identified, told the SCMP that its systems could be provided with support for local languages, including Russian, and that the company also offered comprehensive training on how to use the equipment.

Beijing has meanwhile continued to expand security cooperation with Central Asian and African countries, including exchanges and training programmes.

item.title: [SCMP] How China harnesses AI microdramas to shape public opinion at home and abroad
item.description:
Beijing is rapidly scaling up the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to produce short-form videos and microdramas in its publicity campaigns, aligning with directives stressing technology’s role in strengthening ideological work and guiding public opinion.

In contrast to sensational tropes dominating AI content across Chinese media platforms – such as Cinderella romance, rebirth for revenge and post-apocalyptic survival – a new wave of AI-generated miniseries weaves Chinese culture, policies and initiatives, developmental achievements and revolutionary history into engaging storylines.

They are mostly produced by Chinese publicity authorities and official media, usually in cooperation with private production studios and digital creators.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing is rapidly scaling up the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to produce short-form videos and microdramas in its publicity campaigns, aligning with directives stressing technology’s role in strengthening ideological work and guiding public opinion.

In contrast to sensational tropes dominating AI content across Chinese media platforms – such as Cinderella romance, rebirth for revenge and post-apocalyptic survival – a new wave of AI-generated miniseries weaves Chinese culture, policies and initiatives, developmental achievements and revolutionary history into engaging storylines.

They are mostly produced by Chinese publicity authorities and official media, usually in cooperation with private production studios and digital creators.

The latest example is Tie Ji De, or The Iron Remembers, an AI microdrama created by the news media centre of the People’s Liberation Army. Its first episode was released last Thursday.

The series features a unit of 128 troops safeguarding a telegraph transmitter and a hand-cranked generator with their lives during the Long March, a large-scale retreat between 1934 and 1936 by the Communist Party’s Red Army to evade the ruling Kuomintang forces during the Chinese civil war.

These state-backed AI productions form part of Beijing’s broader push to modernise its official messaging, leveraging emerging technologies to steer public opinion and make national narratives more engaging to audiences at home and abroad.

Beijing considers the efforts vital to maintaining political stability, fostering loyalty to the leadership and reinforcing its discourse power globally – to counter Western mainstream narratives that often frame China as threatening and authoritarian.

At a 2019 study session of the Politburo, the party’s top decision-making body, Chinese President Xi Jinping urged mainstream media to boldly adapt new technologies, mechanisms and models to maximise publicity outcomes.

Noting that fast-evolving technologies such as 5G, big data, cloud computing and AI were driving the expansion of mobile media, Xi pointed to the need for a “mobile-first strategy”.

“By leveraging mobile dissemination, mainstream media should firmly secure the strategic high ground in guiding public opinion, providing ideological orientation, transmitting culture and serving the public,” Xi said.

He reiterated the message at another Politburo study session in February last year, saying authorities “must step up positive publicity and public opinion guidance and focus on using modern science and technology to enhance social governance”.

In response to top-level directives on innovative publicity, local governments and official media across China have continually refreshed their dissemination toolkits to amplify the reach of state-sanctioned ideological and cultural content.

These updated channels range from building proprietary mobile apps that feature media convergence to introducing immersive virtual-reality news videos and launching digital collectibles that immortalise historical news moments.

Now, with generative AI technology flourishing, the spotlight has shifted to AI-generated content.

China rolled out its regulations for generative AI in 2023, requiring AI-powered content to conform to “socialist core values” – 12 principles that guide individual morality and public ethics to achieve a prosperous, harmonious and modern society under party leadership.
