Productions like The Iron Remembers, alongside other AI videos unveiled by Chinese publicity bodies, emerged amid the country’s AI microdrama boom.

According to a report from the China Netcasting Services Association in July, 367,000 microdramas debuted in the first half of this year, with over 1,500 new AI-generated series flooding the market daily, accounting for more than 74 per cent of the total.

Microdramas, usually rendered in a vertical format and lasting only a few minutes each episode, gained immense popularity before generative AI was introduced to their production process.

The tool can be used across all stages, from story adaptation and scriptwriting to character and scene generation, all the way to post-production, creating animation or live-action-style dramas.

In May, the National Radio and Television Administration launched a strategy to promote the refinement, popularisation and internationalisation of microdramas. Central to this push is the goal of producing 1,000 high-quality works annually on themes like mainstream values, historical milestones and regional cultures.

The broadcasting regulator has called for leveraging AI to boost efficiency, lower costs and enhance visual quality.

The Iron Remembers comes ahead of the 90th anniversary of the conclusion of the Long March on October 22.

This historical journey – during which Red Army troops travelled roughly 10,000km (6,200 miles) and suffered staggering casualties – has become a symbol of resilience and sacrifice that Beijing and Chinese mainstream media frequently draw upon to bolster patriotism and foster national unity.

According to Chinese media reports, the telegraph transmitter and hand-cranked generator at the centre of the series were the Red Army’s only pieces of communications equipment – so vital that a reinforced company was formed exclusively to protect them throughout the Long March.

The two machines are anthropomorphised with animated eyes and ears through AI, as shown in the first episode, which details the formation of the protection unit and the troops’ plan to dismantle the heavy machinery for a river crossing.

Another AI miniseries, The Hidden Gambit, similarly focusing on the party’s revolutionary history, debuted in September.

Based on a true spy story, the drama follows a female operative who assumes the identity of a high-ranking official to gather pivotal intelligence for the “Yangtze River crossing campaign” – a decisive battle during the civil war’s final stage.

The Hidden Gambit was produced under the guidance of Anhui provincial authorities to commemorate the party’s 105th anniversary.

Publicity bodies are also turning to AI microdramas to advance grass-roots policy initiatives and social governance.

Unveiled in February, the AI miniseries A Story of Town was produced by Yanqing town in Beijing to promote urban civic virtue.

The storyline follows A Niu, a young man who returns to his hometown to launch a business and whose uncivil daily behaviours lead to amusing mishaps.

The series charts A Niu’s growth as he adopts civic virtues, from keeping fire exits clear to avoiding unauthorised flyposting.

AI microdramas are also increasingly harnessed to promote traditional Chinese culture.

The Queen’s Sword, an AI series from state-owned news channel China Global Television Network that debuted on October 2, showcases the Shang dynasty civilisation of 3,000 years ago – an era historically documented primarily through oracle bones and bronze artefacts.

Other recent titles include Illuminating the Lamp of Spatiotemporal Connection, which debuted last Thursday, with backing from local authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province.

It showcases the intangible cultural heritage of gun deng, or “rolling lantern”, through a time-travel narrative spanning the Southern Song dynasty (1127-1279), the Republic of China era (1912-1949) and modern times.

These projects closely align with Beijing’s continuing call to preserve and revitalise Chinese culture, fostering cultural confidence to counterbalance foreign cultural influence.

Other AI microdramas are meant to display regional development.

The Ideal of a Tree, a series set in the Tibet autonomous region and released on September 30, follows a young musician travelling there to find inspiration and connect with her grandmother’s past. In the process, the musician witnesses Tibet’s progress in modernisation and ecological conservation.

The storyline also highlights young people’s reinterpretation of Tibetan culture alongside inter-ethnic exchange, thereby advancing Beijing’s vision of national ethnic unity bound by shared roots and a common future.

Foreign critics and human rights groups frequently accuse Beijing of pursuing forced cultural assimilation in ethnic minority regions like Tibet. Beijing has consistently rejected the accusations.

Beyond these featured productions, however, the rapid boom in AI microdramas has created mounting regulatory headaches for Chinese authorities, ranging from content plagiarism to copyright infringement and unauthorised likeness usage.

Meanwhile, the market’s chaotic expansion has also led to a flood of poorly produced content.

Chinese media reports say that the country’s broadcasting regulator has pulled 68,000 microdramas from the web this year alone, citing content deemed harmful, vulgar, child-inappropriate or copyright-infringing.

To address industry malpractice, regulators and major platforms have stepped in with stricter oversight.

In July, the broadcasting regulator published formal administrative measures regarding prior approval for sensitive or high-budget series, with a rule effective from September mandating explicit labels for AI-generated content.

Streaming platforms are also taking action, banning repetitive “cookie-cutter” characters while deploying automated pre-screening tools to detect copyright infringement and unauthorised likenesses before content airs.

The South China Morning Post previously reported that China’s broadcasting regulator had urged greater support for live-action drama to counter the rapid rise of AI-generated content.

item.title: [SCMP] Unsung turtle conservation heroes in Malaysia’s Sabah unite to fight poachers
item.description:
Roziah Jelali has a tip or two on catching a turtle poacher: carrying a pair of binoculars and having patience in spades are key to doing the job well.

The 36-year-old Malaysian volunteer ranger once spent three months in Sabah tracking a man whom she suspected of illegally capturing protected turtles. Once thriving off the azure seas of Omadal Island in the Malaysian state, many turtles had been hunted down, killed and sold for their meat, according to conservation experts.

Recounting the 2023 incident, Roziah said she patrolled the beach from dawn daily to keep an eye on the poacher. She would scribble detailed notes on her target’s movements at her stilted home, backed by tips from her network of part-time conservationists on nearby islands.
item.content:encoded:
Roziah Jelali has a tip or two on catching a turtle poacher: carrying a pair of binoculars and having patience in spades are key to doing the job well.

The 36-year-old Malaysian volunteer ranger once spent three months in Sabah tracking a man whom she suspected of illegally capturing protected turtles. Once thriving off the azure seas of Omadal Island in the Malaysian state, many turtles had been hunted down, killed and sold for their meat, according to conservation experts.

Recounting the 2023 incident, Roziah said she patrolled the beach from dawn daily to keep an eye on the poacher. She would scribble detailed notes on her target’s movements at her stilted home, backed by tips from her network of part-time conservationists on nearby islands.

“Every day after my patrol, I would sit near my house with my binoculars and watch him. He was initially operating on Bum Bum Island, then he came to Omadal,” Roziah told This Week in Asia.

“He would kill the turtle at sea, then when he returned, he would cut it open and cook it on the boat.”

Her careful surveillance led to the rescue of a live turtle and a crackdown against an illicit ring selling turtle meat in the waters of Omadal and the town of Semporna.

Using Roziah’s information, wildlife officials caught the poacher and an accomplice. They were accused of illegally catching five turtles, four of which were butchered for their meat.

Roziah did not learn the anti-poaching skills on her own. She received training from Sabah’s Wildlife Department and WWF-Malaysia while learning more about the rich biodiversity off the state’s east coast, such as the seagrass, sea grapes and green turtles.

She and four other women are part of a volunteer watchdog committed to protecting the marine life that once thrived around Omadal Island but has been threatened with extinction due to poaching. They are also adept at craftwork, regularly weaving pandan leaves into mats and baskets.

Their husbands also have strong links with the sea, as its sustainability is crucial to their jobs as fishers.

As volunteers with the Women’s Association of Omadal Island (WAPO), the women would share findings with their peers.

According to WAPO chairwoman Sitti Rasah Haji Abdul, the association has not recorded any turtle landings on Omadal and other nearby islands since last year. In the past, turtles would lay their eggs in guarded hatcheries, and this would help prevent attacks by predators like monitor lizards or theft by villagers.

While Sitti is disappointed about the disappearance of nesting turtles, she is determined to do her part to bring about their safe return.

Widespread illegal trading

Sea turtles have been a fully protected species under Sabah’s wildlife conservation laws since 1997.

According to marine life experts, the presence of these turtles is a key sign of a healthy marine environment. Through their grazing, green turtles contribute to the growth of seagrass meadows, which store carbon that is biologically essential for fish and shellfish. Nesting turtles also help move nutrients from the sea onto beaches and keep jellyfish populations in check.

But the threat of illegal trading faced by turtles extends beyond Malaysia’s Borneo shores.

The waters surrounding Sabah form part of the trafficking corridor spanning the Sulu-Celebes Seas between Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia, according to the wildlife trade monitoring group Traffic.

Turtle eggs are particularly prized by poachers, according to Elizabeth John, Traffic’s communications manager.

The Sulu-Celebes Seas accounted for most of the illicit wildlife trade activities involving turtles between June 2003 and September 2021, according to the latest available data in a Traffic report released in 2023.

“Our records from that study period showed cases of stockpiled dead green sea turtles, the discovery of live hawksbill turtles with missing scutes in the north of Sabah and other turtle parts seized several times in the Semporna district,” John said.

While Sabah’s law enforcement agencies have been active, the state continues to be a hotspot for illegal turtle trade.

“The seizure cases in Semporna district included people from island communities instructed by middlemen to poach turtles at turtle foraging grounds,” John said.

In November last year, police and wildlife authorities raided premises in Semporna and seized 570 hawksbill turtle scutes weighing 17.8kg (39lbs) and valued at US$3,450, believed destined for the black market. They arrested two people, including a foreign national.

Daunting challenge

Between eastern Sabah and the southern Philippines, the Celebes-Sulu Sea provides ready cover for wildlife criminal gangs to hide among fishers, cargo and passenger boats, said Ramli Dollah, a lecturer and maritime security expert at the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities in Universiti Malaysia Sabah.

“The same boats, operators, routes, landing points and intermediaries can move people or different types of goods,” said Dollah, who referred to their system of “co-riding and camouflage”.

The vast area in Sabah and beyond poses a formidable challenge for enforcement agencies to catch poachers and smugglers, according to Dollah.

Maritime security specialist Nazery Khalid, an adjunct professor at the University of Malaysia, Terengganu, said the vast Sulu-Celebes Seas were difficult for poorly resourced Malaysian and Philippine authorities to patrol.

“There may be cooperation among them in areas such as intelligence sharing, but without maintaining boots on the ground in the form of operationally fit vessels, traffickers can operate with impunity or outmanoeuvre the enforcement agencies’ vessels,” he said.

Sitti and Roziah consider their roles as complementary to those of the enforcement agencies as they pursue the common goals of boosting Malaysia’s turtle population and conservation of other species.

“If not me, then who will do it for the generations to come?” Sitti said. “As long as I am still able to carry out conservation work, I will continue.”

Sitti added that she and the volunteers faced constant risks of potential confrontation with turtle poachers and stormy weather when they were out on boat patrol.

These challenges do not faze Roziah. “We must have courage and determination. That is the most important thing,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why warm welcomes can’t stop Malaysia’s doctor exodus from Borneo
item.description:
On Facebook, public hospitals in Malaysia’s Bornean states have been rolling out “Selamat Datang” [welcome] banner posts to embrace medical staff reporting for duty.

Tawau Hospital on Sabah’s east coast recently published a group photograph welcoming newly arrived medical officers. Kinabatangan Hospital posted similar banners hailing arrivals across various departments, while in neighbouring Sarawak, Kapit Hospital accompanied its greeting with a portrait of a newly arrived doctor.

But behind the warm online welcomes lies a dilemma for Malaysia’s healthcare system: more than a third of doctors offered permanent posts in Sabah and Sarawak have failed to report for duty.
item.content:encoded:
On Facebook, public hospitals in Malaysia’s Bornean states have been rolling out “Selamat Datang” [welcome] banner posts to embrace medical staff reporting for duty.

Tawau Hospital on Sabah’s east coast recently published a group photograph welcoming newly arrived medical officers. Kinabatangan Hospital posted similar banners hailing arrivals across various departments, while in neighbouring Sarawak, Kapit Hospital accompanied its greeting with a portrait of a newly arrived doctor.

But behind the warm online welcomes lies a dilemma for Malaysia’s healthcare system: more than a third of doctors offered permanent posts in Sabah and Sarawak have failed to report for duty.

The no-shows highlight the difficulty of persuading medical professionals to relocate to the country’s Bornean states. Doctors cite family separation, uncertain career prospects and difficult working conditions as major hurdles – with many questioning whether to stay even after heeding the call.

Speaking in parliament on Thursday, Malaysian Health Minister Dzulkefly Ahmad said 382 out of 1,055 medical officers offered permanent appointments in East Malaysia had not reported for duty.

While the 36 per cent no-show rate was an improvement from 42 per cent in 2025, Dzulkefly said it was still not a result to be proud of.

Hard choices

For Dr S*, accepting a permanent appointment in Sabah meant leaving her family in Kelantan to build a new life alone.

The doctor moved from Kota Bharu to Sabah’s east coast in late September after her family encouraged her to accept the permanent offer. She said she had initially considered remaining on a contract in her home state.

Malaysia introduced fixed-term contracts for junior doctors in 2016 amid a shortage of permanent positions, making permanent appointments highly sought-after for their greater job security.

But accepting the post came at a price: moving from Kelantan to Sabah cost S nearly a month’s salary. Even after subsidies and reimbursements, she was still about 2,000 ringgit (US$489) out of pocket, mainly covering upfront rent and basic necessities.

“I have been adapting to the new environment, culture and language. The workload is demanding because we have a shortage of medical officers,” S said. “But I also have support from my specialists, nurses and fellow doctors … Even small things, like invitations to share meals, are very meaningful when you are far from family.”

Despite the support, S does not envisage staying indefinitely. “For now, I see about two years as the maximum period I can serve away from my family,” she said, adding that while she might consider staying up to five years if her family could join her, her ultimate goal was to return to Kelantan.

Other doctors have chosen not to take the leap at all. Dr AN*, another contract doctor, declined a permanent appointment in Sarawak to continue serving in Kelantan.

“My own health needs and my mother’s illness factored into my decision to stay in Kelantan as a contract [doctor],” she said.

AN appealed the placement decision, but after this was rejected, she chose to remain a contract employee and reapply for a permanent position in the future. Asked if she would have accepted under different circumstances, AN said: “My decision is final. I want to continue serving in my home state.”

The limits of incentives

The experiences of S and AN reflect the reasons outlined by Health Minister Dzulkefly in his response to Pulai MP Suhaizan Kayat in parliament.

Besides family separation, health and financial and logistical challenges, Dzulkefly said that doctors often declined postings due to a preference for urban facilities, concerns over future specialist training and difficulties ensuring eventual transfers back home.

To address these concerns, Dzulkefly said he had directed the ministry to study and implement a dedicated 30 per cent quota for specialist training for medical officers serving in Sabah and Sarawak.

“Today, our Hadiah Latihan Persekutuan [Federal Training Award] has 1,650 places, so 30 per cent – around 500 places – will be specifically for those who are in Sabah and Sarawak,” he told parliament.

Sarawak MP Kelvin Yii welcomed the announcement but added that stronger career incentives should be accompanied by better pay, improved accommodation and clearer posting terms.

“Each posting should state the specific location and the duration of service from the start,” Yii said in his statement on Thursday.

Dr A. Iswaran, who now works in private practice in Kuala Lumpur, described a different frustration: wanting to stay in East Malaysia but being unable to secure a permanent role.

After serving as a contract house officer and medical officer in Sarawak and Sabah, Iswaran contacted health authorities in 2021 offering to remain in Sabah if allocated a permanent position. His request was not granted and he later declined an extension of his contract.

Official correspondence he shared directed him to the standard federal appointment process, explaining that permanent roles fell under the health ministry subject to approval from the Public Service Commission.

Iswaran also recalled having to rent private housing with colleagues because staff quarters were not provided, noting that the additional allowances failed to cover rent, utilities and security deposits. During all of this, Iswaran was single. “I only had myself to look out for,” he said.

Dr R. Dinesh, a private doctor from the Klang Valley, was posted to Sarawak in 2014 – before the 2016 introduction of the contract system for junior doctors.

“If you [were] single and male, you [were] gonna be posted to Sabah or Sarawak,” Dinesh said, recalling the expectation among his peers after they completed their housemanship training in Putrajaya. Though he preferred Peninsular Malaysia, he decided to see the move as an adventure.

That included squatting at a friend’s place for a fortnight while starting work because there was no initial lodging and local hostels were full, and having to wait two months for relocation expense reimbursements.

Beyond reporting for duty

To ease the transition for new hires, Dzulkefly told parliament that the ministry had begun releasing placement results earlier and allowing eligible officers to claim full transfer allowances covering travel, meals and hotel accommodation.

But the Malaysian Medical Association (MMA) warned that official placement numbers might not necessarily reflect the reality on the ground.

In a statement on Thursday, MMA president Dr Sivanaesan Letchumanan said that feedback from the association’s Sabah branch suggested several hospital departments were experiencing a net reduction in medical officers. As a result, some doctors were forced to work on-call shifts every other day, with individual shifts lasting between 24 and 33 hours.

“Are the reported placements translating into an actual increase in doctors serving at healthcare facilities where they are most needed?” the statement said.

The association called for a facility-level breakdown of arrivals and departures, including clarification on whether official figures included doctors already serving in Sabah who had chosen to remain.

Addressing broader healthcare reforms, the government committed under Malaysia’s 2027 budget, tabled on Friday, to offer permanent positions to more than 9,000 contract doctors next year.

While the MMA welcomed the commitment in a statement on Friday, it stressed that job security alone will not solve regional shortages unless backed by a comprehensive workforce-retention strategy. The association also called for better incentives, improved working conditions and clearer career-development opportunities in Sabah and Sarawak.

“Ultimately, progress must be measured not merely by the number of doctors reporting for duty but by whether healthcare facilities have sufficient manpower to deliver safe, timely and quality care to the rakyat [public],” the MMA added.

For doctors like S in Sabah, while her colleagues’ support has helped her settle in, accepting a posting was different from deciding to stay.

“In the long run, I still want to return to serve in my home state and be closer to my family,” S said.

*Names have been changed to pseudonyms as the doctors are employed by the Ministry of Health and are not authorised to speak publicly.

item.title: [SCMP] As AI and the Iran war loom, China’s energy technocrats are on the fast track
item.description:
This is a special contribution from the Centre on Contemporary China and the World at the University of Hong Kong. Read the full report at the end of the article. It will be available on the institute website cccw.hku.hk from October 13.

With the rising strategic significance of energy, especially due to the need to support China’s artificial intelligence (AI) development, members of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee with energy backgrounds – the country’s “movers and shakers” in this strategic sector – merit closer attention.

Among them are former or current power-company executives, petroleum managers, nuclear-safety officials and specialists in water administration. Many built their expertise over decades, establishing themselves as energy technocrats before taking on responsibilities beyond their original industries. Their biographies reveal a recurring route into political leadership – deep specialisation first and diversification of political experience later, highlighting the growing presence and power of this leadership cohort.
item.content:encoded:
This is a special contribution from the Centre on Contemporary China and the World at the University of Hong Kong. Read the full report at the end of the article. It will be available on the institute website cccw.hku.hk from October 13.

With the rising strategic significance of energy, especially due to the need to support China’s artificial intelligence (AI) development, members of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee with energy backgrounds – the country’s “movers and shakers” in this strategic sector – merit closer attention.

Among them are former or current power-company executives, petroleum managers, nuclear-safety officials and specialists in water administration. Many built their expertise over decades, establishing themselves as energy technocrats before taking on responsibilities beyond their original industries. Their biographies reveal a recurring route into political leadership – deep specialisation first and diversification of political experience later, highlighting the growing presence and power of this leadership cohort.

More experience, greater representation

Our data set identifies 34 energy sector members, including 21 full members and 13 alternates. They account for 10.2 per cent of the 205 full members, 7.6 per cent of the 171 alternates and 9 per cent of the combined membership. Three of them were elected to the Politburo in October 2022, representing 12.5 per cent of its 24 members. As of this year, their median ages are 64 among full members and 60 among alternates.

By October 2022, 29 of the 34 had at least 10 years of energy experience. This included 16 of the 21 full members. Nineteen had careers spanning 20 years or more.

The comparison with earlier committees further illustrates the long tenure and solid leadership experience of these energy technocrats, especially among the full members. In the energy cohort, the share with at least 10 years of energy experience was 75 per cent in the 18th committee, falling to 67.7 per cent in the 19th before reaching 85.3 per cent in the 20th. Among full members, the number with energy backgrounds increased from 15 in the 19th committee to 21 in the 20th committee; within that group, the number with at least 10 years of experience increased from nine to 16.

A long apprenticeship

The career of Zhang Yuzhuo, president and Communist Party secretary of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, is illustrative. He began work at a coal research institute in 1985, combining research with progressively greater institutional responsibilities. In 2002, he moved to Shenhua Group, where he held senior management positions before becoming chairman in 2014. When he joined Tianjin’s municipal party leadership and became party secretary of the Binhai New Area in March 2017, he brought more than three decades of coal-related research and enterprise experience into local government.

That was a specialised career, but not a narrow one. Zhang’s progression from research to institute leadership and then corporate management placed him at different points in the relationship between technology and industrial production. The professional foundation remained rooted in the energy industry as the scale of his responsibilities expanded.

This is an important feature of deep specialisation. Remaining within an industry can involve considerable movement across functions – from solving technical problems to managing people, allocating capital and taking responsibility for operations. Each role exposes a different part of the same system and offers opportunities to understand how an engineering choice becomes a financial commitment, an organisational challenge and, eventually, an operating result.

The resulting knowledge is both technical and managerial. A manager who understands why a grid connection is delayed – whether due to network capacity, equipment procurement or the timing of another investment – can ask better questions of the organisations involved.

Read in this light, the long careers represent an extended apprenticeship in complex systems. Their significance lies in sustained exposure to implementation – what it takes to turn a plan into a functioning operation. Repeated responsibility for delivery can sharpen judgment about whether a timetable is credible and whether the organisations involved can meet their commitments. For those who later enter government, this experience provides a practical and solid foundation for much broader and more strategic decisions.

From an industry to governance

The next stage changes the scope of responsibility. Among the energy cohort in the 20th Central Committee, 22 had acquired party-government experience by the 20th party congress in 2022, in local or central posts. Their careers connect prolonged work within an industry with appointments spanning a broader range of public responsibilities.

Career diversification, in this context, means an expansion of governing responsibilities. The transition from responsibility for a particular enterprise or administrative field to responsibility for a wider set of institutions, interests and public priorities is a demanding task. China’s personnel framework provides institutional channels for such movement. The Communist Party has an established tradition of recruiting leaders from enterprises, universities and research institutions and allows exchanges across organisational boundaries. Technical experience can enter leadership selection through a system of party appointment and evaluation.

Liu Ning, who until recently served as Henan’s provincial party secretary, illustrates the scale of that transition. He began work in the Yangtze water-planning and design system in 1983 and later became chief engineer and vice-minister at the Ministry of Water Resources. After roughly 34 years in water-related work, he moved to Qinghai province in 2017. He subsequently served as governor of Qinghai and then Liaoning before becoming Guangxi’s party secretary in 2021. By the 2022 party congress, a long specialist career had been followed by senior responsibilities in three different provincial settings.

His trajectory illustrates two stages of increasing complexity. Water administration already requires decisions across connected territories and competing uses, whereas provincial leadership extends that problem across the whole economy. A water official may approach a proposed project through its implications for supply, flood protection or infrastructure. A provincial leader must place those considerations alongside employment, public finances, industrial development and social services. Earlier expertise remains useful, but its holder must now decide how much weight it deserves among competing claims.

Yang Jinbai, deputy secretary of Hainan’s provincial party committee and concurrently secretary of its Political and Legal Affairs Commission, followed a parallel route through electricity. He began work in power dispatch in 1994, progressing through technical and operational positions before taking senior roles at Guizhou Power Grid, China Southern Power Grid and State Grid. In 2018, after 24 years in the power sector, he became a vice-chairman of the Guangxi regional government. He became a vice mayor of Beijing in 2020 and was elected an alternate member of the 20th Central Committee.

His industrial career had already widened from dispatch and engineering to strategic planning and corporate management. The move into government expanded its scope again. In Guangxi, he concurrently headed the office responsible for planning and construction in the Beibu Gulf Economic Zone. Now his responsibilities on the Hainan party committee encompass public security, social stability and coordination across law-enforcement and judicial institutions.

Yang’s trajectory makes the distinction between the two stages particularly clear. Within the power sector, his responsibilities grew around a connected set of technical and commercial problems. His move into government transferred that experience to the regional economic agenda. His subsequent appointment in Hainan shows that diversification can extend across distinct functions of party-state governance.

A city cannot be governed like an enlarged enterprise. Its leadership must consider firms with conflicting interests, residents affected by development and public bodies pursuing different objectives. An investment that makes commercial sense for one company may impose costs elsewhere. A project that promises industrial growth may compete with housing, transport or public services for land and funding.

For an energy veteran, this changes the central question. Experience in industry helps explain how a project can be delivered. Governing requires deciding whether it deserves to be a priority, how its costs should be distributed and what other commitments must accompany it. This is precisely the substance of the second apprenticeship of governing. Higher office calls for negotiation across departments, choices under budget constraints and engagement with interests outside the original professional community.

The two stages reinforce each other. Professional depth provides a basis for scrutinising technical advice. Wider governing experience places that advice within a larger set of economic and social choices. The sequence is essential because depth and breadth address different weaknesses. Rapid movement across unrelated posts can produce extensive exposure without sustained understanding.

Energy technocrats, China’s security and AI capacity

This combination of deep energy expertise and broad governing experience helps officials manage the complex demands of energy security and AI development. It contributes to the rapid industrial deployment of cost-efficient open-source models, despite US chip export curbs. Energy veterans who developed technical competence alongside political judgment are uniquely prepared to anticipate and manage risks and to pursue long-term strategies. Power plants, grids and reserves take time to build, so waiting until a need becomes urgent can leave few options. Officials must judge when the benefits of early investment justify its costs and when preparing for a possible shortage is necessary.

Expanding AI capacity, for example, requires power infrastructure to be planned alongside computing facilities. In Guian, Guizhou, the supercomputing centre handles AI training orders from across China. As the surrounding data centre cluster expanded, a new 500-kilovolt substation entered service three months ahead of schedule to meet demand. The project illustrates the value of coordinating power and computing investment to bring computing capacity into use sooner and provide reliable electricity for training and running AI models.

Energy security also depends on investments made ahead of need. During the recent US-Iran war, oil stocks accumulated before the conflict helped China weather disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the International Energy Agency. Accumulating oil before the crisis illustrated the foresight energy planning requires – weighing demand prospects against the risk of interrupted supply. Using reserves effectively also calls for coordination across enterprises and government. China’s energy veterans can bring both industrial knowledge and governing experience to such decisions, helping the country prepare for external shocks while investing in future growth.

It is no coincidence that China has excelled in energy security while confronting the dual challenges of a global oil shortage and the massive electricity demands of the AI revolution.

item.title: [SCMP] How shadow banking feeds Myanmar while starving its military
item.description:
On a recent Friday night in a Bangkok dive bar, a group of young Myanmar exiles sang softly along to a mournful ballad played on an acoustic guitar.

None among the crowd had any plans to leave, either for their homeland or home for bed. They fled war, a broken economy and forced conscription into a military that seized power in the 2021 coup.

While their future in Thailand is uncertain, their ties to home are kept alive by the hard currency they send back each month to parents and siblings left behind in devastated village economies.
item.content:encoded:
On a recent Friday night in a Bangkok dive bar, a group of young Myanmar exiles sang softly along to a mournful ballad played on an acoustic guitar.

None among the crowd had any plans to leave, either for their homeland or home for bed. They fled war, a broken economy and forced conscription into a military that seized power in the 2021 coup.

While their future in Thailand is uncertain, their ties to home are kept alive by the hard currency they send back each month to parents and siblings left behind in devastated village economies.

Aung*, a 31-year-old from the government-controlled Bago region, used to work at a state-owned bank. But since fleeing Myanmar he has relied on a shadow banking system to bypass state-sanctioned remittance channels that take a hefty cut.

That means most of the 3,000 to 5,000 baht (US$90-US$150) he sends home every month reaches his mother and sister.

“I only use the agent in my home village. The exchange rate is better and the military does not get the money,” he said.

Village-level agents are the front end of Myanmar’s “hundi” system, a network built on kinship, trust and community that can deliver money to remote hamlets within a day or two, even amid conflict.

“My agent is like my brother, I trust him 100 per cent,” Aung said.

Rules enacted in 2024 require migrant workers to send at least 25 per cent of their earnings home through Myanmar’s official banking channels, with non-compliance punishable by travel bans and passport confiscation.

Last year, such remittances totalled US$5.6 billion, or about 38 per cent of foreign inflows, according to non-public Finance Ministry data cited by Bloomberg.

That pales in comparison to the US$8 billion that Myanmar’s government estimated was remitted in 2015, though this did include money sent through both official and unofficial channels.

A decade ago, total remittances were thought to account for as much as 13 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product. It is not known what that percentage is today, but it is almost certainly higher given the millions based abroad sending money back home.

Foreign direct investment, by comparison, barely topped US$1 billion last year, by Myanmar state media’s own admission.

The government, desperate for foreign currency to pay for essential imports, sees remittances as a quick and reliable source of cash.

Money sent by relatives abroad is also a lifeline for those left behind in a nation where inflation spiked to nearly 25 per cent in June, according to the World Bank.

The kyat, Myanmar’s currency, has lost about three-quarters of its value against the US dollar since the coup, its worth battered by conflict, natural disasters and economic mismanagement.

Giant currency swaps

Money sent home by Myanmar’s migrant workers through the unofficial hundi system rarely, if ever, crosses the border as physical cash.

Instead, it operates more like a giant currency swap. In Thailand, small sums of baht collected from migrants are pooled in border towns like Mae Sot and Mae Sai to pay Thai exporters directly for goods. Myanmar importers then hand over the equivalent value in kyat to hundi agents, who distribute it to migrants’ families while charging a transaction fee of around 2 to 2.5 per cent.

In Myanmar, a country that has been at war with itself for generations, this informal system has been in operation, in one form or another, for decades. It now dwarfs official banking channels and works, by comparison, like clockwork. Customers get a better deal too, enjoying an exchange rate that can be twice as high as the official rate of around 2,100 kyat to the US dollar.

It works just as well for Myanmar nationals living and working in Malaysia.

Ju*, a migrant from Yangon, said the hundi system was as easy to use as walking into a shop in Kuala Lumpur’s Pudu district or elsewhere in the Klang Valley, with the money arriving fast, at a better rate and without the daily withdrawal limits imposed by conventional banks.

Some people “have been cheated before”, Ju conceded. “So usually, we test an unfamiliar agent by sending a smaller amount first. Usually it arrives within a day.”

Chasing foreign cash

In Naypyidaw, former military chief Min Aung Hlaing’s government would like some of that money.

The coup leader swapped his fatigues for the title of president in April and his administration – civilian in name but military in character – needs foreign currency to pay for imports.

Thailand, meanwhile, wants the influx of Myanmar migrants in the country, nearly all of whom work, to be regularised, moving millions from the shadow economy into one that is taxable, or at least more visible.

As many as 4.6 million Myanmar nationals were based in Thailand as of September last year, according to the International Organization for Migration – forming what Thai government-linked think tank the Institute for Strategic Policy called “the largest single migrant-worker corridor in Southeast Asia” in a report published last month.

Their remittances “are a critical source of household income and national foreign exchange for Myanmar,” the report said. “Yet the overwhelming majority of these flows continue to move through informal channels – principally the hundi system – rather than through banks or licensed money transfer operators.”

Some Thai banks have partnered with Myanmar digital payment platforms such as KBZPay and AYA Pay to offer cross-border transfers at rates that now compete with the black market.

But opening a Thai bank account requires a passport and other documents issued or notarised by the Myanmar embassy, creating an impossible hurdle for exiles who crossed the border illegally or fled conscription into the military.

Thai authorities would also like the legions of migrant workers from Myanmar to pay into social security or health schemes so they do not place a strain on public services intended for Thai citizens.

“The issue for the Thai side is we have to find a way to pay for their health, education and social facilities,” said Pana Janviroj, executive director of the Institute for Strategic Policy, suggesting that employers could start paying a small monthly contribution to welfare funds for legal employees.

In the meantime, some of those who did use the hundi system “may be charged more, some are taken advantage of”, Pana warned, adding that both governments had a security interest in monitoring cross-border money flows because “a lot of grey money goes into this system”.

None of this is persuading the exiles back at the bar in Bangkok. Mistrust of Myanmar’s military-backed government just runs too deep.

“If I register, the government will know about me,” said Mark*, using an anglicised nickname. “Then I will have to fight in the army or they can cause trouble for my family.”

He had a more fundamental objection as well. “I don’t want to give the government any money to buy more guns and bombs to use on us.”

*Name changed to protect interviewee’s identity

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Bangkok’s World Gourmet Festival, where top chefs share the kitchen
item.description:
The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld.

Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner.

The pressures of collaboration
item.content:encoded:
The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld.

Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner.

The pressures of collaboration

Beyond now commonplace four-hands dinners and chef residencies, the World Gourmet Festival presents a unique set of challenges. Chefs must traverse language barriers, unfamiliar ingredients, and sky-high expectations from some of the industry’s most trained palates. For many, this tests more than culinary skill; it also challenges adaptability and creativity.

Josiah Citrin, chef-owner of restaurants Mélisse and Citrin in Los Angeles, acknowledges the pressure this event brings. “The expectation is always high, but that’s what makes these events exciting,” he explains. “In the kitchen, food becomes its own language quickly. Once you start cooking together, you find a rhythm, and that’s part of the fun of doing these events around the world.”

This balancing act – maintaining one’s gastronomic identity while embracing the unknown – is central to the festival’s spirit.

Pastry chef Puyachart “Boy” Puttawong of Saneh Jaan in Bangkok frames the goal precisely. “A successful collaborative menu should allow guests to recognise each chef’s individual personality while still experiencing a clear and harmonious connection from the first course to the last.”

Weaving a comprehensive throughline that connects each course, rather than jockeying for attention, helps diners understand the interplay between both cuisines and each chef’s culinary ethos. “Our intention is not to make every dish taste Thai, but to allow Thai culinary knowledge and ingredients to become part of the creative conversation,” Puttawong stresses.

Creating a cohesive dining experience amid such diversity can be daunting. Chefs must develop a menu together that reflects their individual styles while maintaining culinary continuity across courses. “Menu development begins with understanding each chef’s strengths,” remarks chef Pilaipon “Toi” Kamnag of Saneh Jaan. “Compromise doesn’t mean weakening anyone’s culinary identity; it’s about making thoughtful adjustments.”

Clavijo stresses the importance of listening rather than competing for space on the same plate: “I wouldn’t really call it ‘compromise’. If both chefs are trying to prove their identity in every single course, the guest feels that tension. A good partnership requires enough confidence to know when to speak and when to let the other person speak.”

Communicating can be a challenge in itself, with chefs from so many different countries taking part. But for many involved, food serves as a universal tongue, reducing friction.

Thanh Vuong Vo, executive chef of Coco Dining in Ho Chi Minh City, shares his perspective: “In a professional kitchen, communication goes beyond spoken language. You communicate through technique, timing, gestures, tasting and repetition,” he says. “If there is a difference in interpretation, we taste together and use the food itself as the common vernacular.” This fluidity allows chefs to communicate through actions and shared experiences rather than relying solely on verbal exchanges.

Zee Zheng, chef-owner of Fabula in Shanghai, observes, “I believe a chef is simply a messenger of nature. My role is to act as a bridge – connecting dishes while weaving in subtle local touches that add a sense of discovery.

“It’s all about both chefs working together to allow the ingredients to speak for themselves; that is what defines high-level cuisine.” This synergy cultivates an environment where innovation thrives despite the pressures of the event.

Ingredient-led approaches

Despite the challenges, one of the event’s most exciting aspects is the opportunity to experiment with niche Thai ingredients, from produce to proteins. For the chefs involved, these ingredients offer both inspiration and a challenge. Says Vo, “I want to understand the Thai ingredients and techniques first, then see how they can enter my own culinary language naturally.”

His goal is to create something that feels like a genuine conversation between Vietnam and Thailand, rather than simply combining ingredients from both countries. “Understanding their role in Thai cooking allows me to incorporate them into my own cuisine in a meaningful way while keeping the Vietnamese perspective at the heart of my cooking.”

This mindset of exploration is essential for chefs seeking to create dishes that resonate with both their own background and the local culture.

Clavijo’s approach at his restaurant, El Chato, is deeply rooted in Colombia’s ecological variety, and he sees Thailand as a mirror rather than a contrast. “Even though Colombia and Thailand are far apart, there are many similarities in our ingredients as both countries share a tropical climate,” he says. “Rather than forcing Colombian and Thai cuisines together, I prefer to find natural connections and let the products guide us.”

Julien Royer, chef-owner of Odette in Singapore, echoes this sentiment, emphasising the importance of understanding local flavours. “My culinary ideology revolves around the principle that ingredients are a reflection of terroir. My grandmother, Odette, was the one who taught me that respect for seasonality,” he says. For Royer, cooking with Thai ingredients is about respect and balance – finding a natural connection between two cuisines and letting them meet on equal terms.

The costs and benefits of participation

While the festival offers significant exposure and brand building, it also comes with sacrifices. Chefs must balance their responsibilities at home with the demands of such high-profile events. Citrin acknowledges this cost, stating, “Leaving your restaurant means leaving your team, your business, and your family. It has to have a meaningful purpose that extends beyond that one single event.”

Clavijo agrees, explaining that collaboration must go further than mere visibility. “The real value is exchange,” he says. “The lasting benefits of meeting other chefs, discovering new products, and creating ongoing relationships are what make these experiences worthwhile for chefs and attendees alike.”

A celebration of gastronomy

The World Gourmet Festival mirrors the evolving culinary landscape in Bangkok and Asia. As local chefs collaborate with international talents, they bring new perspectives and techniques to the fore. “As Thai chefs, we are proud to be part of the hosting city,” says chef Toi. “Bangkok is no longer simply a destination where international cuisine is presented; it has become an active and influential participant in the global culinary conversation.”

item.title: [SCMP] The EU’s China dilemma: how to counter Beijing without alienating friends
item.description:
In September, the Jaecoo 7 – a budget SUV from China’s Chery Automobile – made headlines when it shifted more than 10,000 units to become Britain’s bestselling car.

Christened the “Temu Range Rover” online, a nod to the cheap goods available on the Chinese online marketplace and the luxury 4X4 made by Jaguar Land Rover that it resembles, its success showed British drivers’ new-found taste for cut-price Chinese cars.

Overall, 23 per cent of new cars bought in Britain last month were Chinese models, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, with several electric and hybrid models ranking highly.
item.content:encoded:
In September, the Jaecoo 7 – a budget SUV from China’s Chery Automobile – made headlines when it shifted more than 10,000 units to become Britain’s bestselling car.

Christened the “Temu Range Rover” online, a nod to the cheap goods available on the Chinese online marketplace and the luxury 4X4 made by Jaguar Land Rover that it resembles, its success showed British drivers’ new-found taste for cut-price Chinese cars.

Overall, 23 per cent of new cars bought in Britain last month were Chinese models, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, with several electric and hybrid models ranking highly.

But days later, the booming Chinese car market was caught up in a wider European trade dispute.

Britain was considering matching EU tariffs of up to 45 per cent on Chinese-made electric vehicles to gain access to European manufacturing subsidies, The Times reported.

Brussels is also weighing import restrictions on Chinese-made hybrids, a category that includes the plug-in version of the Jaecoo 7. If adopted, London could be under pressure to follow suit.

The EU had long wanted Britain to align on EV tariffs, fearing that the country, which left the EU in 2020, would become an entrepot for cheap Chinese cars, which it says are flooding the European market.

Now, with its proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), the bloc potentially has a tool with which it can strong-arm London to follow suit.

“The UK example shows that you can have a negotiation position with the IAA,” said Nils Redeker, acting co-director of the Jacques Delors Centre, a think tank.

Redeker argued that the law could give Brussels leverage to pressure Britain into taking a tougher stance on Chinese car imports.

The act is the EU’s major foray into industrial policy after a decades-long love affair with neoliberal governance, during which the very term “industrial policy” became dirty words.

Yet, it has also raised questions among political groups in Europe and among its allies whether, in its frenzied efforts to protect its industry from China, the EU is mirroring the US policies it previously railed against.

“The IAA should not – even inadvertently – penalise the companies of close partners, which have invested deeply in Europe and become part of its industrial networks simply because their headquarters happen to be elsewhere,” wrote Kazutoshi Aikawa, Japan’s ambassador to the EU, in the Financial Times last month.

“Trusted international partners are part of Europe’s industrial strength,” he added.

Aikawa compared the law with former US president Joe Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act, a green-oriented stab at industrial policy that alienated Tokyo and Brussels alike.

The bloc’s recent steel restrictions, aimed at curbing the impact of Chinese overcapacity, led other partners including South Korea and Turkey to complain they were caught in the crossfire.

When adopted, the IAA would create rules through which EU funds, public contracts and other incentives are funnelled to EU-made products in sectors like EVs, steel, cement and clean technology, while speeding up permits for new industrial projects.

The aim is to bolster European manufacturing and reduce the bloc’s dependence on foreign suppliers, particularly China.

It would also impose strict conditions on large investments from countries dominating global production in strategic sectors, again primarily targeting Beijing.

“European workers and the firms must benefit … China has applied this logic for 30 years,” said Anna Cavazzini, a Green member of the European Parliament, involved in drafting the chamber’s own version of the law.

“The only shocking fact for me is that it took us so long to even consider investment conditionalities.”

But it is not without controversy.

A European preference would also disadvantage companies from partners such as Britain, Japan and South Korea, their governments argue, unless they secure exemptions, leading to negotiating scrambles such as the UK-EU talks.

This has sparked a vigorous debate as to just how much the EU, in its efforts to counter China’s industrial prowess, can and should cut itself off from the rest of the world.

Ignacio Garcia Bercero, formerly a top EU trade negotiator, said the bloc needed to be “extremely careful” that it does not throw the baby out with the bathwater as it heads in new policy directions.

“We must not have a situation where because of legitimate concerns relating to China … we are going to be fundamentally undermining the value of [free-trade] agreements,” Garcia Bercero said.

“It would be a huge mistake to … disrupt our relationship with those countries that normally [are] close allies of the EU because of these concerns.”

At the EU level, some members led by Germany want to allow countries with which the EU has made a free-trade agreement to be given access to the benefits of IAA.

“If you say this is all about China, then why is the Japanese ambassador writing concerned letters to the Financial Times? Why is the South Korean government telling us last week in Seoul there will be countermeasures to these proposals because this is simply an attack on us?” asked Dirk Gotink, a Dutch member of the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), at a recent debate.

This week, the EPP took it further: a small group of influential lawmakers from the group proposed scrapping the IAA altogether.

On the other side of the ledger sits a coterie of nations led by France who want the plan to be narrow geographically and broad in scope.

“This [allowing FTA partners in] would open up provisions to over 80 countries, 27 from the EU,” said Christophe Grudler, a centrist French lawmaker involved in drafting the parliament’s counterproposal.

“That’s about 110 countries out of 190 in the UN. So, it’s no longer made in the EU. It’s no longer made with the EU. It’s made everywhere.”

Research commissioned by the parliament suggested, however, that the debate showed Europe obsessing over details that barely move the needle economically.

An EU-only “Made in Europe” scenario would increase GDP by 0.13 per cent and employment by 0.11 per cent, according to the study’s modelling. And a “Made with Europe” scenario, including selected trading partners, would lift GDP by 0.19 per cent and employment by 0.16 per cent.

item.title: [SCMP] Are Chinese military aircraft already using a new joint air facility in Laos?
item.description:
Chinese military aircraft may already be using a new joint aviation facility in Laos, with satellite imagery showing twice as many K-8/JL-8-family trainer aircraft there as the Laotian air force is assessed to possess.

Eight of the two-seat trainer and light-attack aircraft were visible at Ban Keun Airport in commercial satellite imagery taken on September 30, according to Reuters, which first reported the images. More than two dozen military and support vehicles were also visible.

The image was taken a day after the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Centre and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy formally began operations at the airport, with a People’s Liberation Army delegation attending the inauguration.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese military aircraft may already be using a new joint aviation facility in Laos, with satellite imagery showing twice as many K-8/JL-8-family trainer aircraft there as the Laotian air force is assessed to possess.

Eight of the two-seat trainer and light-attack aircraft were visible at Ban Keun Airport in commercial satellite imagery taken on September 30, according to Reuters, which first reported the images. More than two dozen military and support vehicles were also visible.

The image was taken a day after the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Centre and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy formally began operations at the airport, with a People’s Liberation Army delegation attending the inauguration.

Beijing says the jointly maintained and operated centre is intended to strengthen training for Laotian air force pilots.

The Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force is assessed by the IISS Military Balance 2026 to operate about four K-8Ws.

The South China Morning Post could find no public record of Laos acquiring a new batch of K-8-family aircraft.

Possible explanations for the discrepancy include additional Laotian aircraft not reflected in published inventories, aircraft assigned to the new academy or the presence of Chinese military aircraft.

Chinese military aviation analyst Andreas Rupprecht said he believed PLA Air Force aircraft were among the eight visible at Ban Keun.

“In my opinion, not only possibly but certainly, since there are eight aircraft to be seen there and Laos itself only owns four,” he said, adding that the imagery could show four Laotian K-8Ws alongside four JL-8s from the PLA Air Force.

Rupprecht also pointed to apparent differences in their colour schemes, noting that Laotian K-8Ws had been seen in camouflage while PLA aircraft of the type commonly use a much lighter-coloured livery.

A satellite imagery expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, was more cautious in his assessment.

The expert said four aircraft were covered by tarpaulins, while the remaining four appeared lighter in colour – possibly consistent with Chinese aircraft – but sunlight reflection prevented a definitive identification.

Timothy Heath, China expert and founder of security research firm Perceptum, called the four-and-four interpretation “very plausible”.

But according to Brian Hart, deputy director of the CSIS China Power Project, even if some of the aircraft were operated by the PLA, their presence would not necessarily signal a significant expansion of Chinese air power in the region.

“These aircraft do not provide China any significant new ability to project air power in the region,” Hart said. “They are primarily trainer aircraft.”

The imagery also shows Ban Keun has the capacity to accommodate considerably more aircraft than Laos’ existing jet-trainer fleet, which Military Balance lists as comprising about four K-8Ws and three Yak-130s.

The satellite imagery expert said the apron appeared to contain about 24 marked parking positions suitable for small aircraft such as the K-8/JL-8. Few other facilities were yet visible, although construction was continuing, and the number of positions could indicate that aircraft would travel to Ban Keun for training, with enough space to accommodate joint training.

More broadly, Ban Keun occupies a distinct place in China’s small overseas military footprint.

Hart said in an interview when the centre opened last month that Ban Keun was China’s first acknowledged overseas military facility centred on air power.

According to official Laotian reporting, cooperation at the centre will include joint training and exercises, personnel development, humanitarian assistance and other areas.

If PLA aircraft were among those visible, their presence would demonstrate actual Chinese military aviation access to Ban Keun, said Isaac Kardon, an adjunct professor at Johns Hopkins University’s school of advanced international studies.

“Training and a strategically useful military presence can coexist,” Kardon added, saying that the main questions were who operated the aircraft, under whose command and with what permissions.

In January 2024, nine JL-8s from the PLA Air Force’s Red Falcon aerobatic team flew to Laos for celebrations marking the Lao People’s Army’s 75th anniversary, showing that Chinese military aircraft could operate from Laotian territory temporarily.

PLA aircraft have also temporarily used partner airfields in countries including Russia, Pakistan and Thailand for exercises and training.

What would distinguish Ban Keun from those temporary deployments, Kardon said, is whether the PLA had “reliable access” – an arrangement allowing it “to return and use the facility predictably, rather than negotiating each deployment as a separate event”.

He said an enduring PLA operating location would require three elements together: “reliable access, sustained support and a recurring operational role”, including personnel and facilities capable of maintaining, fuelling and supporting Chinese aircraft over time.

Kardon said fuel storage, maintenance facilities and communications would be relevant indicators, although they could also support an ordinary training establishment.

Calling Ban Keun a PLA aviation base would require clearer evidence about its standing mission, command arrangements and China’s control of the facilities, he added.

Hart said the joint facility’s location meant that even if China stationed more capable aircraft there in future, it would not fundamentally change the PLA’s ability to project air power in the region because Chinese aircraft could already reach the area from bases in China.

“Still, operating from there could help China to build experience with overseas basing – a valuable stepping stone if the PLA seeks to open bases farther afield in the future,” he added.

Whatever Ban Keun’s eventual status, the facility’s significance was primarily political and institutional, Heath said.

“This base not only shows China’s growing influence in Southeast Asia,” he said. “It clearly demonstrates China’s expectations of its Belt and Road Initiative partners.”

At the same time, Kardon cautioned that permission to train Laotian pilots did not automatically imply permission for Chinese aircraft to conduct regional intelligence or combat operations.

Ban Keun could represent “an aviation application of the Ream model”, he said, referring to the China-Cambodia Joint Training and Support Centre at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base.

“A standing, jointly supported aviation facility that enables repeated or extended Chinese deployments would be a meaningful development,” Kardon added. “Whether Ban Keun meets that description remains to be established.”

item.title: [SCMP] How a museum masterpiece’s life-size replica sparked rare US-China collaboration
item.description:
For anyone who has visited the Chinese galleries at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, there is one work that stops them in their tracks.

Stepping into Gallery 206, home to Chinese Buddhist art, visitors are met by a monumental wall – over 15 metres wide and 7.5 metres tall (nearly 50 feet by 25 feet) – covered in a Buddhist assembly so vast and majestic that it momentarily erases the Manhattan bustle outside.

Here stands the Medicine Buddha, a 14th century Yuan dynasty (1279-1368) mural originally from Guangsheng Temple in central China’s Shanxi province, glowing with mineral pigments and filled with serene deities.
item.content:encoded:
For anyone who has visited the Chinese galleries at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, there is one work that stops them in their tracks.

Stepping into Gallery 206, home to Chinese Buddhist art, visitors are met by a monumental wall – over 15 metres wide and 7.5 metres tall (nearly 50 feet by 25 feet) – covered in a Buddhist assembly so vast and majestic that it momentarily erases the Manhattan bustle outside.

Here stands the Medicine Buddha, a 14th century Yuan dynasty (1279-1368) mural originally from Guangsheng Temple in central China’s Shanxi province, glowing with mineral pigments and filled with serene deities.

The work left a lasting impression on Zhang Jian, director of the Meticulous Painting Institute at the Chinese National Academy of Arts, who visited the Met three times before 2023.

“The moment you step into the hall, you are overwhelmed by its awe-inspiring energy and ancient brilliance,” Zhang said.

“But back then, I never connected it to my own work. It was only when I later stood inside the dilapidated main hall of Guangsheng Temple in Shanxi that the two spaces clicked in my mind.”

The revelation sparked a groundbreaking journey.

Over the next three years, Zhang led a team of Chinese artists and scholars in working just inches away from the masterpiece, painstakingly recreating every crack, faded line and historical scar to render a life-size replica.

Most surprisingly, they even uncovered mistakes the Met’s own restorers never saw.

The 700-year-old treasure left China in 1928, was cut into sections and sold by impoverished monks for 1,600 silver coins to repair a collapsing temple roof.

More than 10 million Chinese cultural artefacts have been lost overseas since the opium wars of the mid-19th century, mostly through wartime looting and illegal trafficking.

After changing hands through international dealers, Medicine Buddha was officially donated to the Met in 1965 by Dr Arthur M Sackler.

While the physical repatriation of lost relics remains an arduous task, Zhang proposed an ingenious alternative: a visual homecoming through forensic, research-based copying – an exacting art form that replicates not just lines but hundreds of years of decay and restoration.

At a time when US-China relations face headwinds across trade, technology and geopolitics, cultural collaboration has carried on without fanfare.

On September 24, the first day of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US, the fruits of this cross-continental effort were unveiled in an exhibition at the China National Arts and Crafts Museum in Beijing.

Featuring a life-size replica of the mural among a collection of traditional Chinese and Buddhist paintings, the exhibition is scheduled to run until November 15.

“This systematic research-based copying is both an academic challenge and a cultural responsibility,” Zhang said at the opening ceremony.

“We are exploring a wall painting protection methodology with distinct Chinese academic characteristics, allowing ancient murals to re-enter contemporary cultural life,” he added.

Jason Sun, the Met’s curator of Chinese art, described the results achieved by the team in Beijing as having “profound historical and practical significance”.

“They offer deep insights and guidance for the future restoration and resplicing of ancient wall paintings at the Met,” Sun said. “We look forward to continued friendly cooperation.”

The project is the culmination of an initiative launched by the Chinese National Academy of Arts.

In line with Beijing’s broader strategy to elevate cultural heritage preservation as a pillar of national rejuvenation, the institute launched its mural initiative in 2016.

The effort was backed in 2017 by the China National Arts Fund, a state-endowed philanthropic fund established in 2013 and approved by the State Council, China’s cabinet.

For 13 years, central fiscal allocations have poured billions of yuan into hundreds of thousands of projects preserving national treasures and nurturing conservators.

This momentum was reaffirmed in September, when Beijing issued its 15th five-year plan for cultural heritage protection and preservation.

The sweeping joint directive explicitly prioritises the systematic conservation of ancient murals and ancient architecture, urging the leveraging of national funds and cross-border partnerships to build autonomous knowledge systems and talent pipelines.

The document also emphasises intensifying research into Chinese artefacts held overseas, tracing their provenances and deepening international cooperation in restitution and museum exchanges.

Over the past decade, the institute has surveyed and copied classic murals across more than 40 cave temples, monasteries and tombs along the ancient Silk Road in Shanxi, as well as Gansu province, the Tibet autonomous region and the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region.

By 2023, with help from the US embassy and consulates across China, academic links were established with the Met.

In 2024, the partnership was formalised, with the Met granting full authorisation and sharing ultra-high-resolution digital images.

Zhang’s team travelled to New York five times, spending seven to 10 days during each trip inside the Chinese gallery. The Met granted them unprecedented access – “the only such conditions in the world”, as Zhang put it – allowing them to set up isolated work zones and use specialised hydraulic lifts to examine high sections up close.

“The Met staff actively coordinated with visitors for us,” said Meng Ying, an artist on the team. “Though our lifts and lighting equipment occasionally blocked sightlines, visitors were remarkably understanding.”

“Many Chinese and foreign tourists came up to greet us warmly when they realised we were recreating this masterpiece for audiences back home,” Meng added.

While most mural reproductions are painted on smooth paper or silk, Zhang’s team insisted on the ancient technique of painting directly on a mud-and-straw plaster base. To ensure absolute authenticity, they sourced raw soil from the immediate vicinity of the original temple.

Most clay-based copies only reach about 80 per cent accuracy, but the team pushed for 95 per cent.

Matching colours under dim museum lighting was a challenge. On every trip to New York, the artists carried dozens of handmade mud test tiles and giant prints to lay on the gallery floor, comparing them directly against the original.

“It wasn’t just about picking a colour,” explained Han Maoyuan, another artist on the team. “Lighting, digital cameras and printing all change how a colour looks. We had to tweak our paints over and over again on site.”

Rather than painting on a smooth modern wall, the team layered their mud base in two stages to copy both the original texture and the scars left by past restorers.

“Real accuracy means respecting every chapter of the painting’s history, including its scars,” Han said.

According to Wei-Cheng Lin, an associate professor of Art History at the University of Chicago and faculty director of the Dispersed Chinese Art Digitisation Project (DCADP), such physical marks bear unique historical weight.

Fragmentation was the “necessary evil” that allowed these fragile images to be separated from crumbling walls and kept alive in art museums today, Lin said.

“The indelible cuts witnessed a tumultuous period of the early 20th century, when the cultural significance of ancient Chinese artefacts was still in limbo,” he added. “That fragmentation transformed the mural painting from a religious image into an artwork.”

The most surprising finding came when the team discovered that the Met’s earlier restorers had made several errors when reassembling the fragments.

In one case, the restorers decades ago misread the neck lines and misaligned the Medicine Buddha’s head by 5cm (about 2 inches).

“Western restorers are masters of chemistry and material conservation, but they were less familiar with the compositional logic of traditional Chinese brushwork and central-axis symmetry,” Meng said. “In Buddhist iconography, the central Buddha must project a dignified, perfectly aligned presence.”

When Zhang presented digital reconstructions to Met curators, initial surprise gave way to realisation. Curators accompanied the Chinese artists back into the gallery to inspect the mural at close range.

“They were astonished and admitted the tilt was real,” Meng recalled with a smile. “When we returned to New York for our next trip, a Met expert joked: ‘Ever since you pointed out that the Buddha’s head was shifted, the more I look at it every day, the more crooked it seems.’”

Far from causing friction, the discovery strengthened mutual respect.

“They truly appreciated our academic rigour and our willingness to point out and correct errors,” Meng said. “After all, this is what true academic exchange is all about. Meaningful academic exchange thrives precisely on asking questions and raising doubts.”

The team’s traditional craftsmanship has also been amplified by 21st century technology. They used high-precision cameras and MacBooks for data capture and iPads on lifts for colour matching.

The blend of ancient heritage and modern tech caught international attention when Apple executive chairman Tim Cook visited the team’s project workshop during his trip to Beijing for the China Development Forum in March.

Cook observed how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital tools were being applied to cultural preservation, from colour correction to virtual image reconstruction, according to Chinese media reports.

“I see AI as an amplification of the human, not as a replacement of humans,” Cook was quoted as saying after observing the workflow.

“You saw today some things that were being done to make life much easier in terms of recreation … whether it’s colour correction and some of the things that you saw posted here, all of those things can be driven by AI. I would advise, ‘Don’t fear it, embrace it.’”

Cook later shared his thoughts on social media, saying: “A new generation of art researchers is bringing China’s cultural treasures back to life.”

Digital projects aimed to “re-envision our cultural heritage in a virtual world that transcends spatial and temporal limits”, added Lin, whose team at the University of Chicago has extensively digitised other dispersed Guangsheng Temple murals across American institutions.

“At this level of understanding, collaboration on a global scale becomes necessary, and the digital paradigm we try to build could be extended to other cultures as well,” he said.

DCADP seeks to digitally restore scattered Chinese relics to their original heritage sites. It has collaborated with multiple Chinese institutions, including the Taiyuan University of Technology, the Tianlong Mountain Grottoes Museum, Tsinghua University and Xian Jiaotong University.

Across the United States, the Beijing team’s work has triggered a ripple effect. They helped the Cincinnati Art Museum in Ohio and the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Missouri reidentify the exact original positions of their own Guangsheng Temple mural fragments.

Inspired by the Met project, both institutions are now actively negotiating with the Chinese National Academy of Arts to initiate similar research-based copying projects for their collections, according to Han.

Later in October, the Met is to co-host an international symposium in Beijing about Chinese murals with the academy, marking the first time the New York institution has jointly held a major academic conference in China with a national research body.

The debut of the exhibition at the China National Arts and Crafts Museum also took place against a broader diplomatic backdrop.

On September 24, the first ladies of China and the US toured Chinese artworks and a gallery dedicated to Asian design at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art. Peng Liyuan praised the US for returning lost Chinese artefacts in recent years and urged both sides to forge deeper cooperation on cultural heritage.

Cultural heritage preservation has emerged as a fruitful front in Sino-American cooperation.

Since signing their intergovernmental memorandum of understanding to prevent the illegal import of Chinese cultural artefacts in 2009, the US has facilitated the return of more than 700 lost artefacts to China.

And just days before the exhibition in Beijing opened, US Homeland Security Investigations handed over 58 cultural relics and fossils at a ceremony at the Chinese embassy in Washington.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘A Hawaiian son’: Honolulu honours Sun Yat-sen as his landmarks vanish
item.description:
Eddie Flores pressed the button at a pedestrian crossing on King Street, then pointed across the road.

In the spring of 1910, Chinese revolutionary Sun Yat-sen lodged over there, on the second floor of a shop owned by a friend and fellow party member.
