“The government has also taken the issue directly to headquarters,” Unggul said, noting that the communications minister met representatives from Meta’s global public policy and safety leadership team in New York last month to push for faster deactivation of underage accounts.

“Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost,” he added.

Still, Indonesia’s proposed fine framework has yet to be legally codified and many question marks remain over how it will ultimately be implemented.

Unresolved issues include how to collect fines from companies with no local assets, how to accurately verify global revenue “and what due process exists when the same ministry writes the rules, judges compliance and imposes the sanction”, Unggul said.

Blocking sites, meanwhile, “hurts Indonesian users more than the companies”, he said. “And the government can order [content] removals, but it still has little visibility into how the platforms are actually designed.”

The threat of high fines could push platforms to invest more in safety-by-design and high-privacy defaults for children, said Indriyatno Banyumurti, executive director of ICT Watch, an Indonesian civil society organisation focused on digital literacy.

But he warned that legal clarity and consistent enforcement were key, stressing that child safety “should not depend solely on voluntary corporate commitments”.

Indriyatno said much would depend on how violations were defined, how compliance was monitored, how evidence was assessed and whether sanctions could be applied fairly and consistently.

Regional rules

Indonesia’s social media ban may have been Southeast Asia’s first, but it is far from alone in trying to make Big Tech take responsibility for children’s safety online.

In Malaysia, rules in force since June now bar under-16s from opening or maintaining social media accounts and require platforms to verify users’ ages. Companies that fail to comply face fines of up to 10 million ringgit (US$2.5 million), with further penalties for ignoring regulatory directives.

Vietnam is considering a draft decree that would limit under-16s to a view-only mode of social media, preventing them from posting content, commenting, sharing or reacting to other posts. Accounts would have to be registered using a parent or guardian’s details under the proposed rules, with platforms compelled to block age-inappropriate material and place caps on children’s online gaming time.

The Philippines’ approach has been more piecemeal. It already legally forces internet providers to block child sexual abuse material or face heavy penalties and has used regulatory pressure to squeeze direct concessions from platforms. Lawmakers are also considering introducing age limits and other measures.

In August, Meta and Roblox agreed to strengthen age checks, parental controls and content takedowns following talks with Philippine authorities over child safety and online radicalisation. A spate of school shootings this year also spurred officials in Manila to order Reddit and Discord to appoint local representatives to coordinate on online threats. Discord was briefly blocked before agreeing to cooperate.

Singapore requires social media giants to shield users, including children, from harmful material under its Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act that came into effect in 2023, with non-compliance carrying a financial penalty of up to S$1 million (US$781,500).

App stores have been legally required to verify the ages of users who want to download age-restricted material in the city state since April this year. And an Online Safety Commission, launched in June under legislation passed last year, has the power to order the immediate removal of harmful content and restrict offending accounts.

While these efforts have helped effect some change, analysts say the results have been uneven.

“Platforms do respond, but market size is a factor they consider,” said regional tech policy adviser Paco Pangalangan, a technology and human rights fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School in the US. “A large market might get more attention, while a smaller one might get a slower, more minimal version. Whether there’s a law matters too.”

By his count, most of the big social media companies do not even have in-country representatives in five of Asean’s 11 member states.

“So there’s often no real channel for regulators or civil society to raise problems,” Pangalangan said.

Strength in numbers

Individual governments, especially those that represent sizeable markets with credible enforcement mechanisms, may be able to force social media platforms to comply with their rules.

But global technology companies can also opt to deal with countries one by one, which analysts and advocates say makes it harder for smaller markets to exert sustained pressure. One solution could be to present a more united front.

“A regional coalition can push Big Tech to create child-friendly ecosystems in ways no single country can,” Unggul said. “Individually, each Asean country is a market platforms can afford to deprioritise. Together, the region is not.”

Pangalangan said that, taken as a whole, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations could leverage the region’s more than 400 million social media users to strengthen its hand in negotiations..

“Collectively, we have a market that platforms can’t afford to simply deprioritise,” he said.

“If we can agree on common standards, including requirements around how platforms are designed, there’s less room for platforms to play one country off against another or just wait things out.”

Allan Cabanlong, Asean regional director for cybersecurity and cloud services provider CyberCX’s regional cyber advisers programme and a former assistant secretary at the Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology, agreed that collective action could hand regional governments greater bargaining power.

“A broom with one strand cannot sweep,” he said. “We have hundreds of millions of users in Asean. If the Philippines were to stand alone, it would not be listened to.”

As this year’s Asean chair, the Philippines could push the protection of children online higher up the regional agenda, Cabanlong said, while the bloc could also work to strengthen its existing mechanisms for digital regulation.

Asean would not be starting from scratch. Its declaration on the protection of children from online exploitation and abuse, adopted in 2019, and associated regional plans of action already recognise online harm to children as a cross-bogrder issue.

Other frameworks on personal data protection – and a declaration on safe and responsible social media use, adopted last October – widen that scope to include online radicalisation and AI-related risks.

But few observers expect a single, regional law on children’s social media use to be the end result.

“Asean does not necessarily have to start by creating one identical social media law for all member states,” said Ysrael Diloy, executive director of Stairway Foundation, a non-profit children’s rights organisation in the Philippines.

“Given differences in national legal systems, regulatory structures and capacities, that may not be the most realistic starting point.”

Indriyatno agreed that a more realistic approach would be for Asean to agree on common expectations for factors such as risk assessments, minimum standards of platform accountability, privacy defaults for children and cooperation on cross-border cases.

“Regulators could also develop more compatible requirements for platform transparency and information sharing,” he said.

Alejandro Reyes, chief strategic officer of non-profit organisation AI Safety Asia, said national regulators would also need to share information and cooperate more closely.

“If Singapore identifies a serious failure in a platform’s child-safety systems, its counterparts in Malaysia, the Philippines and elsewhere should have access to those findings,” he said.

“Joint investigations, shared technical expertise and coordinated enforcement would make it harder for companies to exploit differences between national regulatory regimes.”

Such a baseline would not demand identical laws, but it would provide common ground in dealing with companies that straddle borders.

It would also carry risks. “The concern here is that child protection is part of a much broader framework of government control over online content and expression,” Reyes said, urging caution given the differences in countries’ legal systems, political priorities and enforcement capacity.

Other issues, according to Unggul, include the fact that Asean members currently compete for technology investment, have very different track records when it comes to free expression and make decisions as a bloc by consensus.

“Collective leverage only works if it is credible and rights-based, and that is where civil society across the region must make sure the coalition strengthens accountability rather than state control over content,” he said.

“Child safety must not become cover for censorship. Bargaining power comes not only from penalties but from legitimacy.”

Limits of laws

Governments can restrict access, require age verification and impose penalties on platforms, but they cannot regulate the behaviour of children and families, online child safety experts say.

Fandy Zulmi, programme manager at the Centre for Child Study and Protection in Indonesia, pointed to recent Communications Ministry data showing that three out of five Indonesian children had falsified their age to access restricted platforms.

Without stronger digital literacy, parental involvement and robust reporting mechanisms, Indonesia’s social media ban for children might simply move the risks “somewhere else”, he said.

“It is still too early to conclude that the policy has effectively deterred children from going online,” Fandy said.

Indonesia’s implementation challenge begins with the fact that there are between 60 million and 80 million children in the country whose circumstances differ enormously, according to Diena Haryana, founder of the Sejiwa Foundation, a Jakarta-based child welfare organisation.

“Where they live, what education their parents have, what digital parenting awareness the parents have, whether the parents themselves have digital skills – all of that varies massively, especially between somewhere like Jakarta and rural areas,” she said.

Some parents used social media platforms to keep children occupied while they worked, Diena said, while others were more aware of the risks involved with giving their children unfettered access.

“We all need to work much harder to make sure children understand what the regulation is, why it exists and how implementation should actually work,” she said.

But ultimately, it is the platforms themselves that bear the brunt of the responsibility for child safety, according to Pangalangan.

“They already know where many of the harms are,” he said. “They don’t need a law to fix things they control in their own products.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia budget: healthcare boost, Malay businesses to get more public projects
item.description:
Malaysia’s government will boost spending on social welfare while maintaining subsidies to rein in the cost of living under its 2027 Budget unveiled on Friday, as Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim seeks to shore up public support while under pressure to call for an early general election.

Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) has suffered bruising defeats in a series of state elections since December, as voters expressed disapproval of his administration’s failure to deliver on promises of reforms, which had helped the ruling coalition to secure the largest share of parliamentary seats in the 2022 polls. Malaysia’s next general election is due by February 2028.

He faces the prospect of presenting possibly the last budget of his term, as his federal partner but state electoral rival Umno demands immediate snap polls, emboldened by its decisive victories over PH in the recent Johor and Negeri Sembilan elections.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s government will boost spending on social welfare while maintaining subsidies to rein in the cost of living under its 2027 Budget unveiled on Friday, as Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim seeks to shore up public support while under pressure to call for an early general election.

Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) has suffered bruising defeats in a series of state elections since December, as voters expressed disapproval of his administration’s failure to deliver on promises of reforms, which had helped the ruling coalition to secure the largest share of parliamentary seats in the 2022 polls. Malaysia’s next general election is due by February 2028.

He faces the prospect of presenting possibly the last budget of his term, as his federal partner but state electoral rival Umno demands immediate snap polls, emboldened by its decisive victories over PH in the recent Johor and Negeri Sembilan elections.

Anwar, who is also finance minister, presented an expansionary budget of 460 billion ringgit (US$112.6 billion), with increased spending on education, healthcare and infrastructure along with higher wages and aid for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

“It must be stressed that the national budget is a moral statement of a responsible government. Malay traditional intelligentsia has long placed justice and trust as the core of governance,” Anwar said when presenting his budget in parliament.

He said the government expected to spend at least 80 billion ringgit (US$19 billion) on subsidies next year. This includes an estimated 40 billion ringgit to sustain fuel subsidies at pump stations and a 6.7 per cent increase in cash handouts to 16 billion ringgit.

The higher subsidy bill takes into account expectations of a prolonged energy crisis caused by the US-Israel war on Iran, which has already forced Malaysia to revise its 2026 budget estimates higher to 444.1 billion ringgit, Anwar said, from the initial target of about 419 billion ringgit.

“We have to remember that the cost-of-living issue is already there even before the Iran war started in February this year,” Irwan Shah Zainal Abidin, a senior associate fellow at Universiti Utara Malaysia’s Economic and Financial Policy Institute, told This Week in Asia.

“Maintaining the fuel subsidies is more about not making things worse rather than addressing the issue of living costs pressure.”

Middle-class Malaysians will benefit from a 1 per cent reduction to their 2027 income tax assessment, and there will be a new tax relief ceiling of 12,000 ringgit to accommodate additional categories including maternity care and elderly care for grandparents, AI subscriptions and vaccination for pets.

The package will offer some relief, but its impact on middle-income purchasing power will be modest, according to Doris Liew, an economist specialising in Southeast Asian development.

Those earning below the taxable threshold would not benefit from the tax relief, while families facing high housing, childcare and eldercare costs could remain under pressure, particularly single-earner households and workers with irregular income, she said.

“For these households, stronger earnings and more affordable essential services matter more than modest tax saving.”

The government will also raise the minimum wage for unskilled workers to 2,000 ringgit from 1,700 ringgit currently from June next year, while the wage floor for semi-skilled workers will be set at 2,500 ringgit for the first time.

Anwar said the government, supported by government-linked firms and major corporations in primary sectors such as banking and oil and gas, had paved the way for more reasonable wages in the country.

“Hence, I urge all private employers to do the same,” he said, adding that companies could only claim tax breaks on salaries paid through bank accounts to close loopholes that had long enabled the hiring of undocumented workers.

To win over the country’s Malay-Muslim majority, the government will expand their business access to nearly 70 billion ringgit worth of small-scale public projects, funding and investments, besides procurement opportunities with national energy giant Petronas and government-linked companies.

The country’s Malays account for 60 per cent of Malaysia’s 34 million population and whose support is vital for political parties to secure legitimacy to rule.

The government will also cut the cost of elderly care, allowing full service tax exemption for annual care centre fees of up to 96,000 ringgit. The government will also allocate 1.3 billion ringgit for cash aid targeted at elderly citizens.

The budget will allocate 1.5 billion ringgit for welfare aid for the disabled, including raising the wage floor by 300 ringgit to 2,000 ringgit for companies claiming benefits for their disabled employees and a 600 ringgit monthly payout for families and caregivers of disabled and bedridden individuals.

“The continued move towards more targeted assistance should help improve the efficiency of government support while reducing leakages. Subsidy reform continues to protect vulnerable households without unduly increasing the cost of living,” said Arshad Mohamed Ismail, group chief executive at local ratings firm Malaysian Rating Corporation.

To boost healthcare, the government will spend 47.7 billion ringgit in 2027 to build and upgrade facilities and improve access to primary and outpatient care and recruit at least 9,000 doctors on a full-time basis in the public health sector.

Education will get a combined budget of nearly 100 billion ringgit, to cover the construction of new schools and food aid for students at primary, secondary and university levels, besides lower repayment requirements for government student loans and tax breaks for companies that help their workers with government-back study loan repayments.

For local businesses, income taxes for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) will be brought down by 1 per cent to help cushion the blow from rising operating costs, while factories can claim sales tax refunds for machinery, spare parts and equipment sourced from local traders or distributors.

The Malaysian central bank will also offer an additional 5 billion ringgit in funding in 2027 for SMEs affected by the Iran war, adding to the 5 billion ringgit set aside for this year.

A total of 6 billion ringgit will be set aside to develop tech capabilities among Malaysians, which includes providing 100,000 free subscriptions to new AI applications on the market.

In an uncharacteristically blunt assessment of its own performance, the government said in its 2027 Economic Outlook Report that it had fallen short of delivering on promises to keep prices low, narrow the wage gap and improve healthcare access.

The report, released ahead of Friday’s budget, cited limited welfare coverage for self-employed and informal workers, fragmented delivery of targeted cash aid, substandard student performance, a chronic shortage of specialist doctors and escalating medical costs.

“Despite significant progress, Malaysia’s social protection landscape continues to face challenges in providing adequate and comprehensive protection across different forms of employment and household circumstances amid the rising cost of living,” the report said.

The government said it was on track to narrow the country’s deficit to 3.3 per cent next year through more efficient subsidy mechanisms, improving on the revised target of 3.6 per cent for 2026.

Inflation is expected to range between 1.8 and 2.8 per cent in 2027, likely tracking higher in the first half of the year due to carry-over effects from higher energy, food and other input costs before easing as the year progresses.

The economy is forecast to grow by 4.8-5.3 per cent this year before moderating slightly to 4.2-5.2 per cent in 2027, buoyed by resilient domestic demand and sustained global demand for Malaysia’s semiconductors and AI-related products.

item.title: [SCMP] Why a ‘confrontational posture’ won’t help China in the Arctic
item.description:
China should avoid taking a “confrontational posture” over a new security pact between the United States, Denmark and Greenland as it might end up being excluded from engagement on the emerging Arctic order.

That was the warning from Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies (NISS), a Chinese think tank, in a report released on Wednesday.

It also said the US was unlikely to turn the northern polar region into its “exclusive strategic backyard”. The report noted that Russia as well as America’s Nato allies including Canada and European nations could constrain how far a “northward Monroe Doctrine” would go.
item.content:encoded:
China should avoid taking a “confrontational posture” over a new security pact between the United States, Denmark and Greenland as it might end up being excluded from engagement on the emerging Arctic order.

That was the warning from Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies (NISS), a Chinese think tank, in a report released on Wednesday.

It also said the US was unlikely to turn the northern polar region into its “exclusive strategic backyard”. The report noted that Russia as well as America’s Nato allies including Canada and European nations could constrain how far a “northward Monroe Doctrine” would go.

The new pact signed by the US, Denmark and Greenland on September 22 allows America to establish two new military bases in Greenland and gives it a formal say in vetting foreign investment in “sensitive” sectors on the world’s largest island, an autonomous Danish territory. Those sectors include but are not limited to critical infrastructure and resource extraction.

The deal also bans states outside the Nato transatlantic security alliance from establishing military installations or deploying troops in Greenland without the consent of all three parties.

Observers have said the agreement could have an impact on Beijing’s engagement in the Arctic because its activities in the region could face more scrutiny, while its efforts to develop polar shipping routes could be challenged.

The NISS report echoed those views, saying that the deal would raise the political bar for Chinese capital, research and infrastructure projects to enter parts of the Arctic.

“But China still has considerable policy space,” the institute said in the report, which was posted on social media.

It noted that the Greenland agreement would not alter the rights of countries outside the region to take part in scientific research, navigation and global governance in the Arctic under international law. It said the pact also did not empower the US to close off the Arctic Ocean’s high seas or legitimate international shipping lanes.

But the institute did caution against two “misjudgments” when assessing the impact of American policy on Chinese interests in the Arctic.

“First, overestimating the speed of ice melt and the commercial value of shipping routes, leading to duplicated investment,” the report said.

“Second, treating all Western restrictions as a denial of China’s legitimate rights and interests, thereby reinforcing the other side’s security concerns through a confrontational posture.”

Still, the report said China remained the extra-regional force that the US was “most explicitly” seeking to guard against in the Arctic.

The Donald Trump administration has designated the western hemisphere as Washington’s top foreign policy priority.

That approach was framed in the 2025 National Security Strategy as the “Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine”, invoking a policy from more than 200 years ago that warned European powers against interfering in the affairs of the Americas.

Before the agreement was reached with Greenland and Denmark last month, Trump had repeatedly threatened to annex Greenland, citing national security concerns and the need to counter potential influence from Beijing and Moscow in the melting Arctic.

Unlike the US and Russia, China is not an Arctic littoral state. Beijing described itself in a 2018 white paper as an “important stakeholder” in the region and a “near-Arctic state”.

The NISS report said the Greenland security deal was a sign that the Monroe Doctrine’s scope – which traditionally focused on Latin America – was extending further north.

“[Washington] is taking the Arctic as an extension of North America’s homeland security perimeter, using military denial, investment screening and alliance rules to restrict foreign activities at the northern end of the Americas,” the institute said.

“Greenland’s particular value lies precisely in the convergence there of minerals, infrastructure and Arctic-North Atlantic routes, making it the most direct intersection of resource security and military security in the US ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’.”

But the report also noted that the Arctic was not a no man’s land that the US could unilaterally carve up, and most of the land and offshore resources in the region were already subject to clearly defined sovereignty and jurisdiction.

“The ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’ also has clear limits,” it said.

The report was released a day before the Arctic Circle Assembly – the biggest annual international gathering on Arctic affairs – began in Reykjavik, Iceland on Thursday.

American activities in the Arctic and China’s role in the region’s affairs are both on the agenda at the conference, which runs until Saturday.

The Arctic has become a new flashpoint for great-power rivalry in recent years, as climate warming and record-low sea ice open the region to shipping and resource extraction.

In its report, the NISS said the Greenland deal was unlikely to change Russia’s established presence in the region, but it could help the US to restrict rival powers’ access to strategic space in the northern reaches of North America.

Russia has the world’s densest network of Arctic ports and the largest icebreaker fleet, while the Arctic shipping corridor known as the Northern Sea Route runs along its coast.

The report also pointed to Canada’s long-standing claim that another sea lane – the Northwest Passage – lies within its territorial waters, noting that Ottawa could be wary of Washington trying to dominate the Arctic.

In addition, the NISS noted that Finland, Sweden and Norway all had their own resource, shipping, local governance and security interests in the Arctic, and that they could seek to retain a degree of policy autonomy while maintaining security cooperation with the US under the Nato framework.

It also argued that, given the European Union’s increased investment in recent years in Greenland’s communications, energy, mining and infrastructure, it might be hard for the US to “unilaterally securitise” those areas in future.

“Russia’s coastal advantages, Canada’s sovereignty claims, the autonomous interests of the Nordics and the EU and China’s continued participation all limit the expansion space of the ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’,” the NISS said.

“The US can strengthen its influence on specific areas, but it will find it difficult to turn the entire Arctic into an exclusive strategic backyard.”

It said the key to China’s future policy on the Arctic would be improving scientific research and shipping, expanding industrial cooperation, taking part in multilateral rule-making and continuing Arctic engagement.

“[China should] avoid being excluded from the process of shaping the future Arctic order while respecting Arctic states’ sovereignty and local community interests,” the report concluded.

It said China should continue investing in areas including polar science, sea-ice forecasting and ecological monitoring, improve the foundations for its involvement in Arctic shipping, and increase the transparency of commercial projects.

The institute also called on Beijing to remain involved in setting international rules on Arctic shipping, fisheries, environmental protection and ocean governance.

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s new air force base in Laos could rattle Vietnam
item.description:
A newly opened China-backed air force training centre in Laos could unsettle Vietnam, even as it aims to modernise Vientiane’s military and balance defence ties among Beijing, Moscow and Hanoi, observers say.

China’s National Defence Ministry said last Tuesday that the joint support and training facility at Ban Keun Airport in the Laotian capital would strengthen the expertise of local air force pilots and was “not directed against any third party”.

“The establishment and operation of the two institutions reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, aligning with domestic laws of both countries, as well as international law and common practices,” the ministry said in a statement.
item.content:encoded:
A newly opened China-backed air force training centre in Laos could unsettle Vietnam, even as it aims to modernise Vientiane’s military and balance defence ties among Beijing, Moscow and Hanoi, observers say.

China’s National Defence Ministry said last Tuesday that the joint support and training facility at Ban Keun Airport in the Laotian capital would strengthen the expertise of local air force pilots and was “not directed against any third party”.

“The establishment and operation of the two institutions reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, aligning with domestic laws of both countries, as well as international law and common practices,” the ministry said in a statement.

It added that the installation, widely described as China’s third overseas defence base, “contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation, as well as promoting regional peace and stability”.

China’s other two military facilities are in East Africa’s Djibouti and Ream Naval Base in Cambodia.

Operational activities have already begun at Ban Keun, with satellite images taken on September 30 by Vantor showing what security analysts believe are eight K-8 light attack jets ‌and more than two dozen support vehicles on a runway that is still being built.

Abdul Rahman Yaacob, a research fellow at the Rabdan Security and Defence Institute in the United Arab Emirates, said the facility indicated that Laos was looking to juggle defence relations between China, Russia and Vietnam.

“As Vietnam continues to maintain close defence partnerships with Russia, Laos could look to China as a counter balance,” Rahman said.

Modernising its air force and roping in China as a potential supplier and partner were also high on Vientiane’s agenda, but the move has another dimension: “a competition between Vietnam and China for influence in Laos”, he said.

Given Vietnam’s long history of exercising political, military and strategic sway in Laos, Rahman said Hanoi may see the latest development as “China encroaching into its area of influence”.

He added that Beijing could also monitor military activities in southern Vietnam by developing Cambodian naval and air defence facilities.

“Vietnam could be surrounded by China from the north and China-friendly regimes in Laos from the west and Cambodia from the south,” Rahman said.

‘Chosen partner’

Beyond keeping an eye on Vietnam, the Laos facility signalled China’s deepening competition with the United States for influence in mainland Southeast Asia, he said.

Hanoi and Beijing maintain a quietly tense relationship driven by a complex strategy of balancing intense economic interdependence against maritime territorial disputes in the South China Sea.

Rahman noted that China has the ability to monitor air activities deep into Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam if it decides to install the 700km (434 miles) YLC-8B long-range radar system.

Security analyst Olli Pekka Suorsa said from Vientiane’s perspective, Beijing appeared as an ideal partner to help develop the country’s small, capacity-constrained air force, which has sent its pilots to China for training.

“The [facility] is of great importance to the [Laos air force] and its future development road map,” Suorsa said.

The assistant professor of security at the Rabdan Academy in Abu Dhabi said “China has become the chosen partner” for the modernisation of Laos’ air force, whose SAIC LE500 and Hongdu K-8 jets are also Chinese-made.

He added that Chinese flight instructors would be sent to the new facility in the future, allowing local pilots to complete their military flight training syllabus entirely in Laos.

Vientiane could also seek to acquire budget-friendly Chinese combat jets, including the JF-17 and FTC-2000, Suorsa said.

Describing reports that the airfield would be occupied by Chinese combat aircraft as implausible, Suorsa said the facility had limited infrastructure and runway to support a large Chinese air force contingent.

With a single 2,000-metre runway, Suorsa said it was relatively short for military operations as Chinese airbases under the Southern Theatre Command generally had runways of about 2,500 metres.

In addition, China already had a significant airbase network close to Laos and Vietnam across Yunnan and Guangxi provinces, as well as on Hainan Island, under the Southern Theatre Command, he noted.

“For operations in mainland Southeast Asia, the PLA Air Force has a broad network of bases that provide it with significant reach,” Suorsa said, adding that China’s growing fleet of aerial refuelling aircraft could further extend the reach of its tactical and strategic aircraft without the need to base them in Laos.

“Taken together, the fear of China using the new facility as a forward base is likely overblown,” he said, adding that China’s military and civilian aid to Laos had been extensive over the past two decades, including in the Kingdom’s aviation sector.

Simon Creak, an associate history professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore and modern Southeast Asia historian, said the training, equipment and infrastructure benefits for Laos were clear.

“A joint facility like this delivers something Laos cannot develop by itself,” Creak said.

Though Laos has similar arrangements with China in other areas of development and infrastructure, it was the first time the country used this model to strengthen its military capacity, he said.

“It is unprecedented in this sense.”

Laos and China have long-standing defence ties that include holding the “Friendship Shield” drills and providing modern military equipment, maintenance support and training to Vientiane.

Keith Barney, an associate professor at the Australian National University and country expert on Laos, said there was a broader connection between the Ban Keun air facility and the US$6 billion Laos-China Railway, both built with Chinese support.

During the 2024 exercise near Vientiane, the rail link was used to move personnel and military equipment. Vehicles were unloaded at a station some 25km from Ban Keun.

Ban Keun’s under-construction runway could potentially be extended from 2,000 metres to 3,000 metres (9,842 feet), enabling longer-range aircraft to operate from there, Barney said.

“Infrastructure can have both civilian and military uses and infrastructure can become strategic,” he said, adding that the facility could potentially acquire wider logistical or operational functions over time.

Barney said Laos’ need for Chinese financial support might constrain its room for manoeuvre in negotiations with Beijing, including over military cooperation and access to infrastructure.

“I would not assume that this means China has imposed particular terms on Laos in the case of Ban Keun, but the wider debt relationship is relevant to understanding the context in which such agreements are made.”

Laos faces a severe debt crisis with public and external debt exceeding up to 118 per cent of its gross domestic product, struggling to meet its financing and repayment obligations.

Massive financial losses in the state-run energy sector and heavy infrastructure overborrowing from Chinese banks have largely contributed to the situation.

item.title: [SCMP] Taipei’s dilemma over history deepens with Xi-Trump praise of WWII Flying Tigers
item.description:
Taipei’s dilemma over its history during World War II appeared to deepen as Beijing and Washington looked to the Flying Tigers as a source of connection and goodwill during last month’s Xi–Trump summit.

US President Donald Trump’s description of China as an American ally during the war has raised concerns in Taiwan that what could have been a valuable historical connection with the United States ended up benefiting Beijing’s ties with Washington.

The dilemma resurfaced after Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping repeatedly invoked wartime Sino-US cooperation during Xi’s visit to Washington last week.
item.content:encoded:
Taipei’s dilemma over its history during World War II appeared to deepen as Beijing and Washington looked to the Flying Tigers as a source of connection and goodwill during last month’s Xi–Trump summit.

US President Donald Trump’s description of China as an American ally during the war has raised concerns in Taiwan that what could have been a valuable historical connection with the United States ended up benefiting Beijing’s ties with Washington.

The dilemma resurfaced after Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping repeatedly invoked wartime Sino-US cooperation during Xi’s visit to Washington last week.

Trump described China and the US as World War II allies and praised the Flying Tigers – a unit of American military personnel who helped defend mainland China against Japanese air attacks – while Xi recalled the two countries fighting “side by side” against Japanese militarism.

A White House fact sheet later said the two leaders recalled that the US and China “were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war”.

The episode has put Taiwan’s independence-leaning ruling Democratic Progressive Party in an awkward position.

Some argue that the island’s long-running efforts to emphasise a distinct Taiwanese identity over the pre-1949 history of the Republic of China (ROC) – Taiwan’s official name – have inadvertently created space for Beijing to claim that legacy.

When China fought Japan alongside the Allies, it was represented by the ROC government, which was overthrown in 1949 on the mainland when Communist forces won the civil war and established the People’s Republic of China (PRC).

Taipei objected to the wartime reference during the Xi-Trump summit, with Deputy Foreign Minister Wu Chih-chung accusing Beijing of trying to replace the ROC’s wartime role and describing the effort as part of Beijing’s “narrative diplomacy”.

The dispute has in fact exposed a dilemma for the DPP, which is now invoking the ROC’s wartime legacy internationally after years of seeking to distinguish Taiwan’s history and identity from that of mainland China.

Taiwan’s main opposition party, the Kuomintang, which ruled the ROC during the war, accused the William Lai Ching-te administration of invoking the pre-1949 republic only when politically useful.

The KMT government retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, and the island retains ROC as its formal name.

KMT communications director Chen I-hsin said Lai had emphasised the “end of the second world war” – a term Japan uses for its defeat – during last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations rather than “victory in the war of resistance against Japan”.

Chen accused the DPP of deliberately distancing itself from the ROC’s mainland-era history.

However, Chuang Jui-hsiung, the DPP’s legislative caucus chief executive, said the “China” that fought alongside the US was indeed the ROC and that “diplomatic language between major powers is often deliberately vague and should not be overinterpreted”.

The controversy has nevertheless highlighted a broader contest between Taipei and Beijing over who inherits the international historical identity of wartime China.

According to Wang Hsin-hsien, director of the National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations in Taipei, while Beijing has long maintained this wartime narrative, what sets this instance apart is that the American account also referred simply to “China” in the context of World War II.

“Trump wants something in the short term, while Xi wants a long-term discourse and narrative,” Wang said.

Washington appeared interested in invoking wartime cooperation to help stabilise Sino-US relations, he added, and Beijing was pursuing a broader historical argument involving the second world war, Taiwan and the post-war international order.

Together with Beijing’s commemorations of what it has called Taiwan’s “restoration” to China following Japan’s surrender in 1945, such arguments were gradually forming a “legal chain”, Wang continued.

If Washington increasingly accepted the same historical framework, the ROC’s role could be “taken away wholesale”, he said.

Yen Chen-sheng, a researcher at the same institute, added that the DPP’s distancing Taiwan from ROC history risked abandoning a valuable historical connection with the US.

That relationship stretched from wartime cooperation and the ROC’s status as a founding member of the United Nations to close political and security ties between Taipei and Washington after the Chinese civil war, Yen said.

The ROC was a founding member of the UN before the global body voted in 1971 to recognise the PRC as the only lawful representative of China at the United Nations.

The debate has also spread online, where critics have accused the DPP of protesting against Beijing’s “erasure” of the ROC while playing down the same name itself.

“On the one hand, they’re quietly pushing Taiwan independence and de-Sinicisation,” one critic said. “On the other, they pretend to be deeply upset and aggrieved. It’s really ugly.”

Beijing has rejected Taipei’s objections. Its Taiwan Affairs Office said victory in the war belonged to the entire Chinese nation while acknowledging that Communist and Nationalist or KMT forces fought on different battlefronts.

It also said the establishment of the PRC in 1949 represented a change of government rather than a change in China’s international legal identity, underpinning Beijing’s status as the inheritor of the historical role of the wartime Chinese state.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The historical dispute could become more consequential if Washington increasingly adopted the same terminology, analysts said.

Wang said repeated American references simply to “China” – without distinguishing the wartime ROC from today’s PRC – could gradually strengthen Beijing’s ability to define that history internationally.

“At least on the issue of the second world war, we really need to be careful.”

item.title: [SCMP] PAS wants urban Malaysia’s vote. Can it win over urban Malays?
item.description:
A string of electoral victories in recent years has inspired the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) to go for more urbanised and developed states in the run-up to Malaysia’s next general election. PAS’ strategy is straightforward: besides leveraging its religious credentials, it also seeks to underscore its ability to govern well. The problem here, however, is that PAS might not have a solid technocratic record to sell to voters.

PAS was established by the ulama (religious scholars) wing of the United Malays National Organisation. As part of an Islamic resurgent wave starting in the 1980s, the ulama leadership began to shape PAS into a movement that represented the “authentic Islam”, as opposed to the more “Westernised” and “secular” Umno.

PAS became synonymous with the image of a party that exclusively focuses on matters of faith and whose solutions to real-world problems can only be found in religious texts. Consequently, the general public perceives PAS’ ulama leadership to be ill-equipped to deal with the complex challenges of modern life.
item.content:encoded:
A string of electoral victories in recent years has inspired the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) to go for more urbanised and developed states in the run-up to Malaysia’s next general election. PAS’ strategy is straightforward: besides leveraging its religious credentials, it also seeks to underscore its ability to govern well. The problem here, however, is that PAS might not have a solid technocratic record to sell to voters.

PAS was established by the ulama (religious scholars) wing of the United Malays National Organisation. As part of an Islamic resurgent wave starting in the 1980s, the ulama leadership began to shape PAS into a movement that represented the “authentic Islam”, as opposed to the more “Westernised” and “secular” Umno.

PAS became synonymous with the image of a party that exclusively focuses on matters of faith and whose solutions to real-world problems can only be found in religious texts. Consequently, the general public perceives PAS’ ulama leadership to be ill-equipped to deal with the complex challenges of modern life.

Currently, PAS controls the state governments of Kedah, Kelantan, Perlis and Terengganu. In the 2022 general election and various state polls the following year, PAS made inroads into states previously controlled by Umno, such as Perak, Pahang and Selangor. These states, however, are more urbanised, economically developed and demographically diverse, and campaigning on a platform of Islamic credibility to govern was not enough to attract Malay voters there. They may be religiously conservative but will not blindly vote based on faith alone.

The results of the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state elections this year show that the more urbanised west coast and southern states pose a challenge for PAS. The only way for PAS to expand its presence is by allying with Malay nationalist parties such as Umno and the newly formed Wawasan.

A nationwide poll in April by the Merdeka Centre showed that 81 per cent of Muslim Malays listed economic concerns as the country’s main challenge. About 53 per cent of Malays feel the country is going in the wrong direction. Most of those making less than 4,000 ringgit per month (US$980), many of whom are Malays, feel the same. PAS is targeting these voters, and it is clear that their top priority is the economy. PAS’ aim is to show them it has a sound and feasible economic agenda and, more importantly, the technocratic chops to carry it out.

At its annual congress, or muktamar, last month, PAS sought to convince the Malaysian public of its ability to govern. The party put forth reformist-like motions, such as the creation of a Royal Commission of Inquiry on the so-called corporate mafia; increasing protection of healthcare workers and ramping up rice production to augment food security. Whether PAS can convince voters of this reformist, welfare-focused vision remains a challenge in the months leading up to the general election.

PAS has some ground to cover from its posturing of the past decade. After purging the “professional” faction in 2015, PAS has since adopted a more ethno-religious stance. It has fused Islamism and Malay nationalism and coalesced around its hardline president, Abdul Hadi Awang. The image turns off many Malays who are pious but do not buy into PAS’ divisive rhetoric. Hence the appeal of technocrats in PAS who are seen as the party’s moderate face.

Since 2018, PAS has been showcasing technocratic leaders such as Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar, the chief minister of Terengganu, and Syahir Sulaiman, MP of Bachok in Kelantan. Ahmad Samsuri holds a PhD in aerospace engineering from the University of Leeds and is a protege of Abdul Hadi. Syahir has a private sector background, having worked with the Sime Darby Group before becoming a full-time politician in 2018.

PAS regularly uses the Samsuri administration in Terengganu as an example of the party’s governing achievements. But PAS might be overstating its case. As an oil-producing state, Terengganu is highly dependent on oil royalties from the federal government, which make up about 80 to 90 per cent of its budget. Such royalties played a big role in the Samsuri administration’s ability to fulfil its populist agenda in its first term from 2018 to 2023. This was primarily due to the unimpeded flow of revenue from the then Perikatan Nasional federal government, of which PAS was part.

The dynamic changed after 2022 when the current Madani federal government took over. These royalty payments are now subjected to onerous conditions set by Putrajaya. This affects the Samsuri administration’s visibility significantly, as the federal government can now claim credit for the payments. The federal government has also opted to develop the state directly by funding myriad projects such as a new hospital in Dungun and a 60 million ringgit (US$14.7 million) poverty eradication programme.

But are the technocrats in PAS actually more religiously moderate compared with the hardline ulamas in the party? Given that PAS seeks to propel an ideologically driven movement, party members must go through a regimented indoctrination process, such as regularly attending usrah (guided study sessions). In short, a PAS technocrat can be as dogmatic as a religious scholar; the only difference is that one wears a suit and a tie while the other wears a robe and a turban. Authority over matters of faith and ideological underpinnings still resides with the ulama council. Economic policies formulated by the party’s technocrats have to get a religious imprimatur from the ulamas.

As Malaysia heads into the 16th general election, PAS needs to make a case for its governing ability to hesitant Malay voters in urban and semi-urban areas. This is especially so when development in PAS strongholds still lags behind Pakatan Harapan-governed areas like Selangor and Penang.

Working with Umno would help PAS leverage the former’s vast experience and proven track record in government. In the 2022 general election and various 2023 state polls, PAS combined forces with Bersatu, allowing it to penetrate Malay-majority areas outside its strongholds. As a result, PAS increased its parliamentary seats from 18 to 43 and made inroads in Perak, Selangor and Pahang.

There is a similar dynamic now with Umno, but a key difference is that Umno is stronger than Bersatu and would not want to play second fiddle to PAS in this partnership. The tussle for dominance will be a key dynamic as the general election looms closer. If PAS decides not to ally itself with Umno, it would face a tough challenge in persuading the sceptical Malay electorate to put their trust in its mixed technocratic record.

Dr Azmil Tayeb is a Visiting Senior Fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is an Associate Professor at the School of Social Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia. This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea struggles to curb sexual exploitation sites 10 years after Soranet scandal
item.description:
A decade after the shutdown of Soranet – a sprawling online hub for secretly filmed and non-consensual sexual videos that became a symbol of South Korea’s digital sex-crime crisis – the country is still struggling to stamp out similar networks and copycat sites that have emerged in its wake.

Their prevalence reflects the difficulties of deterring such illegal activities, policing the online space and changing societal attitudes towards women.

Last month, a man was detained over an alleged Soranet offshoot that investigators said shared more than 2,000 sexually explicit videos, illegally filmed material and deepfakes.
item.content:encoded:
A decade after the shutdown of Soranet – a sprawling online hub for secretly filmed and non-consensual sexual videos that became a symbol of South Korea’s digital sex-crime crisis – the country is still struggling to stamp out similar networks and copycat sites that have emerged in its wake.

Their prevalence reflects the difficulties of deterring such illegal activities, policing the online space and changing societal attitudes towards women.

Last month, a man was detained over an alleged Soranet offshoot that investigators said shared more than 2,000 sexually explicit videos, illegally filmed material and deepfakes.

The site also allegedly recruited participants for partner-swapping sessions that were later filmed and uploaded, while members shared photographs of family members and acquaintances so users could rate their bodies.

The case highlights the challenge South Korea faces in tackling the darker side of the online space despite tougher laws and more aggressive police investigations.

Soranet was home to thousands of illegal pornographic videos viewed and shared by more than a million users in South Korea. The site featured videos secretly filmed in toilets and changing rooms, as well as intimate footage posted by former partners without the consent of the women recorded. Some victims who appeared in the videos later took their own lives.

A public outcry, including large street protests organised by women’s groups, put pressure on the government. Authorities later arrested Soranet’s operators and shut down the site in 2016.

But the closure did not prevent similar sites from emerging, particularly small networks that have eluded the scrutiny of authorities.

Tougher laws

In May, police shut down a Soranet-inspired site known as the “Honours Club” after discovering that about 6,300 members had shared and watched photographs and videos of group sex and orgies facilitated through the platform.

Another infamous site, Yadong Korea, resurfaced last month under the same name after it was shut down in August, prompting the country’s feminist political group, the Women’s Party, to urge the police to reopen investigations into illegal pornography networks.

A police officer in Seoul was recently detained on suspicion of creating and distributing hundreds of AI-generated sexually explicit deepfakes and possessing about 5,600 illegal sexual images and videos.

The officer was caught following an undercover investigation by the Busan Metropolitan Police Agency into a Telegram chat room where such images were circulated. He was also suspected of possessing child sexual exploitation material and creating more than 400 AI-generated images and videos depicting acquaintances as nude.

During the molka, or spycam, crisis of the 2010s, the government strengthened laws against non-consensual distribution of intimate images, regardless of who originally recorded them.

In 2020, the Nth Room case further exposed how online platforms could be used to produce, sell and blackmail victims with sexually exploitative material. It led to the so-called “Anti-Nth Room Act”, which expanded criminal liability beyond creators and distributors to buyers and viewers.

Purchasing, downloading or knowingly viewing illegally filmed sexual exploitation material carries a sentence of up to three years in prison or a fine of 30 million won (US$22,440).

South Korea subsequently overhauled its laws on deepfakes following public outrage over Telegram-based sex crime rings that distributed doctored images of women and girls.

Creating sexually explicit deepfakes carries up to seven years in prison or a fine of 50 million won, while possessing, purchasing, storing or knowingly viewing such material can also result in criminal penalties.

An Gab-chul, a lawyer at Gammyung Law Firm who specialises in sexual crimes, said the law was now clearer on such offences.

“There are cases where the footage was originally recorded with the person’s consent. But if that material is later distributed without the person’s consent, that in itself constitutes a violation of the law,” An said.

But tougher laws have not eliminated the need for improved investigative tactics as perpetrators are often caught only following reports by victims, according to An.

Undercover investigations, once uncommon in South Korea, were authorised in 2021 for crimes involving minors and expanded last year to cover digital sexual offences involving adult victims.

A representative of the National Police Agency told This Week in Asia that a team of 20 investigators across four regional police agencies was established this month to investigate illegal websites promoting sexual exploitation.

“The more actively we investigate these cases, the more criminals try to evade detection, whether by using overseas servers or adopting other methods to prevent their activities from being traced,” the representative said.

“These cases are becoming increasingly difficult to investigate, but we are also working hard to keep pace with those changes.”

Eluding police crackdown

However, An is not optimistic that the underground networks will disappear any time soon.

“What I found through my research is that whenever one of these sites is shut down, another one keeps appearing,” he said. “They disappear, and then they are created again.”

“There are people who demand these services, and there are people who see an opportunity to make money from them. As long as that structure remains in place, these sites will continue to be created.”

An said the problem extended beyond dedicated pornography sites, with online communities and open chat rooms becoming gateways to sexual exploitation and prostitution.

“Some of our most popular chat services seem to have essentially turned into platforms for prostitution,” he said.

Joohee Kim, an assistant professor of women’s studies at Duksung Women’s University in Seoul, said online sexual exploitation cases in South Korea had exposed the limitations of its legal understanding of sexual violence.

“The legal understanding of sexual violence has historically focused more on whether an act was forced through violence or threats than on whether the woman consented.”

Kim cited choehyeobui-seol, the legal interpretation under which rape or indecent assault was established only when a perpetrator’s violence or threats were serious enough to make it impossible or extremely difficult for the victim to resist.

The interpretation dominated South Korea’s criminal justice practice and legal scholarship for decades, and its influence remains despite a 2023 Supreme Court ruling that lowered the threshold for establishing indecent assault.

“Online sexual exploitation can be understood as a problem in which this disregard for consent is repeatedly amplified through digital technology,” Kim said.

Kim Yeo-jin, director of the Korea Cyber Sexual Violence Response Centre, linked the problem to the country’s online culture, particularly how technology had been used to sexualise women.

Male-dominated online forums, such as DCinside and FMkorea, have helped spread misogynistic language and a culture of sexualising women through lewd images and videos shared in open chats, according to Kim Yeo-jin.

“The biggest underlying problem is that attitudes towards sexually objectifying women without their consent have not fundamentally changed,” Kim said

“Ordinary members of the public need to change how they perceive and treat victims of sexual exploitation. Only then can we truly understand the magnitude of these crimes and have deeper discussions on how we can change for the better.”

item.title: [SCMP] How expanded Japan-US military exercises could complicate PLA planning over Taiwan
item.description:
Japan and the United States will rehearse moving anti-ship missiles, air defences and communications networks onto islands near Taiwan this month in an expanded military exercise that analysts say could complicate Beijing’s planning for a Taiwan or East China Sea conflict.

Keen Sword 27, which runs from October 19 to 29, will involve about 45,000 Japanese personnel, 6,100 vehicles, 40 ships and 260 aircraft, up from about 33,000 personnel, 30 ships and 250 aircraft in 2024.

About 12,000 US troops are reportedly expected to take part. France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines, which were observers in 2024, are listed as participants this year alongside Australia and Canada.
item.content:encoded:
Japan and the United States will rehearse moving anti-ship missiles, air defences and communications networks onto islands near Taiwan this month in an expanded military exercise that analysts say could complicate Beijing’s planning for a Taiwan or East China Sea conflict.

Keen Sword 27, which runs from October 19 to 29, will involve about 45,000 Japanese personnel, 6,100 vehicles, 40 ships and 260 aircraft, up from about 33,000 personnel, 30 ships and 250 aircraft in 2024.

About 12,000 US troops are reportedly expected to take part. France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines, which were observers in 2024, are listed as participants this year alongside Australia and Canada.

Christopher Hughes, a professor of international politics and Japanese studies at the University of Warwick, said Japan and the US were “building out their ‘wall’ strategy in the East China Sea”.

He said that meant reinforcing and “fortifying” Japan’s southwest islands and rapidly moving forces and anti-ship weapons there to hinder the movement of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) through nearby straits during a Taiwan contingency.

“The operational problem Keen Sword is built around is clearly the one the PLA poses,” said Masashi Murano, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute.

He said that meant “holding the southwest islands, defending them against missile and air attack” and keeping Chinese surface ships at risk along the first island chain.

Japan does not present Keen Sword as preparation for war with China; its Joint Staff says the exercise trains responses to “various contingencies”. Tokyo’s latest defence white paper, however, describes China’s military activities as its “greatest strategic challenge”.

The exercise’s clearest link to a potential Taiwan contingency is the activity planned for Yonaguni Island, just over 100km (62 miles) from Taiwan.

Japan will temporarily deploy Type 88 surface-to-ship missiles and Type 03 medium-range air-defence systems, while the US Marine Corps will bring its Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (Nmesis) anti-ship missile platform and its Marine Air Defence Integrated System (Madis).

They will move equipment through Yonaguni Airport and Kubura fishing port. Communications training will connect Yonaguni with Ishigaki and Miyako islands.

Murano described the Type 88 deployment alongside Nmesis as “something like a test of a Japanese version of EABO”, referring to the US Marine Corps’ concept of Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations – operating mobile forces from dispersed temporary bases in contested maritime areas.

In a conflict, Murano said, Nmesis deployed on Yonaguni could cover waters between the Japanese island and Taiwan, as well as areas to Taiwan’s north and east, including approaches the PLA Navy could use to operate east of Taiwan or enforce a blockade.

Even then, the Taiwan Strait itself would remain “largely out of range”, with Nmesis at most able to reach its northern entrance, he added.

Murano noted that to engage ships beyond the horizon, Nmesis would rely on targeting data from other sensors and platforms.

Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, said the significance of the Yonaguni deployment lay less in exactly which waters the missiles could cover than in showing that US anti-ship capabilities could be “rapidly deployed to an island close to Taiwan”.

Tokyo has said it has no current plan to permanently station anti-ship missiles on Yonaguni. Matsuoka said that made the temporary deployment significant as a test of whether such systems could be moved there quickly during a crisis.

She described the drills as both an “operational rehearsal” and a “political signal”, stressing the “important distinction” between testing an option and committing to it.

Repeated rehearsals, however, could “lower the practical and political barriers” to deploying the systems in a future crisis, she added.

Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo, was more sceptical of the deployments’ military weight.

Given China’s growing missile and naval capabilities, he said, such Japanese and US military assets were “likely irrelevant in halting a Chinese military operation”, but could still affect Beijing’s calculations by raising the risk of drawing Japanese and US troops into any such operation.

The wider international participation in Keen Sword could further complicate Beijing’s calculations.

Hughes said the Philippines’ involvement was particularly significant, as it suggested Japan and the US were extending their “wall strategy” farther south along the first island chain.

Maslow said the wider participation was evidence of an Indo-Pacific security architecture that had “moved beyond symbolism”.

Matsuoka noted that repeated participation in exercises such as Keen Sword could build familiarity among the forces involved without obliging their governments to intervene over Taiwan. For Beijing, she added, it could reinforce perceptions that “a wider group of states is becoming integrated” into a US-Japan-centred regional security network.

Beyond the widening foreign participation, Keen Sword 27 will also be the first iteration of the exercise since Japan established its permanent Joint Operations Command in March last year.

The programme has expanded from 10 training areas in 2024 to 15 this year, including separate cyber, information, space, electromagnetic and distributed-operations components.

Murano said closer coordination between the new command and US forces was likely to concern the PLA because it could allow Japanese and US anti-ship and air-defence capabilities to be employed together “from early in a crisis”.

A distributed posture also meant the PLA “cannot simply concentrate on Taiwan”, he said, but would have to “find, track and suppress many small, mobile targets”, diverting surveillance assets and munitions while stretching its timeline.

However, the measures designed to complicate PLA planning could also deepen strategic mistrust.

Matsuoka warned they could be interpreted in Beijing as preparations for conflict, feeding a cycle of mainland Chinese countermeasures and Japanese and US responses.

Maslow argued that this cycle could also make repeated military deployments to Japan’s southwest islands increasingly routine, embedding them further in Tokyo’s regional contingency planning.

With any further deployments in the area, he said, “security tensions with China are bound to intensify”.

Hughes said that despite concerns in Tokyo over Washington’s security commitments under US President Donald Trump, the military side of the alliance told a different story.

“The substance of US-Japan alliance planning and interoperability is only further tightening and integrating,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] In Indonesia, will VP Gibran’s ‘diploma-gate’ haunt his future after court ruling?
item.description:
A legal challenge to the vice-presidency of Indonesia’s Gibran Rakabuming Raka could haunt his political future even though he has survived damning court findings on his educational qualifications.

The Constitutional Court on Tuesday dismissed a petition to unseat the son of former president Joko Widodo, ruling that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing. But it also found no convincing evidence that Gibran’s overseas education met the minimum high-school qualification required for presidential candidates.

Legal experts say the ruling has shifted the battleground to parliament and law enforcement agencies, potentially opening a Pandora’s box for Gibran.
item.content:encoded:
A legal challenge to the vice-presidency of Indonesia’s Gibran Rakabuming Raka could haunt his political future even though he has survived damning court findings on his educational qualifications.

The Constitutional Court on Tuesday dismissed a petition to unseat the son of former president Joko Widodo, ruling that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing. But it also found no convincing evidence that Gibran’s overseas education met the minimum high-school qualification required for presidential candidates.

Legal experts say the ruling has shifted the battleground to parliament and law enforcement agencies, potentially opening a Pandora’s box for Gibran.

Political observers, however, doubt President Prabowo Subianto would risk a confrontation that could destabilise his government. Gibran, who ran on the 2024 ticket alongside Prabowo – capturing 58.59 per cent of the vote – is likely to retain his office for now, but analysts say he will be dogged by questions over his future political career.

Delivering the judgment on Tuesday, Chief Justice Suhartoyo argued that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing to dispute the presidential election result because they were not contestants in the race.

“Consequently, the court rules that their petition be declared inadmissible,” he said.

Although the court unequivocally stated it was in no position to disqualify the vice-president, it noted there was “no convincing evidence” to confirm that Gibran had completed an education equivalent to Indonesian senior high school.

In a news conference after the ruling, lawyer Refly Harun, one of the plaintiffs, quipped to reporters that it was unprecedented in Constitutional Court history for a ruling to bring celebration to both sides of a trial.

“The defendant is happy because he still gets to keep his vice-presidency, for now. But we are also happy because we’ve satisfactorily proved that he doesn’t have a high school diploma,” Refly said, adding that the ruling should shame Gibran into resigning.

Known locally as “Gibran’s diploma-gate”, the saga erupted on September 10 when 12 plaintiffs, led by constitutional law expert and former deputy minister of law and human rights Denny Indrayana, filed a petition with the court.

In their complaint, they accused Gibran of manipulating his secondary school degree equivalency certification. Under Indonesian election law passed in 2003, presidential and vice-presidential candidates must have completed senior high school or its equivalent.

According to his educational record, Gibran attended Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore, where he completed his O-Levels, before taking a pathway programme at UTS Insearch in Sydney, Australia. He subsequently attained his bachelor’s degree in marketing from the UK’s University of Bradford via the Management Development Institute of Singapore in 2010.

The petitioners asked the court to nullify his vice-presidency on grounds of fraud.

Herlambang P. Wiratraman, an associate professor and director of the Research Centre for Law and Social Justice at Gadjah Mada University in Indonesia, told This Week in Asia that the Constitutional Court had delivered a sound ruling that had gone as far as its legal remit allowed.

“I see it as a vigorous nudge at getting the other state institutions to act on the verdict and do their jobs under the constitution,” Herlambang said.

State administrative law scholar Bivitri Susanti, who testified as an expert witness for the plaintiffs during the court’s two-week proceedings, agreed that the ruling opened up other legal avenues for Gibran’s removal.

“The House of Representatives can now legally start a process of impeachment against the vice-president,” she said, adding that law enforcement agencies should also initiate an investigation into Gibran for alleged forgery to strengthen the impeachment case.

“So the ball is in the politicians’ court now.”

On Wednesday, a group calling itself Advocators For Upholding National Ethics, Morals and Integrity filed a police report against Gibran for falsifying his educational record.

“But I suspect the police will stop short of conducting an actual investigation,” said Made Supriatma, a political analyst and visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

Made said Prabowo would want to prevent the issue from escalating into a full-blown political crisis. “The ramifications for an impeachment process would be too volatile and unpredictable for his administration.”

Prabowo has so far steered clear of the controversy, offering no public comment.

However, Syahganda Nainggolan, recently appointed head of the Government Communications Agency, said in a podcast on Monday that the president had “long been aware of Gibran’s fake diploma, but saw it as a non-priority for the government to tackle”.

Saidiman Ahmad, a researcher and programme manager at Jakarta-based pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting, pointed to another aspect of the debate he believed was being overlooked.

“As a guardian of democracy, the court should’ve borne in mind that limiting elected office to people of certain educational backgrounds is elitist, if not non-inclusive,” Saidiman said. He questioned using formal qualifications as a benchmark for public officials, pointing out that most Western democracies did not impose educational prerequisites on elected political leaders.

He also questioned the plaintiffs’ motives in targeting Gibran’s overseas education as a legal loophole. “It’s obvious they had a target on his back with this manoeuvre, with the end game being his political demise – either through removal from office or by barring him from future elections on technicalities.”

But Made said that what Gibran did with his education documents was essentially illegal. “He sought to circumvent existing regulations through falsification, and that is always wrong.”

Analysts are divided on whether the court’s findings automatically bar Gibran from running again for vice-president or president in the future.

“This constitutional blight on his persona should strongly dissuade political parties from nominating him as a candidate,” Bivitri said.

In contrast, Saidiman saw the ruling as no impediment to Gibran’s future candidacy, provided a proper degree equivalency certificate could be obtained from the Ministry of Education.

Gibran has publicly denied not having completed his secondary education.

“If I hadn’t graduated from high school, I wouldn’t have been able to enrol at a university. Please bear in mind I finished my tertiary education in Singapore,” he told reporters on Wednesday.

Made said that Gibran might retain his current post but would likely not emerge unscathed.

“His political legitimacy will greatly suffer as a result,” Made said. “And this will come back to haunt him again and again.”

item.title: [SCMP] Data centre opposition is growing in Australia. Is there a middle ground?
item.description:
Australia may have vast tracts of land and political will to support the growth of the artificial intelligence industry, but the development of data centres to power the technology is proving more challenging.

Last month, property developer Goodman Group withdrew its application for a 90-megawatt data centre in Lane Cove, on Sydney’s lower north shore, after months of opposition from residents about the potential impact on their electricity and water supplies, noise pollution and other concerns.

In a press statement, Goodman said it had considered changes in the policy and regulatory environment, as well as feedback from residents.
item.content:encoded:
Australia may have vast tracts of land and political will to support the growth of the artificial intelligence industry, but the development of data centres to power the technology is proving more challenging.

Last month, property developer Goodman Group withdrew its application for a 90-megawatt data centre in Lane Cove, on Sydney’s lower north shore, after months of opposition from residents about the potential impact on their electricity and water supplies, noise pollution and other concerns.

In a press statement, Goodman said it had considered changes in the policy and regulatory environment, as well as feedback from residents.

It is not the first time that a developer has pulled the plug on a proposed data centre in Australia this year.

In May, GreenSquareDC shelved its plan for a 120MW data centre in Hazelmere, in Perth’s eastern suburbs. A much smaller proposed data centre in Katoomba, in New South Wales’ Blue Mountains, was also withdrawn by MAK Urban Group in June.

Although the projects were in two different states, residents had raised similar concerns – that the large resource-hungry facilities would be located too close to their homes and schools, and could cause environmental damage.

Rob Nicholls, a senior research associate at the University of Sydney, who recently gave evidence to a New South Wales legislative inquiry on the development of data centres, said these facilities had run ahead of current land-use categories.

Developers typically looked for sites with convenient access to high-capacity electricity networks, fibre-optic connections, water and sewerage, Nicholls said, adding that these requirements favoured established industrial estates.

Yet he said such sites had often been designated for warehouses and lighter industrial uses, located near residential neighbourhoods, schools and waterways.

Existing telecommunications infrastructure could fit into the plans of data centre developers if they were scaled down, Nicholls added.

“I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see lots of Telstra telephone exchange buildings hosting small inference-level data centres.”

Residents push back

Sasha Titchkosky, from the Lane Cove Responsible Planning group, explained to This Week In Asia why residents were up in arms over the data centre plan, saying it would be built just 20 metres (66 feet) away from the nearest house, close to a nursery and conservation bushland.

Residents were concerned about the constant noise and fire hazards created by diesel backup generators, air pollution and water use, Titchkosky said.

While the community was not totally opposed to having a data centre, the scale of the Goodman plan meant it was not suitable for Lane Cove, she added.

“We would say that data centres fit into the heavy-industry kind of classification because of their impact.”

In Hazelmere, community members and Trillion Trees Australia objected to GreenSquareDC’s planned facility, which would have been located near a school, residential areas and Helena River, a major environmental and cultural landmark.

Kate Herren of Trillion Trees Australia said the conservation charity was not wholly against the development of data centres.

“We understand the need for it, but there needs to be very careful consideration of the impact of these developments on the environment and the local community,” she said.

Herren said planning staff from the City of Swan, the local government area in Perth, had recommended rejecting the GreenSquareDC plan, as operating diesel backup generators overnight could exceed the residential noise limit. The developer withdrew the proposal before local authorities could assess the data centre’s feasibility.

Titchkosky and Herren said the communities they served were part of the Australian Community Alliance for Responsible Data Centres, an informal network sharing information and strategies on proposals for such facilities.
